as nullable when its object is freed; a call that never returns (the trap path's `throwJs`), or a block or `if` that always
jumps, ends its statement list, as tsc doesn't narrow in what follows; and the arguments before one that needs a statement
of its own first are evaluated into locals, in order, where the expansion refused the call. Forced only (`AUTO_RC_EXC`)
until R23. *R23: a thrown object built out of line, and fields nothing stores to.* `throw new C(a, b)`, whose lowering is
`{ let t = alloc; t.cid = k; C.ctor(t, a, b); t }` with a constructor that can't throw and each argument a variable, a literal
or a string literal's address, prints as a call of a builder function, `tmkMadeC(a, b)`, tagged `@tsl.noinline`, which makes
the object as the throw made it and returns it; throws of one shape (the constructor, the class id, the size, each literal, and
each variable's type, and a reference's class) share one. tslc's expansion builds a `new` in a frame slot of its function's
entry and moves it into its counted slot (`Rc.make`), so a function that throws, recursive or not, kept that slot, and its
address in a callee-saved register, on every call that didn't throw: `down` in bench/exc/exc_cost.ts was 28.5 instructions a
frame to the direct route's 23.1. The builder has the slot instead; the same object is made by the same steps in the same
order, only in a function of its own, and its arguments are borrowed there as they were in place. And an `unknown`'s reference
field that nothing printed ever stores to (`SuppressedError`'s `error` and `suppressed` in a program that never makes one) is
always null, so it prints as a getter giving null, and its 8 bytes stay as a field that holds no reference
(`error_none: u64 = 0n`): the release function visits only the slots that can hold something, and the object stays the size it
was, in its size class. R22 found that a smaller `Dyn` moved to the 64-byte class, and corpus/lower/exc/exc_exhaust.ts's
`throwAndDrop(20000)` then ran out of pages, as with the collector a size class's chunks stay that class's; with the 8 bytes
kept it completes, and leaving them out (`r23-none-pad`) runs it out again. `auto` takes exceptions in `rc` since R23
(`AUTO_RC_EXC`, M5's R23 record), where it prints the program exactly with strings off, as `AUTO_RC_STRINGS` is.

A small program, as written and as expanded (abridged from `corpus/rc/rc_list.ts`; `tmk compile --emit tsl` lays it out with oxfmt):

```text
class Node {                                  class Node {
  next: Node | null = null;                     next: Counted<Node> | null = null;
  constructor(public v: u32) {}                 constructor(public v: u32) {}
}                                             }
                                              function Node$release(o: Node, at: usize, op: Visit): usize {
                                                const k: usize = 1;
                                                if (at === 0) {
                                                  const x = o.next;
                                                  if (x !== null) Node$rc.visit(x, op);
                                                }
                                                return k;
                                              }
                                              const Node$rc = new Rc<Node>(Node$release);
class List {                                  class List {
  head: Node | null = null;                     head: Counted<Node> | null = null;
  push(v: u32): void {                          push(v: u32): void {
    const n = new Node(v);                        const n: Counted<Node> = Node$rc.make(new Node(v));
    n.next = this.head;                           const $o1 = n.next;
                                                  n.next = this.head === null ? null : Node$rc.share(this.head);
                                                  if ($o1 !== null) Node$rc.drop($o1);
    this.head = n;                                this.head = Node$rc.replace(this.head, Node$rc.take(n));
  }                                             }
  sum(): u32 {                                  sum(): u32 {
    let s: u32 = 0;                               let s: u32 = 0;
    for (let p = this.head; p !== null;           for (let p = this.head; p !== null; p = p.next) {
         p = p.next) s += p.v;                      s += p.v;   // p is a borrow: nothing in sum can drop a count
    return s;                                     }
  }                                               return s;
}                                               }
                                              }
```

On V8 and JSC the expanded program runs with `@tsl/unsafe`'s simulation of memory, which poisons a freed object so any use of it traps
5: that's TSL `rc`'s poisoning build, on every host run. The program as written runs there too, and has to agree on every result that
doesn't read a count.

**`rc` (D39).** Ordinary TS, lowered natively, frees what it allocates, with no tracing collector and no collection pause. What it costs is below, and it's real: counts take time, every block has a 16-byte header, and cycles need the collector below (D41), which has its own costs.

- *What's counted.* Whatever isn't on the stack: class instances, object records, array headers with their buffers, typed arrays, closure environments, and the cells of mutated captures. An object the stack rules allow (no escape, not in a loop, 3.5's rules for down-lowering in 4.5) is never counted, unless it holds something counted: only a count can tell what an object holds that the object has died, so such an object is counted too. `rc` doesn't use the call arena for lowered allocations. That's a change from the order D38 set out, and why is in 4.5.
- *Threading (D40).* One heap per thread, and counts aren't atomic. A counted reference must not cross threads, and nothing lowered today can: lowered code has no threads. When threads arrive, D40's rule is what keeps this true.
- *A block* is `[link: u64][count: u32][meta: u32][object]`, so an object is 16-byte aligned and pays 16 bytes. `meta` is a class and a per-type descriptor, which says where its outgoing references are. A small block is a power of two from 32 to 2048 bytes, one class to a page. A larger one is a run of 2^k pages. An interior pointer, which a `subarray` is, finds its block through a four-level page map, built only if the module has a counted typed array, and that map is also how a static typed array is known not to be counted.
- *Order.* Every store counts the new value before releasing the old one, so `x.f = x.f` and swaps are safe by construction.
- *Deferred frees.* A decrement to zero links the object onto a queue through its own header, and does nothing else: no allocation, no recursion, and no visit to what it holds. `__rc_new` then does at most `RC_BUDGET` steps (32) of freeing before it allocates. A step is one reference slot visited or one block given back. `__rc_cur` and `__rc_idx` hold the object being scanned and how far along it is, so a million-element array is a million steps across many allocations, and a million-node list uses no stack, because each node's successor goes on the queue, not on the stack. Nothing frees between allocations, so a program that stops allocating stops freeing, and `__rc_collect` is there for a caller who wants it done.
- *Worst cases, honestly.* The bound is on freeing work per allocation in steps, not on an allocation's time:
  - An increment or decrement is constant time. On a typed array it's a walk of the page map, four loads.
  - A small allocation is the budget plus zeroing its block, which is at most 2 KiB. Growing from the page source adds the source's own cost, including its zeroing of a page, and the map's up to three new table pages. A large allocation zeroes its size, however it got its pages: that's proportional to what was asked for, and no allocator with zeroed memory avoids it. An array growing past its capacity also copies it.
  - If a program drops faster than 32 steps an allocation can free, the backlog grows, and memory stays in use for that long, with fresh pages taken meanwhile. On exhaustion, when the source has nothing, everything pending is freed in one go before trap 14 is considered. **That drain is the one place with a pause, and it's proportional to what's pending.** A step count is deterministic, and tests pin it. A time isn't: QEMU can't gate it, and a host can preempt a guest. So the latency figures in M5 are figures.
  - `a.length = 0`, `shift` and `splice` are one operation in JS and linear here: each visits or moves what it removes. `shift` on a long array isn't what V8's left-trim makes it.
  - A freed small block goes back to its class, and is never another class's. A freed run goes back to the list for its size, and is cut up only at exhaustion. Nothing coalesces, a page never returns to the source, and a run's size rounds up to a power of two. So trap 14 can come with free memory of the wrong shape, and that's the limit of this allocator, not of counting.
- *Borrowing.* An argument is borrowed: the caller holds a count for the whole call, and a callee takes one only to keep it. A result is owned: the caller gets one count. A value read from a slot stays alive until a slot on the path to it is overwritten, or a local at its root changes. So a local needs no count of its own, and a caller needn't hold an argument it read from memory, where a whole-program fact shows nothing in between can overwrite a counted slot. A call through a closure value is assumed to. `let g = new P(); function f(p) { g = null; return p.x; } f(g)` holds its count across the call, because `f` is exactly what that fact finds.
- **Cycles leak with the collector off.** A cycle's counts never reach zero. That's memory-safe, and it's a limit, not a detail: `class B { op = () => this.k }` is a cycle, and each instance leaks. `tmk lower --report` says which classes can form a cycle, from the type graph, and which allocation sites make them. Being able to form one isn't forming one: every linked list can. So `rc` has a cycle collector, below, and it's on by default. `WeakRef` remains a way to break a cycle.
- **The cycle collector (D41).** `--cycles on|off`, or `"cycles"` in `tsl.json`, on by default. It's trial deletion, as in Bacon and Rajan's synchronous algorithm, implemented from that paper's description, and changed in the one way that makes it safe to run in bounded steps with the program running in between: **it never changes a count.** A scan finds what its candidates reach and counts, on the side, the edges it finds to each object. What's reached only by edges found is garbage.
  - *What's a candidate.* A decrement that leaves a count above zero, on an object whose type the type graph puts in a cycle: a nontrivial strongly connected component of classes, over fields, elements, captures and what environments are really allocated with. A type that can't be in a cycle is decided at compile time: its sites and its descriptors are what they always were, and a test build checks at each such site that the object agrees. If no type in a module can be in a cycle, the collector isn't linked, and the module is the module `--cycles off` gives, byte for byte. A scan only follows a reference within one component, so a ring holding a long-lived object of another type doesn't drag that object's graph in. A mistake in the type graph can only make an edge look external, which leaks, and can't free anything.
  - *State.* Bits in `meta`, whose class needs only 6 of its 8 bits, and whose descriptor index drops to 18 bits (262,143 words, checked where descriptors are made). In a scan, `link` holds the edges found (20 bits) and the next object in the scan, shifted (44 bits), and a weak cell moves to the same field with the next in the cell's spare word. So **a block is what it was, 16 bytes of header, and a scan allocates nothing and can run with memory exhausted.** The candidates are a fixed table of 4096 pointers (32 KiB of `data`, linked only with the collector). A candidate's `link` holds its index, so one whose count reaches zero leaves the table in constant time, with no dangling entry. If the table is full, the entry to replace is chosen round-robin, and that object stops being a candidate until a later decrement. It isn't lost for good: see exhaustion, below.
  - *A scan.* Phase 0 starts it. Phase 5 takes everything in the table as roots. Phase 1 walks what they reach, each slot one step, counting an edge per reference found. Phase 2 marks what's held, in passes over the list of what was reached, reversing it each time: an object is held if its count isn't the edges found, or a count operation touched it, or something held refers to it. A pass in which nothing new is marked is the decision, and from that instant what isn't marked is garbage. Phase 3 clears its weak cells and releases what it holds of everything else. Phase 4 gives back its blocks. Everything held goes back to how it was as phase 3 reaches it. A scan is cut off at a size limit, 64 objects plus its roots at first and four times that at each try after a cut: what's cut off is treated as held, which is sound, and its roots go back in the table.
  - *The barrier: `__rc_touch`.* Every increment, every decrement, and every count-preserving move (an element moved by `shift` or `splice`) on a type that can be in a cycle tests one bit in `meta`, the object being in the current scan, and if it's set, marks the object held. Inline, that's a load and a branch. A decrement that leaves a count above zero on an object in a scan also marks it to be a candidate again once the scan is done.
  - **Why it can't free a live object.** Take an object `w` the scan decides is garbage, at the instant `T` of the decision. Nothing touched `w` from when it joined the scan to `T`, or it would be held. So its count hasn't changed since then, and each edge found to it still exists: taking an edge away is a decrement or a barriered move of `w`, which is a touch. `w` isn't held, so its count equals the edges found, so **every reference `w`'s count stands for is one of those edges**, from an object in the scan, and that object is garbage too, or marking would have reached `w` from it. So at `T` nothing outside the garbage holds a count on any of it: no slot, no local with a count, no global, no result in flight, no native caller, and no object with a count of zero that's waiting to be freed, as each of those would be a count not found as an edge. A local or argument that holds no count is a borrow (below), good only while a path from something with a count to it stays intact, and there's no such path at `T`. The mutator can't make one, as it has nothing to start from: the only other way in is a weak reference, and `__rc_weak_deref` asks whether its target has been decided on. Nothing here depends on when the steps ran relative to the mutator, only on the barrier. An edge that was added after its source was scanned, or a move of a count from a local into a slot, can only leave an object's count above the edges found, which holds it. In the middle of a `splice`, an array can briefly hold a stale copy of a moved element across the allocation for its growth: the array is held by whoever's in that `splice`, so whatever it refers to is held too.
  - *Giving up (R1e).* A decrement to zero on an object in a scan that hasn't decided (phases 5, 1 and 2) gives it up, as `@tsl/gc` does (3.5): its weak cell is cleared, and it goes on the queue and is freed like any other. It stays in the scan's list, since `link` now holds the queue's link: `meta` says *given up* by `SCANNED` without `BLACK`, a pair a scan never makes otherwise, and its next in the scan is in its count word, as an address over 16 in 32 bits (an object whose next is at or above 64 GiB isn't given up; `__rc_cc_set_next` traps if a later next is, which no image here can reach). Phase 1 passes over it, and phases 2 and 3 take it out of the list; freeing gives its block back unless it's still in the list, when `AGAIN` marks it done and the scan gives the block back. The scan decides nothing while `__rc_cc_pend`, what it gave up with references still to drop, isn't zero: a marking pass that marks nothing new waits, taking no step. The argument above holds with that wait for the reason 3.5's case (6) gives: an edge found from an object given up is dropped by freeing before the decision, a count operation on its target. corpus/lower/rc/rc_shared.ts traps 14 without giving up and completes with it; corpus/lower/rc/cyc_giveup.ts puts the drop at every phase, at every budget `interleave` runs; and a scan deciding before what it gave up is freed (`no-giveup-wait`) is caught.
  - *Why it finishes, and what's restarted.* **Nothing is restarted.** A change during a scan marks one object, and the scan carries on. A scan cut off by its limit goes again with a larger one, at most 13 times over. Marking takes at most one pass per object plus one, and a pass that marks nothing ends it. The last decrement to a garbage cycle comes after every other count operation on it, so it either finds the object in no scan, making it a candidate for a later scan, or marks it to be one when this scan ends. That later scan has nothing touching what it finds.
  - *The bound.* One step is one slot read, one object visited in a pass, or one block given back. Each allocation does at most `RC_BUDGET` steps (32) of freeing and collecting together, deterministically, and test builds pin that. There's no stack: it's all cursors. An allocation gives the collector a quarter of the budget plus one, frees one object, frees more if its free list is empty, and gives the collector what's left. After a scan that frees nothing the next waits, 16 allocations per object it visited, or 4 if it was cut off, and 16 times faster with fewer than 16 candidates waiting. So a program whose candidates are all live spends about half a step per allocation on them, and one whose scans find garbage runs them at the full budget. A scan that was cut off, or a program flooding the table with live candidates, delays how soon a cycle goes, not whether.
  - **The honest worst case.** How large a cycle can be: as large as memory. An object with more than 1,048,575 edges to it from one scan is treated as held, so it and what it reaches aren't collected. *Marking* is the one shape that isn't linear: what's held can reach its way through the scan's order in alternate directions, so each pass gets one hop further, and with `n` objects that's `n` passes and about `n²` steps, spread over allocations at no more than the budget each. `buildZigzag` in `corpus/lower/rc/cyc_large.ts` is that shape, and the tests measure it. Rings, doubly linked lists and trees take a handful of passes. *When* a cycle goes isn't bounded by anything but allocation: nothing runs between allocations, and a large cycle in a program flooding the table can take several times its size in allocations, or wait for exhaustion if its candidate was replaced.
  - **Exhaustion: the one permitted pause.** When the page source has nothing, the queue is drained, then the collector runs to completion, with no limits, over everything in the table. If candidates have been replaced since the last time, it then scans again with every live object whose type can be in a cycle as a root, found by walking the page map, which is on in any module with the collector: that's a full pass over the heap, the only one there is, and only here or in a caller's own `__rc_collect`. Only then does trap 14 come. The pause is proportional to what's pending and to what can be reached from it, or to the whole heap in that last case, and in the worst shape above, to its square. `__rc_collect` is the same thing, for a caller who wants it now. A freed block still only goes back to its own class, so trap 14 can still come with free memory of the wrong shape.
  - *What still leaks.* An object with over 1,048,575 edges in a scan, and a cycle through a type the type graph doesn't connect, if there's ever such a thing: both are leaks, and neither is unsafe. Cycles through an object held by a counted root are live, and aren't leaks.
  - *With the collector linked, freeing changes.* A module with the collector frees one object per allocation unless its free list is empty, rather than up to 16: M5's Phase E has why, and it isn't about cycles. `--cycles off` stays as it was.
- *`WeakRef`.* `new WeakRef(x)` is a counted object with a count on a cell that `x`'s header points to, and the cell holds no count on `x`. When `x`'s count hits zero the cell is cleared at that moment, in constant time, so `deref()` gives `undefined` from then on, including while `x` is queued and not yet freed. A target in a garbage cycle has a count above zero: `deref()` can give it until the collector decides, and that count makes it live, legitimately, as nothing has been decided. From the decision, `deref()` gives `undefined`, including while the cycle is partway through being freed and before its cell has been cleared. A target can't be resurrected. A target is a class, an object, an array or a closure: a typed array has no one reference to hold, so that's `TSLD0228`, as is `WeakRef` in any other mode. V8 may keep a target alive for longer (3.10, item 9). `FinalizationRegistry` stays a fallback (`TSLD0229`).
- *Test builds.* The collector's own: `budget` and no pacing, so a test puts user code between any two steps, a counter of everything it does, and faults that can be put into it (`CcFault` in `compiler/host/down-rt.ts`), each of which the tests have to catch. `check` also traps 16 on a count operation or a `deref` on an object that's been decided on, and on a site promising a type that can't be in a cycle getting one that can. `check` poisons a freed block and traps with code 16 on any access through a counted reference to a dead one, and on an increment or decrement of one. `account` keeps counters of live objects, live bytes, increments, decrements and steps. A release module has neither: no `__rc_chk`, no `__rc_s_` global, and no such trap.

**Strings, `Map` and `Set` in the memory modes (D42).** These are ordinary lowered code, from `compiler/rt`, so they follow the rules above: `rc` counts them, `leak` never frees them, and `manual` frees only a vector's old buffer as it grows.

- *A string* is one pointer to immutable UTF-16: `[len: u32][hash: u32][off: i64]`, with its units at `p + off`, so a read is one load and one add with no test. A *flat* string has its units inline (`off` 16). A *view*, `[owner: ptr @16][start: u32 @24]`, has them in its owner's memory. A *buffer* is never a value: `[tail: u32][cap: u32][off = 24][head: u32 @16]` is what views made by concatenation point into. Literals are flat strings in static data, with a block header whose count starts at 2^30, so counting them needs no test and they're never freed. A module with no run-time string has none of this: a string literal type in it is still a small integer.
- *Concatenation, with no ropes.* Up to 64 units it copies. The next concatenation onto a string that came from one makes a buffer with twice the room, and from then on an append to a view that ends at its buffer's tail writes in place: old views can't see past their own length, so sharing a tail is safe, and immutability is kept by construction. A prepend does the same at the head. So `s += x` is linear in all, with no flattening, and reading the string between appends costs nothing, where V8's ropes flatten. The worst cases are below.
- *Substrings* share only if they keep alive at most four times their own length: at least 32 units, and at least a quarter of the owner's capacity. Anything else copies. So a token from a huge text doesn't keep the text, and the bound on what a view keeps is 4 times its length, plus one 64-byte block for the view.
- *Under `rc`,* strings are never candidates: a view refers to its owner and an owner refers to nothing, so that edge is left out of the type graph (`chainOnly`), and a string's sites have no barrier. Dropping a huge array of strings is the array's slots at one step each, as any array is.
- *`Map<K, V>` and `Set<K>`* are `TmkMap<K, V>`, a class of vectors in `compiler/rt/map.ts`, with one instantiation per `K` and `V`, and `Set` is the class with `V = undefined` and no value slots. Keys and values are in insertion order in parallel vectors. `heads` and `chain` hold a chained hash table of positions, where a link to position `i` is `i + 2`, 1 ends a chain and a head of 0 is empty, so a new table's zeroed vectors are already empty; positions only fall along a chain, and `chain[i]` of 0 is a tombstone for a deleted entry, whose slots are released at once.
- *Growth is incremental (D47).* A full table isn't rebuilt in one operation. A new one (`TmkOld` holds the old) is made at its final size, every vector sized once with `__v_size`, so nothing after grows by copying: room for twice what's live, and for the move to finish before what's inserted fills it. Its first positions are kept for what's live. Each insert and delete after moves the next `STEP` (4) old positions in order, a live entry to the next kept position, linked under what's been inserted since so positions still fall, and a tombstone skipped; each old position then holds where it went, as `-(new) - 1`. While a move is on, a lookup, update or delete looks in the new table and then in the old one at or above the move's place, where a chain's first position below it ends the walk. So no operation does work proportional to the table: the most is one hash and a chain walk for each of 4 positions. Compaction is the move, as only live entries go. So a map's counted references are ordinary vector slots: it has descriptors, the collector traces it, a map holding an object that holds the map is a real cycle and is collected, and a value from `get` is owned by the caller, so a callee that deletes the entry can't free it under anyone. Nothing in `rc` knows a map exists.
- *Mutation during iteration.* A cursor is `[pos][cur][gen][done][inOld][curOld]`, and nothing registers it, so a dropped one costs nothing. Positions only change when a move starts or a table clears, which starts a new generation (`TmkGen`). A move's generation holds the old table's chain, where the move writes each old position's new one, so an old cursor walks the chain from its own generation and finds its place in one load per move, and can sleep through any number of them. While a move is on, iteration order is what's been moved, then what hasn't, still in the old table from the move's place, then what's been inserted since: a cursor that reaches the kept positions the move hasn't filled goes on in the old table, and comes back past them. Generations form a chain only ever pointing at something newer, which is the second `chainOnly` edge. A finished cursor stays finished, as JS has it, whatever's added later. A cursor created while no generation exists makes the first one, so a map that's never iterated pays nothing.
- *Keys* are SameValueZero, with `-0` stored as `+0`. A number, string, boolean, null, undefined or object key works, and also `T | null` and `T | undefined` of those. An object's address is hashed inside the table only: iteration is by insertion, so no result can depend on it, and a test moves the addresses and changes the key to show so. A typed array or a function as a key is a fallback: neither has one identity here. A key type mixing kinds, like `string | number`, is `union-mixed`, as it is everywhere.
- *Hash flooding.* Strings use HalfSipHash-1-3 with a 64-bit key, numbers and addresses a keyed MurmurHash3 finaliser, which is fast and isn't a proven defence against an attacker adaptively probing. The key is a default in static data until a caller sets it with `__hash_key_use`, as a guest has no entropy source of its own to ask, so **a program facing untrusted keys has to register a key, or it floods.**
- *Worst cases, honestly.* The map's own work in one operation is bounded (above). What isn't is the allocation that starts a move: four vectors at the new table's size, which the allocator has to hand over zeroed, and zeroing is proportional to them. In the test runtime that's the page source's `mem.fill` of fresh pages, and in `rc` a freed run that's reused. MEASURED (M5's Maps phase), the worst single `set` at 2^20 entries and one more: 19.2 ms before this, of which the rebuild was the larger part, 11.0 ms now, all of it that one allocation, and 23.5 µs with the page source's fill taken out to see it. A page source that hands out pages already zero, as a kernel can with pages it zeroes ahead or on first touch, takes it away; chunked tables would take it away here, at a load on every access, and aren't built. The old table lives until the move finishes, so a map can briefly hold both. `clear` replaces the vectors, so it's constant and the freeing is within the bound. `delete` is the chain's length. A buffer's growth copies the string, doubling, so it's amortised. A `concat` that doesn't extend a tail is a copy of both sides, so `big + x` from one `big` many times is linear each time, where a rope would defer it. There's no flatten, as there are no ropes. `join` sizes once and copies once. `indexOf` is the naive search, so `O(n·m)` on a bad input. Number to text is proportional to the digits and limbs: a random double of ordinary size is about 1.5 µs, against V8's 50 ns, and an extreme exponent is more. A string is UTF-16 always: an ASCII word costs twice V8's bytes, and a block is 16 bytes of header, 16 of string header, and rounds up to a power of two, so a five-letter word is 64 bytes.
- *Fragmentation.* Blocks don't coalesce (above). A churn of varied-length strings doesn't hit a false trap 14: each size's free list refills itself, and M5's Phase F measures how little memory each shape runs in.
- *Copy-on-write.* Only strings share. For arrays, `.slice()` and spread copy. The write test turned out to cost almost nothing, so that isn't the reason: see M5's Phase F for what is.

**Where a mode's memory comes from.** The one thing an environment registers is a page source: the function 3.5's layers already start with,
handing out zeroed runs of pages, or 0 when there are none. `setPageSource(f)` in `@tsl/unsafe` takes a top-level function by name (TSL5009),
and `__page_source_use(code)` is the same thing for a native caller or a test image. There's no registered allocator: `leak` is a bump allocator over
the source, and `manual`'s heap is a size-class allocator in the shape of `ex-heap.ts`, with no block headers and 16-byte alignment, where a run of whole pages isn't reused. Both are a few
dozen lines of TIR, linked only for a module with a mode, so a `strict` module doesn't change by a byte. A heap as the registered thing would need a
`Heap` object or two function pointers before any allocation, and `@tsl/alloc` linked into everything; a page source is what every environment
in the table above has anyway, and a `Heap` of the program's own can share it. The runtime's arena stays too, for what's bounded (4.5). A source
that's never registered is out of memory, so code 14. The bare-metal test runtime registers a range of RAM. `rc` takes its pages from the same source, as its size classes run out.

```ts
// file: ex-heap.ts
import { idiv, toU64, u64, type bool, type usize } from "@tsl/core";
import { copyBytes, elemSize, pageRunFreed, ptrAt, type ElemOf, type Ptr } from "@tsl/unsafe";

export const PAGE: usize = 4096;
const CLASSES: usize = 8; // 16, 32, ... 2048 bytes; anything larger takes whole pages

/** Hands out zeroed runs of pages, or 0n when there are none. This is the only part that differs per environment. */
export type PageSource = (pages: usize) => u64;

function classOf(bytes: usize): usize {
  let size: usize = 16;
  for (let c = 0; c < CLASSES; c++) {
    if (bytes <= size) return c;
    size = size * 2;
  }
  return CLASSES;
}

/** A size-class allocator. Callers pass the size back on free, so blocks carry no headers. */
export class Heap {
  private heads: u64 = 0n; // CLASSES free-list heads, at the start of the first page
  private bump: u64 = 0n;
  private bumpEnd: u64 = 0n;

  constructor(private source: PageSource) {}

  // SAFETY: heads is a whole page from setUp, and c is below CLASSES, so this is within the 64 bytes reserved there.
  private head(c: usize): Ptr<u64> {
    return ptrAt(u64, this.heads + toU64(c * 8));
  }

  private setUp(): bool {
    const first = this.source(1);
    if (first === 0n) return false;
    this.heads = first;
    this.bump = first + 64n;
    this.bumpEnd = first + toU64(PAGE);
    return true;
  }

  /** Returns an address aligned to the block size, or 0n when out of memory. */
  // SAFETY: a free block's first word is its link, and every block is at least 16 bytes, from pages we were given.
  allocBytes(bytes: usize): u64 {
    if (this.heads === 0n && !this.setUp()) return 0n;
    const c = classOf(bytes);
    if (c === CLASSES) return this.source(idiv(bytes + PAGE - 1, PAGE));
    const head = this.head(c);
    const block = head.read();
    if (block !== 0n) {
      head.write(ptrAt(u64, block).read());
      return block;
    }
    const size = 16n << toU64(c);
    const at = ((this.bump + size - 1n) / size) * size;
    if (at + size > this.bumpEnd) {
      const page = this.source(1);
      if (page === 0n) return 0n;
      this.bump = page + size;
      this.bumpEnd = page + toU64(PAGE);
      return page;
    }
    this.bump = at + size;
    return at;
  }

  // SAFETY: the caller gives back a block it got from allocBytes with this size, so the link fits and nothing else has it.
  freeBytes(addr: u64, bytes: usize): void {
    const c = classOf(bytes);
    if (c === CLASSES) return pageRunFreed(addr, idiv(bytes + PAGE - 1, PAGE)); // @tsl/std takes these, and with no std they stay with the domain
    const head = this.head(c);
    ptrAt(u64, addr).write(head.read());
    head.write(addr);
  }
}

// SAFETY: the address is a fresh block of n elements, or null when there isn't one.
export function alloc<T>(heap: Heap, e: ElemOf<T>, n: usize): Ptr<T> | null {
  const a = heap.allocBytes(n * elemSize(e));
  return a === 0n ? null : ptrAt(e, a);
}

export function free<T>(heap: Heap, e: ElemOf<T>, p: Ptr<T>, n: usize): void {
  heap.freeBytes(p.addr, n * elemSize(e));
}

// SAFETY: the caller owns n elements at both pointers.
export function copyElems<T>(e: ElemOf<T>, dst: Ptr<T>, src: Ptr<T>, n: usize): void {
  copyBytes(dst.addr, src.addr, n * elemSize(e));
}
```

`Vec` is safe to use from safe code. Rust stops a slice outliving a reallocation with its borrow checker. Here
a slice is lent through a closure: it can't escape, because slices can't be stored, and growing during the
loan traps.

```ts
// file: ex-vec.ts
import { Trap, trap, type ArrayOf, type bool, type usize } from "@tsl/core";
import { sliceOf, type ElemOf, type Ptr } from "@tsl/unsafe";
import { alloc, copyElems, free, type Heap } from "./ex-heap.ts";

export class Vec<T> {
  private buf: Ptr<T> | null = null;
  private len: usize = 0;
  private cap: usize = 0;
  private borrows: usize = 0;
  private dead: bool = false;

  constructor(private elem: ElemOf<T>, private heap: Heap) {}

  get length(): usize {
    this.check();
    return this.len;
  }

  private check(): void {
    if (this.dead) trap(Trap.Stale);
  }

  // SAFETY: i is below len, which is at most cap, the number of elements buf holds.
  private slot(i: usize): Ptr<T> {
    this.check();
    if (i >= this.len || this.buf === null) trap(Trap.Bounds);
    return this.buf.add(i);
  }

  // SAFETY: slot checked the index, and the Vec is alive.
  get(i: usize): T {
    return this.slot(i).read();
  }

  // SAFETY: slot checked the index, and the Vec is alive.
  set(i: usize, v: T): void {
    this.slot(i).write(v);
  }

  /** False when out of memory, and the Vec is unchanged. */
  // SAFETY: grow left len below cap, so the element at len is ours to write.
  push(v: T): bool {
    this.check();
    if (this.borrows > 0) trap(Trap.Loan);
    if (this.len === this.cap && !this.grow()) return false;
    this.buf!.add(this.len).write(v);
    this.len++;
    return true;
  }

  // SAFETY: len was above zero, so the element now at len was written by push.
  pop(): T {
    this.check();
    if (this.borrows > 0) trap(Trap.Loan);
    if (this.len === 0) trap(Trap.Bounds);
    this.len--;
    return this.buf!.add(this.len).read();
  }

  private grow(): bool {
    const cap = this.cap === 0 ? 4 : this.cap * 2;
    const next = alloc(this.heap, this.elem, cap);
    if (next === null) return false;
    if (this.buf !== null) {
      copyElems(this.elem, next, this.buf, this.len);
      free(this.heap, this.elem, this.buf, this.cap);
    }
    this.buf = next;
    this.cap = cap;
    return true;
  }

  // SAFETY: borrows stops push, pop and free moving the buffer during the loan, and a slice can't be stored.
  withSlice(f: (s: ArrayOf<T>) => void): void {
    this.check();
    if (this.buf === null) return;
    this.borrows++;
    f(sliceOf(this.elem, this.buf.addr, this.len));
    this.borrows--;
  }

  /** Elements it has room for without growing. */
  get capacity(): usize {
    this.check();
    return this.cap;
  }

  /** Gives an empty Vec's buffer back, and leaves it usable: true if there was one. */
  // SAFETY: buf holds cap elements from this heap, and nothing borrows it.
  trim(): bool {
    this.check();
    if (this.len > 0 || this.buf === null) return false;
    if (this.borrows > 0) trap(Trap.Loan);
    free(this.heap, this.elem, this.buf, this.cap);
    this.buf = null;
    this.cap = 0;
    return true;
  }

  free(): void {
    this.check();
    if (this.borrows > 0) trap(Trap.Loan);
    if (this.buf !== null) free(this.heap, this.elem, this.buf, this.cap);
    this.buf = null;
    this.dead = true;
  }

  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    if (!this.dead) this.free();
  }
}
```

`Slab` is safe allocation for objects:

```ts
// file: ex-slab.ts
import { toU64, Trap, trap, u32, u64, type bool, type usize } from "@tsl/core";
import { elemSize, genOf, inlineOf, objectAt, placeObject, ptrAt, retireObject, slotOf, type Elem } from "@tsl/unsafe";
import type { Heap } from "./ex-heap.ts";

const CHUNK_HEADER: usize = 16; // [next chunk: u64][pad]
const SLOT_PREFIX: usize = 16; //  [next free slot: u64][generation: u32][owner: u32], then the object.
const GEN_AT: u64 = 8n; //         an odd generation means occupied
const OWNER_AT: u64 = 12n;
const MAX_GEN: u32 = 0xfffe; //    stored references keep 16 bits of generation

let nextOwner: u32 = 1; // a Slab takes its ID when it first grows, so one that never has owns nothing

/** Chunks come from a Heap and never go back while the Slab lives, so a slot only ever holds a T. */
export class Slab<T extends object> {
  private chunks: u64 = 0n;
  private freeList: u64 = 0n;
  private count: usize = 0;
  private owner: u32 = 0;
  private elem: Elem<T> = inlineOf<T>();

  constructor(private heap: Heap, private chunkSlots: usize) {}

  get size(): usize {
    return this.count;
  }

  private stride(): usize {
    return SLOT_PREFIX + elemSize(this.elem);
  }

  private slotIn(chunk: u64, i: usize): u64 {
    return chunk + toU64(CHUNK_HEADER + i * this.stride());
  }

  // SAFETY: chunk is a fresh block big enough for its header and chunkSlots slots.
  private grow(): bool {
    const chunk = this.heap.allocBytes(CHUNK_HEADER + this.chunkSlots * this.stride());
    if (chunk === 0n) return false;
    if (this.owner === 0) this.owner = nextOwner++;
    ptrAt(u64, chunk).write(this.chunks);
    this.chunks = chunk;
    for (let i = this.chunkSlots; i > 0; i--) {
      const slot = this.slotIn(chunk, i - 1);
      ptrAt(u64, slot).write(this.freeList); // a free slot's link stays out of its object's bytes
      ptrAt(u32, slot + GEN_AT).write(0);
      ptrAt(u32, slot + OWNER_AT).write(this.owner);
      this.freeList = slot;
    }
    return true;
  }

  /** @tsl.moves item */
  // SAFETY: slot came off the free list, so it's in a live chunk, unoccupied, and only ever holds a T.
  add(item: T): T | null {
    if (this.freeList === 0n && !this.grow()) return null;
    const slot = this.freeList;
    this.freeList = ptrAt(u64, slot).read();
    const gen = ptrAt(u32, slot + GEN_AT).read() + 1;
    ptrAt(u32, slot + GEN_AT).write(gen);
    this.count++;
    return placeObject(slot, gen, item);
  }

  /** Traps with code 5 if the item isn't in this Slab, or has already been removed. */
  // SAFETY: slotOf and genOf only accept a slot's own reference, and the owner and generation checks reject the rest.
  remove(item: T): void {
    const slot = slotOf(item);
    const gen = genOf(item);
    if (ptrAt(u32, slot + OWNER_AT).read() !== this.owner) trap(Trap.Stale);
    if (ptrAt(u32, slot + GEN_AT).read() !== gen) trap(Trap.Stale);
    ptrAt(u32, slot + GEN_AT).write(gen + 1); // now even, so every stored reference is stale
    retireObject(item);
    this.count--;
    if (gen + 1 >= MAX_GEN) return; // out of generations: the slot is never reused
    ptrAt(u64, slot).write(this.freeList);
    this.freeList = slot;
  }

  /** Visits occupied slots. Removing the visited object during the call is allowed. */
  // SAFETY: chunks never go back to the Heap while the Slab lives, and an odd generation means the slot holds a T.
  forEach(f: (item: T) => void): void {
    for (let chunk = this.chunks; chunk !== 0n; chunk = ptrAt(u64, chunk).read()) {
      for (let i = 0; i < this.chunkSlots; i++) {
        const slot = this.slotIn(chunk, i);
        if ((ptrAt(u32, slot + GEN_AT).read() & 1) === 1) f(objectAt<T>(slot));
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The one environment-specific part is the page source. For an EL0 domain:

```ts
// file: ex-pages.ts
import { toU64, type u64, type usize } from "@tsl/core";
import { asMap, frameAlloc, type Cap } from "./ex-sys.ts";
import { PAGE, type PageSource } from "./ex-heap.ts";

const HEAP_BASE: u64 = 0x10_0000_0000n;
const MAP_READ_WRITE = 3;

let quota: Cap<"quota"> = 0;
let space: Cap<"addrspace"> = 0;
let next: u64 = HEAP_BASE;

export function setUpPages(q: Cap<"quota">, as: Cap<"addrspace">): void {
  quota = q;
  space = as;
}

export const domainPages: PageSource = (pages: usize): u64 => {
  const frame = frameAlloc(quota, pages);
  if (!frame.ok) return 0n; // the domain's quota is exhausted
  const at = next;
  const mapped = asMap(space, frame.value, at, MAP_READ_WRITE);
  if (!mapped.ok) return 0n;
  next = at + toU64(pages * PAGE);
  return at;
};
```

Using them:

```ts
// file: ex-memory.ts
import { arenaOver, toU32, type bool, type Result, type u32, type u64, type usize } from "@tsl/core";
import type { Heap } from "./ex-heap.ts";
import { Slab } from "./ex-slab.ts";

export enum TimerState { Idle = 0, Armed = 1, Fired = 2 }

export class Domain {
  constructor(public id: u32) {}
}

export class Timer {
  owner: Domain | null = null;
  state: TimerState = TimerState.Armed;
  constructor(public deadline: u64) {}

  expired(now: u64): bool {
    return now >= this.deadline;
  }
}

// Compiles to a small integer, and may be stored.
export type TimerError = "out-of-memory" | "already-expired";

export class Timers {
  private all: Slab<Timer>;

  constructor(heap: Heap) {
    this.all = new Slab<Timer>(heap, 64);
  }

  // A value union: no identity, no address, and the tag stays in registers.
  arm(now: u64, deadline: u64, owner: Domain): Result<Timer, TimerError> {
    if (deadline <= now) return { ok: false, error: "already-expired" };
    const timer = this.all.add(new Timer(deadline));
    if (timer === null) return { ok: false, error: "out-of-memory" };
    timer.owner = owner; // stores owner, so callers can't pass a stack object here
    return { ok: true, value: timer };
  }

  // A capturing closure is fine as long as it's only passed down.
  expire(now: u64, onFire: (t: Timer) => void): void {
    this.all.forEach((t) => {
      if (t.expired(now)) {
        t.state = TimerState.Fired;
        onFire(t);
        this.all.remove(t);
      }
    });
  }

  countExpired(now: u64): usize {
    let fired = 0;
    this.expire(now, () => {
      fired++;
    });
    return fired;
  }
}

type Pair = { readonly lo: u32; readonly hi: u32 };

export function split(x: u32): Pair {
  return { lo: x & 0xffff, hi: x >>> 16 };
}

// A stack object: gone at return, and can't be stored or returned.
export function ownerIdOfLocal(id: u32): u32 {
  const d = new Domain(id);
  return d.id;
}

export function totalLen(scratch: Uint8Array, n: usize): usize {
  using a = arenaOver(scratch);
  const lens = a.u32s(n);
  let total = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    lens[i] = toU32(i) & 0xff; // bitwise ops need 32 bits or fewer, so usize converts first
    total += lens[i]!; // u32 widens to usize
  }
  return total;
}
```

Messages and anything else from outside are declared structs, decoded into value unions. If a layout needs a
tag, you write the tag:

```ts
// file: ex-messages.ts
import { array, assertSize, enumOf, over, pad, u32, u64, u8 } from "@tsl/core";

export enum EventKind { Irq = 1, Block = 2 }

export class EventWire {
  kind = u32(); // a raw u32, not enumOf: this came from outside, so it's validated below
  reserved = pad(4);
  payload = array(u8, 16);
}
assertSize(EventWire, 24);

export class IrqPayload {
  intid = u32();
}
export class BlockPayload {
  sector = u64();
  status = u8();
}
assertSize(BlockPayload, 16);

export type Event =
  | { readonly kind: "irq"; readonly intid: u32 }
  | { readonly kind: "block"; readonly sector: u64; readonly status: u8 }
  | { readonly kind: "bad" };

export function decode(w: EventWire): Event {
  switch (w.kind) {
    case EventKind.Irq:
      return { kind: "irq", intid: over(IrqPayload, w.payload, 0).intid };
    case EventKind.Block: {
      const b = over(BlockPayload, w.payload, 0);
      return { kind: "block", sector: b.sector, status: b.status };
    }
    default:
      return { kind: "bad" };
  }
}

export function statusOf(e: Event): u32 {
  switch (e.kind) {
    case "irq":
      return e.intid;
    case "block":
      return e.status; // u8 widens to u32
    case "bad":
      return 0xffffffff;
  }
}

export enum BlkType { In = 0, Out = 1, Flush = 4 }

// Device-owned memory we wrote ourselves, so enumOf is safe here.
export class BlkRequest {
  type = enumOf(u32, BlkType);
  reserved = pad(4);
  sector = u64();
}
assertSize(BlkRequest, 16);
```

**`@tsl/std` (D43).** The third layer, for TSL programs that aren't the kernel or a driver: collections and text with no heap passed around. `@tsl/core` is what every program has, `@tsl/alloc` is what a program with its own memory uses, and `@tsl/std` is `@tsl/alloc` over one global allocator. `kernel-core` and drivers stay `"noStd": true` and `"memory": "strict"`: the import is TSL1018, directly, by path, through a re-export, or in anything a `noStd` package imports, however far down and in whoever's package. It's ordinary TSL in `packages/tsl-std`, and it runs on V8 and JSC over the host's simulated memory with no `tslc`, as `@tsl/alloc` does. Five modules and a front door, 643 LOC: 72 unsafe, the global allocator, and the other 571 safe code over `@tsl/alloc`.

| What | Does | Passes D24 because |
|------|------|--------------------|
| `Vec<T>` | `new Vec(u32)`, `new Vec(ref<Item>())`: `push`, `pop`, `get`, `set`, `length`, `insert`, `removeAt`, `swapRemove`, `swap`, `clear`, `forEach`, `sortInPlace`, `withSlice`, `free`, `tryPush` | Asked for |
| `Map<K, V>`, `ExactMap<K, V>`, `Set<K>` | `new Map(u32, u32)`, `new ExactMap(ref<Str>(), ref<Node>())`, `new Set(u32)`: `get`, `getOr`, `set`, `has`, `delete`, `size`, `clear`, `forEach`, `free`, `trySet`; `add`, `tryAdd`. `Map` and `Set` are JS's, and `ExactMap` traps (D47, below) | Asked for |
| `Str`, `StrBuilder` | `Str.of(lit("text"))`, immutable UTF-8: `length`, `at`, `slice`, `concat`, `indexOf`, `compare`, `equals`, `split`, `withBytes`, `free`. A builder appends bytes, a `Str`, or a `u32` or `i32` in decimal | A compiler or a system handles names and text |
| `Slab<T>` | `new Slab<T>()`: `add`, `tryAdd`, `remove`, `forEach`, `size` | In `strict` there's no other way for an object to outlive its function, and one with a heap argument would be the one thing here that takes a heap |
| `globalAllocator`, `setHashKey` | Below | The allocator's the point; a hash table facing untrusted keys needs a key, and a guest has no entropy of its own |

Not in it, with no case made: float keys and a float's text (D42's exact-integer printing is 975 lines of `compiler/rt/num.ts`, which isn't TSL, and nothing here needs it), regular expressions, a double-ended queue (a `Vec` and an index), `Rc`-like sharing (`rc` is lowered code's, D39), or iterators (`for...of` over a container would need an escaping object, 3.6, so it's `forEach`).

*How it's built.* Each collection is `@tsl/alloc`'s `Vec` or `Slab` in a field, over the one `heap`. So the safety code is the code that's already tested: a dead-`Vec` check, a bounds check, a loan on `withSlice`. What std adds is what `@tsl/alloc` leaves to its caller: out of memory becomes a trap, and each collection has a `forEach`, which takes a loan too. The price is measured in M5's Phase G: with no inliner, a `Vec.get` is one more call.

*Two maps (D47).* `Map` is JS's: `get` of a missing key gives `undefined`, a `V | undefined` that for a scalar `V` is a flag and a value in two registers and never memory (3.3, rule 12), and for a reference a null pointer, tested with `=== undefined` or defaulted with `??`; and changing it during `forEach` does what JS does, so an entry added is visited, one deleted before it's reached isn't, a value set before it's reached is the one seen, and after `clear` what's added is. Its `forEach` gives the value first, as JS's does. What makes that work is that nothing moves while a `forEach` runs: a growth then doubles without compacting, and `clear` turns every entry into a tombstone and keeps its place. `ExactMap` is the trapping map this layer had before, renamed: `get` of a missing key traps 2, and inserting, deleting or clearing during its `forEach`, which gives the key first, traps 13. It's for code where a missing key is a bug. `Set` is JS's only, as a set has no `get` to miss. Freeing a `Map` during its own `forEach` is trap 13 in both, as `free` isn't JS's. The table under both still grows in one operation, as lowered code's did: making it incremental here would leave `@tsl/alloc`'s `Vec`, which grows by copying, so it isn't done, and a program that can't take that pause sizes its table.

*Reuse, and what it says about D42.* A `Map` here is a third implementation only in name, and it's still the second one this repo holds: `compiler/rt/map.ts` (373 lines, lowered) and `ex-std-map.ts` (208 LOC, TSL). They have one design, entries in insertion order in parallel vectors, a chained table of positions, tombstones, growth that compacts first. They don't share code, and it isn't for want of trying: `compiler/rt/map.ts` can't change, because every lowered module with a `Map` is pinned to its bytes, and a shared core would need a vector abstraction the lowered form doesn't have. Most of its lines (the cursor generations, `TmkGen`, the incremental move, and the iterator objects) have no counterpart here: TSL has no iterators, and the only cursor is a `forEach`'s index, which stays good because nothing moves under one. About 70 lines of the two correspond one for one, and what they share in fact is an oracle: `tools/std-oracle.ts` runs JS's own `Map`, `Set`, `Array` and strings over the same random operations as `corpus/std/model.ts`, and lowered code's are held to V8 by M5's Phase F, so the two agree through that. A generated copy of those 70 lines was considered and isn't worth a tool. Strings share nothing but the hash's arrangement, as `rc`'s are UTF-16 with views and tail sharing, for JS's sake, and these are UTF-8 bytes in a `Vec`. D42 held: a `Map` over `@tsl/alloc` is possible in TSL proper exactly because a stored reference there is a plain 64-bit value with a generation, which `Vec` can copy, and that's the thing a counted reference isn't. Phase G measures this one against `rc`'s: 1.6 to 3.4× slower on the same work, which is the extra calls and checks of building over `Vec`, and which is what D42 said it would cost to have built lowered code's over it.

*What it does when memory runs out (3.10).* `@tsl/alloc` reports it as a normal result. `@tsl/std` traps with code 14, as Rust's global allocator aborts, because a program with no heap in sight hasn't said what it wants done, and nearly all of them can't do anything else: `v.push(x)` with a result nobody reads would drop data silently. A caller who can handle it uses `tryPush`, `trySet`, `tryAdd`, `Str.tryOf` or `tryAppendBytes`. Those return `false` or `null` with the collection as it was: `trySet` undoes its partial pushes, and a failed growth pops what it added. Code 14 was already out of memory (3.10), so this adds no divergence. Under one page source the host and native run the same arithmetic and trap at the same push, for scalars; objects in a `Slab` have a simulated stride on the host (divergence 6), so the same limit is reached at a different count, which is divergence 4. A `@tsl.noalloc` path can't reach any of it: a push is TSL1017 through `Heap`'s function value, and a `get` passes.

*The global allocator.* Named by a tag on a top-level `const`, in a module listed under `"unsafeModules"`, since a page source is trusted (3.8):

```ts
import { globalAllocator } from "@tsl/std";
/** @tsl.global-allocator */
const heap = globalAllocator(domainPages);
```

The tag is what the plan reserved. It wasn't written anywhere in this spec before now, and this is its form. V8 and JSC don't read comments, which is why it's on a call: the host runs that call as the module loads, before anything can allocate, and `tslc` reads the same declaration at compile time, so a `Vec` made in a top-level `const` compiles to static data with the allocator already bound, and nothing is registered at run time natively. There's at most one in a whole program, counting every module it imports: a second is TSL1021 at that declaration, and the message says where the first is. A tag on anything else, or a `globalAllocator` call with no tag or not at the top level, is TSL1020. The argument is a top-level function by name (TSL5009), as for `setPageSource`. An allocator in a module that isn't listed is TSL5001. What's named is a page source, not an algorithm: `Heap` is the one allocator, `@tsl/alloc`'s `Vec` takes a `Heap` and not two function values, and a choice of algorithm isn't worth what D38 rejected it for. The `const` is that `Heap`, so a program can give it to anything of its own.

| With none named | Where its pages come from |
|-----------------|---------------------------|
| On the host | `setPageSource`'s if one was called, or else simulated regions as they're needed, with no limit but the host's (divergence 4) |
| In a bare-metal test image | The range of RAM the runtime registers (`// memory-pages: n` limits it), and `setPageSource` replaces that |
| In an EL0 domain, at M6 | The domain registers `domainPages` (3.5's table) with `setPageSource` at start, or names it, and then it's charged to its quota |
| With nothing registered at all | The first allocation is trap 14, or `false` from a try form (`corpus/std/nosource`). The host has no such state, so that's divergence 4 |

So `setPageSource` and the tag don't compete. `setPageSource` is the environment's: a run-time call that says where `leak`, `manual` and an unnamed `@tsl/std` get pages. The tag is the program's: a compile-time fact, for std alone. With both, `leak` and `manual` use the one and std the other. A program with no `@tsl/std` links none of this, and pays nothing: its TIR is byte for byte what it was, with `Heap` itself the same bytes (below).

*Runs of whole pages.* `@tsl/alloc`'s `Heap` keeps nothing above 2 KiB: "whole-page runs stay with the domain until it dies" is fine for a kernel that sizes things once, and it's wrong for a program. A `Vec` of 1,000 `u32`s made and freed in a loop would run a test image out of memory with nothing leaked (MEASURED, `vecBuffersComeBack`). So `Heap.freeBytes` says `pageRunFreed(addr, pages)`, which tells `@tsl/std`, and in a program with no `@tsl/std` compiles to no code at all, arguments included, so `Heap` stays byte-identical everywhere else. `ex-std-global.ts` keeps runs on 24 lists by the log of their size, takes the first that fits, splits off what's left, and zeroes what it hands out, as a page source promises. Nothing coalesces, as in `rc` (above), so trap 14 can come with free memory of the wrong shape. Taking a run walks one list, and zeroing is proportional to the run.

*In each memory mode.* `@tsl/std` is a `strict` package, whatever imports it: its code doesn't change.

| Package | What `new Vec(u32)` is | Can it go in a field, or be returned? | What it can hold |
|---------|------------------------|---------------------------------------|------------------|
| `strict` | A stack object, or static at the top level, or held in place in a field (D37). Put it in a `Slab<Vec<u32>>` to give it a life of its own | In place, or from a `Slab`. `TSL3002` to return one made in a function, as for anything made in a function | Scalars; references to `Slab` objects, statics and `leak` objects, generation-checked when read |
| `leak` | The same if it stays put, and a leak object if it escapes | Yes | The same, and its own objects, which never go stale |
| `manual` | The same, and if it escapes, an object in the package's heap, which it frees itself with `unsafeFree`, after `free` | Yes | Scalars and `Slab` references. A raw reference has no generation, and a `Vec`'s field is in a `strict` package: TSL3008 at the push, as for any field there |
| `rc` | Not applicable: lowered code has JS's `Map`, `Set` and strings (D42), and `tmk lower` of a module importing `@tsl/std` is TSL1022 | | |

*Safety.* A stored reference in a `Vec` is what any stored reference is, and reading a member through one is checked. Two things are new:

- A closure's parameter is never checked, because it's assumed to be live (`Slab.forEach` only passes what is). A `Vec` or `Map` can hold a stale one, so `forEach` and `sortInPlace` call `checkLive` on each reference before it reaches a closure, and it traps with code 5 there. It's a no-op on a scalar, and it's a descriptor-like builtin in `@tsl/unsafe` that needs no `// SAFETY:`.
- Removing an element frees nothing, since a `Vec` doesn't own what it refers to, and leaves nothing to read: `pop`, `removeAt` and `clear` make its index out of bounds (trap 2), `withSlice`'s slice has the new length, and a deleted `Map` entry is a tombstone `forEach` skips. Freeing a `Str`, or an object in a `Slab`, makes every stored reference trap 5. A `Str` in a local after `free` is divergence 5, like any `Slab` object.

A slice given to a closure can't be kept outside it (TSL3003). That wasn't so before this work: `let kept = EMPTY; v.withSlice((s) => { kept = s; });` compiled, and read freed memory after a `push`, in `@tsl/alloc` too, because "a slice can't be stored" only covered fields and globals. A local a closure captures is now in the rule. Keeping a static array there's still fine.

*Keys.* `keyHash` and `keySame`, in `@tsl/unsafe`, are chosen by the key's type, since generics are concrete when they're elaborated: an integer by value, a class with `hashKey` and `sameKey` by those methods, a dispatch interface (3.4, D70) with both by its classes' through the class-id switch, and any other class or interface by identity, with nothing dereferenced, so a stale key can be looked up and deleted. `Str` has those methods, and so has `@tsl/jsrt`'s `JsString` (D72). A float is TSL2003, reported at the program's own `new Map(...)`: it has two zeros and a NaN that isn't itself. A class with one method and not the other is TSL2003 too. The compiler knows the method names and no class (D30). A hash can depend on an address, which safe code can't otherwise see (3.8), and so the table is in insertion order, and nothing visible depends on one. As in D42, a program facing untrusted keys calls `setHashKey` before it inserts anything, or it floods.

*Escape checking.* Three limits were known, and each was tried against ordinary programs:

- *A stack object holding a stack object.* This one blocked ordinary use: `const w = new Writer(v)`, a small helper over a local `Vec`, was TSL3001, and that's most of what structs are for. It's allowed now. A method's `this.f = param` is recorded apart from other stores, and a caller may pass a stack object or a view to it if the receiver is a stack object of the caller's frame, and that object isn't moved into a `Slab` by `@tsl.moves`, or a field. `holder.f = x` is the same. A field a stack object has been in is known whole-program, and what's read from it is a stack object: no generation check, because there's no prefix, and TSL3001 or TSL3002 if it's stored or returned. `x` made in a loop stays an error, as its slot's reused. A `leak` or `manual` package is unchanged: there the object just escapes. The cost is on that field: anything else put in it, a `Slab` object say, isn't checked either.
- *A local `Heap` with a local `Vec`.* It's the same limit, and it's fixed by the same change. `@tsl/std` never needed it.
- *A stack object passed to a function value.* It stays: a parameter of function type is assumed to store what it's given, and knowing better would take the closures that can reach each call. It doesn't block std, whose callbacks are only ever given values and stored references, and a program's closure can capture a stack object instead.

`@tsl.moves` can be passed on: a function's own moved parameter given to another function's moved parameter is still one object moved once (`Slab.add` over `@tsl/alloc`'s). Static methods are allowed on non-generic classes, as `Str.of` is, and a `lit("...")` can be written in a function: its bytes are static data, one copy per text.

*Threads (D40).* Each thread has its own heap, so the global allocator is per thread in concept, with nothing to build yet. `heap`, its lists of runs, `Str`'s `Slab` and the hash key are plain module state today, which D40's check on state reached from two threads will have to treat as per-thread storage when threads exist: **that's a rule this design makes harder.** A static object at a fixed address needs a thread pointer at M6, and a `Vec` in a static would need to be one per thread, or be rejected. A `Vec` keeps its `Heap` for life, so it can only be freed on its own thread, which is what D40 wants anyway.

*The opt-in shared type, written down and not built.* **`Shared<T>`**, in `@tsl/std`, is `Arc`'s shape, for what D40 lets cross:

- *What it can hold.* `T` is a layout class: scalars, nested layouts and arrays of them, with no reference, no `Ptr` and no `Vec`, and, as the one exception, a field of type `Shared<U>`, which is a handle, checked at compile time. A plain class is an error, as it can hold an ordinary reference. So nothing in one can name a thread's heap.
- *Its memory.* A heap of its own, `SharedHeap`, over `frameAlloc`ed shared frames, with a lock or atomic free lists, one per program. It isn't the global allocator, and it isn't reached through it. A block is `[count: u32, atomic][generation: u32][T]`.
- *What using one looks like.* `Shared.of(T, init)` makes one with a count of 1. `s.clone()` is an atomic increment and gives another handle, which a thread can be given. `s.drop()`, or `using`, is an atomic decrement, and the last one frees it. `s.value` is a view, with 3.9's rules: fields through `atomic.*`, or a plain read with the race rule that already applies. A handle in a thread's own object is a value it holds and must drop: nothing counts for it, and it isn't a counted `rc` reference, so there's no collector, and a cycle of `Shared` leaks.
- *On V8 and JSC.* A block lives in one `SharedArrayBuffer` per heap, which each worker maps, with counts and fields through `Atomics`, and a handle crossing `postMessage` is its offset and generation. That works because `T` is bytes: the same rule that keeps ordinary objects off shared memory natively is what makes it possible at all on an engine, where a JS object can't be shared. A thread on the host is a worker, and `Vec` can't go across, there or natively.
- *What this rules out.* `Shared<Vec<T>>` and `Shared<Str>`. Text or a growing list between threads is a layout class of a fixed size, or a channel of bytes. If a program turns out to need more, that's a new decision.


The global allocator, and what's unsafe in `@tsl/std`:

```ts
// file: ex-std-global.ts
import { Heap, type PageSource } from "@tsl/alloc";
import { idiv, toU64, toUsize, u64, type bool, type u32, type usize } from "@tsl/core";
import { bytesAt, onPageRunFreed, ptrAt, sourcePages } from "@tsl/unsafe";

export { checkLive, keyHash, keySame, ref, type ElemOf } from "@tsl/unsafe";

// SAFETY: the environment registered this source (setPageSource), and it's trusted to return what it promises (3.8).
function registered(pages: usize): u64 {
  return sourcePages(pages);
}

class Source {
  constructor(public from: PageSource) {}
}

// tslc builds this over the program's named source, if it has one, and nothing changes it at run time natively.
const source = new Source(registered);

const PAGE_BYTES: usize = 4096;
const RUN_LISTS: usize = 24; // by the log of the size, as a Heap keeps nothing about a run itself
const runs = new BigUint64Array(24);

function listOf(n: usize): usize {
  let list: usize = 0;
  for (let s = n; s > 1; s = idiv(s, 2)) list++;
  return list;
}

/** A run of whole pages a Heap was given back. `@tsl/alloc`'s Heap keeps none, as a kernel doesn't need it to; a program does. */
// SAFETY: its owner gave it back, so nothing else has it, and every run is at least one page, so its two words fit.
function keepRun(addr: u64, n: usize): void {
  const list = listOf(n);
  ptrAt(u64, addr).write(runs[list]!);
  ptrAt(u64, addr + 8n).write(toU64(n));
  runs[list] = addr;
}

// SAFETY: the run came off a list, and a list only holds what keepRun was given: it's ours, and it's zeroed as a source's is.
function takeRun(n: usize): u64 {
  for (let list = listOf(n); list < RUN_LISTS; list++) {
    let before: u64 = 0n;
    for (let at = runs[list]!; at !== 0n; at = ptrAt(u64, at).read()) {
      const size = toUsize(ptrAt(u64, at + 8n).read());
      if (size >= n) {
        const next = ptrAt(u64, at).read();
        if (before === 0n) runs[list] = next;
        else ptrAt(u64, before).write(next);
        if (size > n) keepRun(at + toU64(n * PAGE_BYTES), size - n);
        bytesAt(at, n * PAGE_BYTES).fill(0);
        return at;
      }
      before = at;
    }
  }
  return 0n;
}

// SAFETY: tslc binds this at compile time, and it's only the two functions above.
export const keepsRuns: bool = onPageRunFreed(keepRun);

function pages(n: usize): u64 {
  const run = takeRun(n);
  if (run !== 0n) return run;
  const from = source.from;
  return from(n);
}

/** The global allocator: one Heap, per thread in concept (D40), over the named page source or else the registered one. */
export const heap = new Heap(pages);

/**
 * Names the program's page source for the global allocator: a top-level `const h = globalAllocator(f)` with the tag
 * above it (3.5), at most one in a program (TSL1020, TSL1021). tslc reads it at compile time, and on V8 and JSC it runs
 * as the module loads, before any exported function can allocate.
 */
export function globalAllocator(named: PageSource): Heap {
  source.from = named;
  return heap;
}

let key0: u32 = 0x243f6a88;
let key1: u32 = 0x85a308d3;

export function hashKeyWord(i: u32): u32 {
  return i === 0 ? key0 : key1;
}

/** No guest has entropy of its own, so a program facing untrusted keys registers some, before it inserts anything (D42). */
export function setHashKey(k0: u32, k1: u32): void {
  key0 = k0;
  key1 = k1;
}

/** A keyed MurmurHash3 finaliser. A hash can depend on an address, and so nothing visible depends on a hash. */
export function mix(x: u32): u32 {
  let h = x ^ key0;
  h = h ^ (h >>> 16);
  h = Math.imul(h, 0x85ebca6b);
  h = h ^ key1 ^ (h >>> 13);
  h = Math.imul(h, 0xc2b2ae35);
  return (h ^ (h >>> 16)) >>> 0;
}
```

`Vec`:

```ts
// file: ex-std-vec.ts
import { Vec as AllocVec } from "@tsl/alloc";
import { idiv, Trap, trap, type ArrayOf, type bool, type i32, type usize } from "@tsl/core";
import { checkLive, heap, type ElemOf } from "./ex-std-global.ts";

/**
 * `@tsl/alloc`'s Vec over the global allocator. Out of memory is trap 14, and `tryPush` is the form that reports it.
 * A loan (`withSlice`, `forEach`, `sortInPlace`) stops anything that moves or removes elements, with trap 13.
 */
export class Vec<T> {
  private v: AllocVec<T>;
  private loans: usize = 0;
  private freed: bool = false;

  constructor(elem: ElemOf<T>) {
    this.v = new AllocVec(elem, heap);
  }

  get length(): usize {
    return this.v.length;
  }

  get(i: usize): T {
    return this.v.get(i);
  }

  set(i: usize, x: T): void {
    this.v.set(i, x);
  }

  private noLoan(): void {
    if (this.loans > 0) trap(Trap.Loan);
  }

  push(x: T): void {
    this.noLoan();
    if (!this.v.push(x)) trap(Trap.OutOfMemory);
  }

  /** False when out of memory, and the Vec is unchanged. */
  tryPush(x: T): bool {
    this.noLoan();
    return this.v.push(x);
  }

  pop(): T {
    this.noLoan();
    return this.v.pop();
  }

  clear(): void {
    this.noLoan();
    for (let n = this.v.length; n > 0; n--) this.v.pop();
  }

  /** Moves everything from i up one place. Traps 2 past the end, and 14 out of memory. */
  insert(i: usize, x: T): void {
    this.noLoan();
    const n = this.v.length;
    if (i > n) trap(Trap.Bounds);
    if (i === n) {
      this.push(x);
      return;
    }
    this.push(this.v.get(n - 1));
    for (let at = n - 1; at > i; at--) this.v.set(at, this.v.get(at - 1));
    this.v.set(i, x);
  }

  /** Keeps the order: moves everything above i down one place, so it's linear. */
  removeAt(i: usize): T {
    this.noLoan();
    const x = this.v.get(i);
    const n = this.v.length;
    for (let at = i + 1; at < n; at++) this.v.set(at - 1, this.v.get(at));
    this.v.pop();
    return x;
  }

  /** Doesn't keep the order: the last element takes its place. */
  swapRemove(i: usize): T {
    this.noLoan();
    const x = this.v.get(i);
    const last = this.v.pop();
    if (i < this.v.length) this.v.set(i, last);
    return x;
  }

  swap(i: usize, j: usize): void {
    const a = this.v.get(i);
    this.v.set(i, this.v.get(j));
    this.v.set(j, a);
  }

  /** A value that's about to reach a closure, whose parameter nothing checks (3.5): a stale reference traps here. */
  private live(i: usize): T {
    const x = this.v.get(i);
    checkLive(x);
    return x;
  }

  forEach(f: (x: T, i: usize) => void): void {
    this.loans++;
    const n = this.v.length;
    for (let i: usize = 0; i < n; i++) f(this.live(i), i);
    this.loans--;
  }

  /** Heapsort: in place, no allocation, so it can't run out, and not stable. cmp is negative, 0 or positive, as JS's is. */
  sortInPlace(cmp: (a: T, b: T) => i32): void {
    this.loans++;
    const n = this.v.length;
    for (let i = idiv(n, 2); i > 0; i--) this.sift(i - 1, n, cmp);
    for (let end = n; end > 1; end--) {
      this.swap(0, end - 1);
      this.sift(0, end - 1, cmp);
    }
    this.loans--;
  }

  private sift(start: usize, end: usize, cmp: (a: T, b: T) => i32): void {
    let root = start;
    for (;;) {
      let child = root * 2 + 1;
      if (child >= end) return;
      if (child + 1 < end && cmp(this.live(child), this.live(child + 1)) < 0) child++;
      if (cmp(this.live(root), this.live(child)) >= 0) return;
      this.swap(root, child);
      root = child;
    }
  }

  /** Scalars only: the slice can't outlive the call, and `push`, `pop` and `free` during it trap 13. */
  withSlice(f: (s: ArrayOf<T>) => void): void {
    this.v.withSlice(f);
  }

  /** Elements it has room for without growing. */
  get capacity(): usize {
    return this.v.capacity;
  }

  /** Gives an empty Vec's buffer back, and leaves it usable: true if there was one (an `rc` release's step, D74). */
  trim(): bool {
    this.noLoan();
    return this.v.trim();
  }

  free(): void {
    this.noLoan();
    this.freed = true;
    this.v.free();
  }

  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    if (!this.freed) this.free();
  }
}
```

`JsArray` (D66), in `@tsl/jsrt` beside `JsString` with JS's other run-time classes, so that `@tsl/std` stays the explicit library: a JS array, with JS's rules where TSL can say them, which class printing prints a lowered program's arrays as (4.5), and which a person can write too. A hole is a zeroed slot, `null` in an array of references; an outgrown buffer goes back to `@tsl/std`'s global allocator (`heap`, which `@tsl/std` exports for it) unless the array was made to keep it, as a `leak` package's lowered arrays are, since the direct route's never give one back. R16: an array is made at its final size in one step (one block of its length or 4 elements, zeroed, no growth), by a constructor inlined where the inliner inlines, as an array literal's length is a constant; `push` is inlined too, a store and the length raised while there's room, its growth (`pushGrow`) a call out of line; `JsArenaArray` below is made and pushed the same way.

```ts
// file: ex-jsrt-array.ts
import { toU64, Trap, trap, u16, u32, u64, u8, type bool, type usize } from "@tsl/core";
import {
  addrInCallRegion,
  bytesAt,
  callRegionBytes,
  copyBytes,
  elemSize,
  inCallRegion,
  ptrAt,
  type ElemOf,
  type Ptr,
} from "@tsl/unsafe";
import { heap } from "@tsl/std";

/**
 * A JS array of T, with JS's rules where TSL can say them (D66): `length`, `push`, `pop`, `shift`, indexing, growth and
 * holes. A hole is a zeroed slot, which reads as `null` in an array of references, as a JS hole reads `undefined`; an
 * array of numbers can't have one, so where JS would make one this traps 15, as lowered code does. Elements live in a
 * buffer from the global allocator that doubles as it fills, from 4, and goes back to it when it's replaced. Lowered
 * programs print their arrays as this class (`tmk lower --emit tsl`), and a person can write it too. An array tslc placed
 * in a lowered package's per-call region (R6) takes its buffers from the region, which the export call gives back whole,
 * so none of those is given back to the global allocator.
 */
export class JsArray<T> {
  private data: u64 = 0n;
  private len: usize = 0;
  private cap: usize = 0;

  /**
   * `length` elements, each zero: JS's `new Array(length)` with its holes, or `[]`. `giveBack` false keeps each buffer
   * the array outgrows, as a `leak` package's lowered arrays always have (3.5), where true gives it back. R17: `holes`
   * says where the zeroing is done. True keeps every slot past the length zero: a shorter length (`pop`, `shift`,
   * `setLength`) zeroes what it drops, and growth what it doesn't copy, so a longer length finds holes there. False, a
   * lowered array of numbers (which can't have a hole: the lowering traps 15 first), zeroes only what a longer length
   * adds, as `setLength` does then: a shorter length leaves what it drops, and growth nothing past what it copies. Every
   * slot below the length reads the same either way; only where the zeroing is paid differs, and a pop, a store of the
   * length, pays none.
   */
  // R16: made at its final size in one step, as the direct route's `__vec_new` makes a vector: one block of max(length, 4)
  // elements, zeroed, and no growth path (an array literal is made at its length and then written, never grown). Inlined
  // at every level that inlines, so a constant length folds.
  /** @tsl.inline */
  // SAFETY: the block holds ncap elements, at least length, from the call region where tslc placed the array there (R6),
  // or the global allocator; nothing else has it.
  constructor(
    private elem: ElemOf<T>,
    length: usize,
    private giveBack: bool,
    private holes: bool,
  ) {
    const ncap = length < 4 ? 4 : length;
    const bytes = ncap * elemSize(elem);
    const block = inCallRegion(this) ? callRegionBytes(bytes) : heap.allocBytes(bytes);
    if (block === 0n) trap(Trap.OutOfMemory);
    bytesAt(block, bytes).fill(0);
    this.data = block;
    this.cap = ncap;
    this.len = length;
  }

  /** @tsl.inline */
  get length(): usize {
    return this.len;
  }

  /** The room the buffer has, in elements: 0 once `trim` gave it back. */
  /** @tsl.inline */
  get capacity(): usize {
    return this.cap;
  }

  /** @tsl.inline */
  // SAFETY: i is at most cap, so the address is in the buffer or just past it: an element step, with nothing to check.
  private slot(i: usize): Ptr<T> {
    return ptrAt(this.elem, this.data).add(i);
  }

  /** @tsl.inline */
  private at(i: usize): u64 {
    return this.slot(i).addr;
  }

  /** `a[i]`; past the end traps 2 (`a[i]!`): a hole reads as zero, `null` for a reference. Inlined at every level that
   * inlines (R4), as JsRoomArray's is: a map's lookups make several a call, and at -O1 each was a call. */
  /** @tsl.inline */
  // SAFETY: i is below len, so its slot is in the buffer.
  get(i: usize): T {
    if (i >= this.len) trap(Trap.Bounds);
    return this.slot(i).read();
  }

  /** `a[i] = v` below the length. Past it, `setLength` first, which is where JS's holes come from. */
  /** @tsl.inline */
  // SAFETY: i is below len, so its slot is in the buffer.
  set(i: usize, v: T): T {
    if (i >= this.len) trap(Trap.Bounds);
    this.slot(i).write(v);
    return v;
  }

  /**
   * Appends v and gives the new length, as JS's `push` does. R16: inlined at every level that inlines, as the direct
   * route's push is: with room left, a store and the length bumped; full, `pushGrow`, out of line.
   */
  /** @tsl.inline */
  // SAFETY: n is below cap, so the slot at n is in the buffer.
  push(v: T): usize {
    const n = this.len;
    if (n >= this.cap) return this.pushGrow(v);
    this.slot(n).write(v);
    const m = n + 1;
    this.len = m;
    return m;
  }

  /** `push` on a full array: the buffer doubled (`grow`), then the store. Out of line, so `push` stays small. */
  /** @tsl.noinline */
  // SAFETY: grow left room for one more, so the slot at len is in the buffer.
  private pushGrow(v: T): usize {
    const n = this.len;
    this.grow(n + 1);
    this.slot(n).write(v);
    const m = n + 1;
    this.len = m;
    return m;
  }

  /**
   * The last element, removed; on an empty array, `none`, and the array stays empty, as JS's `pop` gives `undefined`.
   * R17: inlined at every level that inlines, as `push` is; an array with no holes (`holes` false) only lowers its length,
   * as the direct route's pop is a store of it: n - 1 is below the room, and the slot it drops needn't be zeroed.
   */
  /** @tsl.inline */
  // SAFETY: n is above zero, so the slot at n - 1 is in the buffer.
  pop(none: T): T {
    const n = this.len;
    if (n === 0) return none;
    const v = this.slot(n - 1).read();
    if (this.holes) this.setLength(n - 1);
    else this.len = n - 1;
    return v;
  }

  /** The first element, removed, with every other moved down one; on an empty array, `none`, as JS's `shift`. */
  // SAFETY: n is above zero, so slots 0 to n - 1 are in the buffer, and the copy moves n - 1 of them down one.
```
