```ts
// file: ex-std-map.ts
import { Vec } from "@tsl/alloc";
import { toU32, Trap, trap, u32, u8, type bool, type usize } from "@tsl/core";
import { checkLive, heap, keyHash, keySame, mix, type ElemOf } from "./ex-std-global.ts";

const TOMB: u32 = 0xfffffffe;
const NONE: u32 = 0xffffffff;
const MIN_BUCKETS: usize = 4;

/**
 * A map where a missing key is a bug (D47): `get` traps 2 for one, as an index past the end does, and inserting, deleting or
 * clearing during `forEach` traps 13. A hash table in insertion order, arranged as compiler/rt/map.ts's tables are (D42):
 * keys and values in parallel vectors, and `heads` and `chain` a chained table of positions, with TOMB for what's deleted.
 * A key is an integer, a reference by identity, or a class with `hashKey` and `sameKey`, which `Str` has.
 */
export class ExactMap<K, V> {
  private keys: Vec<K>;
  private vals: Vec<V>;
  private chain: Vec<u32>;
  private heads: Vec<u32>;
  private count: usize = 0;
  private loans: usize = 0;
  private freed: bool = false;

  constructor(k: ElemOf<K>, v: ElemOf<V>) {
    this.keys = new Vec(k, heap);
    this.vals = new Vec(v, heap);
    this.chain = new Vec(u32, heap);
    this.heads = new Vec(u32, heap);
  }

  get size(): usize {
    return this.count;
  }

  // SAFETY: the hash can depend on an address. It only chooses a chain, and iteration is by position, so no result can.
  private hash(k: K): u32 {
    return mix(keyHash(k));
  }

  private find(k: K, h: u32): u32 {
    const b = this.heads.length;
    if (b === 0) return NONE;
    let i: u32 = this.heads.get((h & toU32(b - 1)) >>> 0);
    while (i !== NONE) {
      // SAFETY: comparing keys is a question about values: identity, or sameKey, which is the key's own method.
      if (keySame(this.keys.get(i), k)) return i;
      i = this.chain.get(i);
    }
    return NONE;
  }

  has(k: K): bool {
    return this.find(k, this.hash(k)) !== NONE;
  }

  /** Traps 2 if the key isn't there, as an index past the end does. */
  get(k: K): V {
    const i = this.find(k, this.hash(k));
    if (i === NONE) trap(Trap.Bounds);
    return this.vals.get(i);
  }

  getOr(k: K, otherwise: V): V {
    const i = this.find(k, this.hash(k));
    return i === NONE ? otherwise : this.vals.get(i);
  }

  set(k: K, v: V): void {
    if (!this.trySet(k, v)) trap(Trap.OutOfMemory);
  }

  /** False when out of memory, and the Map has the same entries. */
  trySet(k: K, v: V): bool {
    const h = this.hash(k);
    const i = this.find(k, h);
    if (i !== NONE) {
      this.vals.set(i, v);
      return true;
    }
    if (this.loans > 0) trap(Trap.Loan);
    if (this.keys.length >= this.heads.length && !this.grow()) return false;
    if (!this.keys.push(k)) return false;
    if (!this.vals.push(v)) {
      this.keys.pop();
      return false;
    }
    const b = (h & toU32(this.heads.length - 1)) >>> 0;
    if (!this.chain.push(this.heads.get(b))) {
      this.keys.pop();
      this.vals.pop();
      return false;
    }
    this.heads.set(b, toU32(this.keys.length - 1));
    this.count++;
    return true;
  }

  /** Full: drops what's deleted, and doubles if that doesn't free half. One operation, linear in the table, as D42's is. */
  private grow(): bool {
    const used = this.keys.length;
    const old = this.heads.length;
    let want = old;
    if (want === 0) want = MIN_BUCKETS;
    else if (this.count * 2 > used) want = want * 2;
    for (let i = old; i < want; i++) {
      if (!this.heads.push(NONE)) {
        for (let n = i; n > old; n--) this.heads.pop();
        return false;
      }
    }
    if (this.count < used) this.compact(used);
    for (let i: usize = 0; i < old; i++) this.heads.set(i, NONE);
    const mask = toU32(want - 1);
    const n = this.keys.length;
    for (let i: usize = 0; i < n; i++) {
      const b = (this.hash(this.keys.get(i)) & mask) >>> 0;
      this.chain.set(i, this.heads.get(b));
      this.heads.set(b, toU32(i));
    }
    return true;
  }

  private compact(used: usize): void {
    let to: usize = 0;
    for (let i: usize = 0; i < used; i++) {
      if (this.chain.get(i) === TOMB) continue;
      if (to !== i) {
        this.keys.set(to, this.keys.get(i));
        this.vals.set(to, this.vals.get(i));
      }
      to++;
    }
    for (let n = used; n > to; n--) {
      this.keys.pop();
      this.vals.pop();
      this.chain.pop();
    }
  }

  delete(k: K): bool {
    if (this.loans > 0) trap(Trap.Loan);
    const b = this.heads.length;
    if (b === 0) return false;
    const at = (this.hash(k) & toU32(b - 1)) >>> 0;
    let i: u32 = this.heads.get(at);
    let prev = NONE;
    while (i !== NONE) {
      const next = this.chain.get(i);
      // SAFETY: as in find.
      if (keySame(this.keys.get(i), k)) {
        if (prev === NONE) this.heads.set(at, next);
        else this.chain.set(prev, next);
        this.chain.set(i, TOMB);
        this.count--;
        return true;
      }
      prev = i;
      i = next;
    }
    return false;
  }

  /** In insertion order. Setting a key that's there is allowed: nothing moves. */
  forEach(f: (k: K, v: V) => void): void {
    this.loans++;
    const n = this.keys.length;
    for (let i: usize = 0; i < n; i++) {
      if (this.chain.get(i) === TOMB) continue;
      const k = this.keys.get(i);
      const v = this.vals.get(i);
      checkLive(k);
      checkLive(v);
      f(k, v);
    }
    this.loans--;
  }

  clear(): void {
    if (this.loans > 0) trap(Trap.Loan);
    for (let n = this.keys.length; n > 0; n--) {
      this.keys.pop();
      this.vals.pop();
      this.chain.pop();
    }
    for (let n = this.heads.length; n > 0; n--) this.heads.pop();
    this.count = 0;
  }

  free(): void {
    if (this.loans > 0) trap(Trap.Loan);
    this.freed = true;
    this.keys.free();
    this.vals.free();
    this.chain.free();
    this.heads.free();
  }

  dispose(): void {
    if (!this.freed) this.free();
  }

  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    this.dispose();
  }
}

/**
 * JS's `Map` (D47): `get` of a missing key gives `undefined`, and changing the map during `forEach` does what JS does. An
 * entry added is visited, one deleted before it's reached isn't, a value set before it's reached is the one seen, and after
 * `clear` what's added is visited. That needs a position to stay good while a `forEach` runs, so then nothing moves: a
 * growth doesn't compact, and `clear` leaves tombstones. The same table as ExactMap's otherwise.
 */
export class Map<K, V> {
  private keys: Vec<K>;
  private vals: Vec<V>;
  private chain: Vec<u32>;
  private heads: Vec<u32>;
  private count: usize = 0;
  private loans: usize = 0;
  private freed: bool = false;

  constructor(k: ElemOf<K>, v: ElemOf<V>) {
    this.keys = new Vec(k, heap);
    this.vals = new Vec(v, heap);
    this.chain = new Vec(u32, heap);
    this.heads = new Vec(u32, heap);
  }

  get size(): usize {
    return this.count;
  }

  // SAFETY: the hash can depend on an address. It only chooses a chain, and iteration is by position, so no result can.
  private hash(k: K): u32 {
    return mix(keyHash(k));
  }

  private find(k: K, h: u32): u32 {
    const b = this.heads.length;
    if (b === 0) return NONE;
    let i: u32 = this.heads.get((h & toU32(b - 1)) >>> 0);
    while (i !== NONE) {
      // SAFETY: comparing keys is a question about values: identity, or sameKey, which is the key's own method.
      if (keySame(this.keys.get(i), k)) return i;
      i = this.chain.get(i);
    }
    return NONE;
  }

  has(k: K): bool {
    return this.find(k, this.hash(k)) !== NONE;
  }

  /** `undefined` if the key isn't there. A scalar's is a flag and a value in registers, never in memory (3.3, rule 12). */
  get(k: K): V | undefined {
    const i = this.find(k, this.hash(k));
    if (i === NONE) return undefined;
    return this.vals.get(i);
  }

  getOr(k: K, otherwise: V): V {
    const i = this.find(k, this.hash(k));
    return i === NONE ? otherwise : this.vals.get(i);
  }

  set(k: K, v: V): void {
    if (!this.trySet(k, v)) trap(Trap.OutOfMemory);
  }

  /** False when out of memory, and the Map has the same entries. */
  trySet(k: K, v: V): bool {
    const h = this.hash(k);
    const i = this.find(k, h);
    if (i !== NONE) {
      this.vals.set(i, v);
      return true;
    }
    if (this.keys.length >= this.heads.length && !this.grow()) return false;
    if (!this.keys.push(k)) return false;
    if (!this.vals.push(v)) {
      this.keys.pop();
      return false;
    }
    const b = (h & toU32(this.heads.length - 1)) >>> 0;
    if (!this.chain.push(this.heads.get(b))) {
      this.keys.pop();
      this.vals.pop();
      return false;
    }
    this.heads.set(b, toU32(this.keys.length - 1));
    this.count++;
    return true;
  }

  /** Full: drops what's deleted, unless a forEach is running, and doubles if that doesn't free half. */
  private grow(): bool {
    const used = this.keys.length;
    const old = this.heads.length;
    const settled = this.loans === 0;
    let want = old;
    if (want === 0) want = MIN_BUCKETS;
    else if (this.count * 2 > used || !settled) want = want * 2;
    for (let i = old; i < want; i++) {
      if (!this.heads.push(NONE)) {
        for (let n = i; n > old; n--) this.heads.pop();
        return false;
      }
    }
    // Compacting leaves no tombstones, and `chain` stale: every link is made again. Without it, a tombstone stays one.
    const compacted = settled && this.count < used;
    if (compacted) this.compact(used);
    for (let i: usize = 0; i < old; i++) this.heads.set(i, NONE);
    const mask = toU32(want - 1);
    const n = this.keys.length;
    for (let i: usize = 0; i < n; i++) {
      if (!compacted && this.chain.get(i) === TOMB) continue;
      const b = (this.hash(this.keys.get(i)) & mask) >>> 0;
      this.chain.set(i, this.heads.get(b));
      this.heads.set(b, toU32(i));
    }
    return true;
  }

  private compact(used: usize): void {
    let to: usize = 0;
    for (let i: usize = 0; i < used; i++) {
      if (this.chain.get(i) === TOMB) continue;
      if (to !== i) {
        this.keys.set(to, this.keys.get(i));
        this.vals.set(to, this.vals.get(i));
      }
      to++;
    }
    for (let n = used; n > to; n--) {
      this.keys.pop();
      this.vals.pop();
      this.chain.pop();
    }
  }

  delete(k: K): bool {
    const b = this.heads.length;
    if (b === 0) return false;
    const at = (this.hash(k) & toU32(b - 1)) >>> 0;
    let i: u32 = this.heads.get(at);
    let prev = NONE;
    while (i !== NONE) {
      const next = this.chain.get(i);
      // SAFETY: as in find.
      if (keySame(this.keys.get(i), k)) {
        if (prev === NONE) this.heads.set(at, next);
        else this.chain.set(prev, next);
        this.chain.set(i, TOMB);
        this.count--;
        return true;
      }
      prev = i;
      i = next;
    }
    return false;
  }

  /** In insertion order, value first as JS has it, with what the callback adds, and without what it deletes first. */
  forEach(f: (v: V, k: K) => void): void {
    this.loans++;
    for (let i: usize = 0; i < this.keys.length; i++) {
      if (this.chain.get(i) === TOMB) continue;
      const k = this.keys.get(i);
      const v = this.vals.get(i);
      checkLive(k);
      checkLive(v);
      f(v, k);
    }
    this.loans--;
  }

  /** During a forEach, every entry becomes a tombstone, so its position still counts and what's added after is visited. */
  clear(): void {
    if (this.loans > 0) {
      for (let i: usize = 0; i < this.keys.length; i++) this.chain.set(i, TOMB);
      for (let i: usize = 0; i < this.heads.length; i++) this.heads.set(i, NONE);
      this.count = 0;
      return;
    }
    for (let n = this.keys.length; n > 0; n--) {
      this.keys.pop();
      this.vals.pop();
      this.chain.pop();
    }
    for (let n = this.heads.length; n > 0; n--) this.heads.pop();
    this.count = 0;
  }

  /** Not JS's: what a forEach is reading can't be freed under it, so that's trap 13. */
  free(): void {
    if (this.loans > 0) trap(Trap.Loan);
    this.freed = true;
    this.keys.free();
    this.vals.free();
    this.chain.free();
    this.heads.free();
  }

  dispose(): void {
    if (!this.freed) this.free();
  }

  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    this.dispose();
  }
}

/**
 * JS's `Set` (D47): a Map with a byte for a value, so changing it during `forEach` does what JS does. There's no trapping set:
 * with no `get` to miss, it would differ only there. `compiler/rt/map.ts` has no value slots for a Set, and that's not worth
 * a second table here.
 */
export class Set<K> {
  private m: Map<K, u8>;

  constructor(k: ElemOf<K>) {
    this.m = new Map(k, u8);
  }

  get size(): usize {
    return this.m.size;
  }

  has(k: K): bool {
    return this.m.has(k);
  }

  add(k: K): void {
    this.m.set(k, 1);
  }

  tryAdd(k: K): bool {
    return this.m.trySet(k, 1);
  }

  delete(k: K): bool {
    return this.m.delete(k);
  }

  forEach(f: (k: K) => void): void {
    this.m.forEach((_v, k) => {
      f(k);
    });
  }

  clear(): void {
    this.m.clear();
  }

  free(): void {
    this.m.free();
  }

  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    this.m.dispose();
  }
}
```

`Str` and `StrBuilder`:

```ts
// file: ex-std-str.ts
import { Slab as AllocSlab, Vec as AllocVec } from "@tsl/alloc";
import { idiv, toI32, Trap, trap, u8, wrapU32, wrapU8, type bool, type i32, type u32, type usize } from "@tsl/core";
import { heap, hashKeyWord } from "./ex-std-global.ts";
import type { Vec } from "./ex-std-vec.ts";

/**
 * A run-time string: immutable UTF-8 bytes in a slot of a Slab of its own, so it can be stored and returned in `strict`,
 * and every stored reference to it traps 5 once it's freed. Reading is by byte, as lit() gives UTF-8.
 */
export class Str {
  private b: AllocVec<u8> = new AllocVec(u8, heap);
  private hashed: bool = false;
  private h: u32 = 0;

  /** Copies the bytes. Traps 14 out of memory. */
  static of(bytes: Uint8Array): Str {
    const s = Str.tryOf(bytes);
    if (s === null) trap(Trap.OutOfMemory);
    return s;
  }

  /** Null when out of memory. */
  static tryOf(bytes: Uint8Array): Str | null {
    const s = strs.add(new Str());
    if (s === null) return null;
    for (const x of bytes) {
      if (!s.b.push(x)) {
        s.free();
        return null;
      }
    }
    return s;
  }

  /** A copy of a Vec's bytes, which is what a builder has. */
  static ofVec(v: AllocVec<u8>): Str {
    const s = strs.add(new Str());
    if (s === null) trap(Trap.OutOfMemory);
    v.withSlice((a) => {
      s.pushBytes(a);
    });
    return s;
  }

  private pushBytes(a: Uint8Array): void {
    for (const x of a) {
      if (!this.b.push(x)) trap(Trap.OutOfMemory);
    }
  }

  get length(): usize {
    return this.b.length;
  }

  at(i: usize): u8 {
    return this.b.get(i);
  }

  /** The bytes, lent: the slice can't be stored or outlive the call, and `free` during it traps 13. */
  withBytes(f: (s: Uint8Array) => void): void {
    this.b.withSlice(f);
  }

  equals(o: Str): bool {
    return this.b.length === o.b.length && this.compare(o) === 0;
  }

  /** By byte, then by length, which is UTF-8's order of code points. */
  compare(o: Str): i32 {
    const n = this.b.length;
    const m = o.b.length;
    const shortest = n < m ? n : m;
    let out: i32 = 0;
    this.withBytes((a) => {
      o.withBytes((c) => {
        for (let i: usize = 0; i < shortest && out === 0; i++) {
          if (a[i]! !== c[i]!) out = a[i]! < c[i]! ? -1 : 1;
        }
      });
    });
    if (out !== 0) return out;
    if (n === m) return 0;
    return n < m ? -1 : 1;
  }

  /** From start up to end, copied. Traps 2 if that's not within it. */
  slice(start: usize, end: usize): Str {
    if (start > end || end > this.b.length) trap(Trap.Bounds);
    const s = strs.add(new Str());
    if (s === null) trap(Trap.OutOfMemory);
    this.withBytes((a) => {
      s.pushBytes(a.subarray(start, end));
    });
    return s;
  }

  concat(o: Str): Str {
    const s = strs.add(new Str());
    if (s === null) trap(Trap.OutOfMemory);
    this.withBytes((a) => {
      s.pushBytes(a);
    });
    o.withBytes((a) => {
      s.pushBytes(a);
    });
    return s;
  }

  /** The first place o is, from `from` on, or -1. The naive search, so O(n·m) on a bad input. */
  indexOf(o: Str, from: usize): i32 {
    const n = this.b.length;
    const m = o.b.length;
    if (m === 0) return from <= n ? toI32(from) : -1;
    let out: i32 = -1;
    this.withBytes((a) => {
      o.withBytes((c) => {
        for (let i = from; i + m <= n && out < 0; i++) {
          let j: usize = 0;
          while (j < m && a[i + j]! === c[j]!) j++;
          if (j === m) out = toI32(i);
        }
      });
    });
    return out;
  }

  /** Each run between `sep`s goes in `out` as a new Str, empty runs too. */
  split(sep: u8, out: Vec<Str>): void {
    const n = this.b.length;
    let start: usize = 0;
    for (let i: usize = 0; i <= n; i++) {
      if (i === n || this.b.get(i) === sep) {
        out.push(this.slice(start, i));
        start = i + 1;
      }
    }
  }

  /** HalfSipHash-1-3 (D42), under the same key as other keys, and kept: a Str doesn't change. */
  hashKey(): u32 {
    if (!this.hashed) {
      this.h = halfSip13(this);
      this.hashed = true;
    }
    return this.h;
  }

  sameKey(o: Str): bool {
    return this.equals(o);
  }

  /** Gives back its bytes and its slot. Every stored reference to it traps 5 from now on. */
  free(): void {
    this.b.free();
    strs.remove(this);
  }

  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    this.free();
  }
}

const strs = new AllocSlab<Str>(heap, 32);

function halfSip13(s: Str): u32 {
  const k0 = hashKeyWord(0);
  const k1 = hashKeyWord(1);
  let v0: u32 = k0;
  let v1: u32 = k1;
  let v2: u32 = (0x6c796765 ^ k0) >>> 0;
  let v3: u32 = (0x74656462 ^ k1) >>> 0;
  const round = (): void => {
    v0 = (v0 + v1) >>> 0;
    v1 = ((v1 << 5) | (v1 >>> 27)) >>> 0;
    v1 = (v1 ^ v0) >>> 0;
    v0 = ((v0 << 16) | (v0 >>> 16)) >>> 0;
    v2 = (v2 + v3) >>> 0;
    v3 = ((v3 << 8) | (v3 >>> 24)) >>> 0;
    v3 = (v3 ^ v2) >>> 0;
    v0 = (v0 + v3) >>> 0;
    v3 = ((v3 << 7) | (v3 >>> 25)) >>> 0;
    v3 = (v3 ^ v0) >>> 0;
    v2 = (v2 + v1) >>> 0;
    v1 = ((v1 << 13) | (v1 >>> 19)) >>> 0;
    v1 = (v1 ^ v2) >>> 0;
    v2 = ((v2 << 16) | (v2 >>> 16)) >>> 0;
  };
  let word: u32 = 0;
  let shift: u32 = 0;
  s.withBytes((a) => {
    for (const x of a) {
      word = (word | (x << shift)) >>> 0;
      shift += 8;
      if (shift === 32) {
        v3 = (v3 ^ word) >>> 0;
        round();
        v0 = (v0 ^ word) >>> 0;
        word = 0;
        shift = 0;
      }
    }
  });
  word = (word | (wrapU32(s.length) << 24)) >>> 0;
  v3 = (v3 ^ word) >>> 0;
  round();
  v0 = (v0 ^ word) >>> 0;
  v2 = (v2 ^ 0xff) >>> 0;
  round();
  round();
  round();
  return (v1 ^ v3) >>> 0;
}

/** Text made a piece at a time: a growable buffer, which `finish` copies once, so appending isn't quadratic. */
export class StrBuilder {
  private b: AllocVec<u8> = new AllocVec(u8, heap);
  private freed: bool = false;

  get length(): usize {
    return this.b.length;
  }

  appendByte(x: u8): void {
    if (!this.b.push(x)) trap(Trap.OutOfMemory);
  }

  appendBytes(a: Uint8Array): void {
    for (const x of a) this.appendByte(x);
  }

  append(s: Str): void {
    s.withBytes((a) => {
      this.appendBytes(a);
    });
  }

  /** False when out of memory, with as much appended as fitted. */
  tryAppendBytes(a: Uint8Array): bool {
    for (const x of a) {
      if (!this.b.push(x)) return false;
    }
    return true;
  }

  /** In decimal. */
  appendU32(x: u32): void {
    if (x >= 10) this.appendU32(idiv(x, 10));
    this.appendByte(wrapU8(48 + x % 10));
  }

  appendI32(x: i32): void {
    if (x < 0) this.appendByte(45);
    this.appendU32(x < 0 ? ((~x >>> 0) + 1) >>> 0 : x >>> 0); // -x overflows at the least i32
  }

  /** A new Str with what's been appended, and the builder can go on. Traps 14 out of memory. */
  finish(): Str {
    return Str.ofVec(this.b);
  }

  free(): void {
    this.freed = true;
    this.b.free();
  }

  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    if (!this.freed) this.free();
  }
}
```

### 3.6 What TSL allows and bans

**Allowed:** `function`, arrow functions and classes as described in 3.4 and 3.5; `const`/`let`; `if`, `for`,
`while`, `do`, `switch` on
integers, enums, literal unions or tags; `for…of` over typed arrays (containers use `forEach` and indexed
loops, because the iterator protocol would need an escaping object); labelled `break`/`continue`; `?.` and
`??` on nullable references (`?.` gives `undefined` in JS, which isn't a value here, so it must be read at once by `??` or `!`, or
stand as a statement; otherwise TSL1008), and
`!` (traps with code 6 on null); destructuring of value records and of scalar fields; `import`/`export` of
named bindings; type aliases; generics monomorphised with `T` bound to a scalar or an object type (`Scalar` in
Appendix A is the layout-helper type, not a constraint) (limit of 128 instantiations per function, TSL4001, a guard against the generics blow-up
Midori reported [P3]); `using` on arenas and on any class with a `[Symbol.dispose]()` method;
JS typed arrays as slices; `Math.imul/clz32/fround/floor/ceil/trunc/sqrt/abs/min/max` on scalars (`imul` yields
`i32`, `clz32` yields `u8`, `fround` yields `f32`, `floor/ceil/trunc/sqrt` take a float and yield `f64`, and
`abs/min/max` keep an integer's type).

Two array literals are constant data, not plain `Array`s, and only at the top level: the elements of a static typed
array (`const K = new Uint32Array([0x428a2f98, …])`, which becomes initialised bytes) and a dispatch table of
non-generic top-level functions (`const OPS: readonly BinOp[] = [add, sub]`, read as `OPS[i]!`, TIR-lowered to a
helper switching on the index).

**Strings exist only at compile time and in logs**, and a run-time string is `Str`, a class in `@tsl/std` (3.5). A string literal is allowed as a literal-union value, as
an argument of a compile-time built-in
(`lit("...")`, `offsetOf(T, "x")`, `atomic.*(r, "field", …)`), and as a value-union discriminant. A template
literal is allowed only as the direct argument of `log()` or `panic()`,
with holes that are integers, bools, enums or literal unions. `lit("...")` can be written anywhere: its bytes are static data, one copy per text (D43). It was top-level only before. Natively these format into a fixed stack buffer
with no allocation and write to a sink set by `setLogSink`.

**Banned, with stable codes:**

| Code | Construct | Reason, or what to use |
|------|-----------|------------------------|
| TSL1001 | Any inheritance (`extends`; `implements` is a check only, D70), `abstract`, `new` of a typed array inside a function | No dynamic dispatch and no hidden allocation. A dispatch interface (3.4, D70) for calls to one of several classes |
| TSL1003 | `any`, `unknown`, `as` on anything except numeric-to-`number` | Types must be exact to compile statically |
| TSL1004 | `throw`, `try`, `catch`, `finally` | They need unwinding. `Result` values, `trap(code)`, `panic(msg)` |
| TSL1005 | Object literals outside value records, and so an object literal with methods given where a dispatch interface goes (D70) | `new`, or `make(T, …)`; a class with the methods |
| TSL1006 | Plain `Array`, JS's own `Map` and `Set`, `Object.*`, `JSON`, `Reflect`, `Proxy`, and `Symbol` other than `Symbol.dispose` | They need a runtime or hidden allocation. `Vec`, `Slab`, typed arrays, and `Map` and `Set` imported from `@tsl/std`, which are ordinary classes |
| TSL1007 | Runtime `string`, template literals outside `log` and `panic` | `lit`, `Uint8Array` |
| TSL1008 | `undefined`, and `null` except on references or to test a nullable scalar (3.3, rule 12) | Sentinels, `Result` |
| TSL1009 | `async`, generators, `yield`, `await`, dynamic `import`, `eval`, `with`, `var`, `delete` | They need a runtime, or defeat static compilation |
| TSL1010 | Non-constant top-level initialisers; module cycles | No run-time module init (a Midori code-size lesson [P3]) |
| TSL1011 | Namespaces, decorators, `const enum`, string enums, reverse enum mapping, `#private` | No static meaning worth its cost |
| TSL1012 | Recursion in `@tsl.noalloc` paths | Bounded stack |
| TSL1013 | Float types or ops in a package with `"noFloat": true` | Integer maths |
| TSL1018 | Importing `@tsl/std` in a package with `"noStd": true`, or in anything such a package imports, however far down and in whoever's package (D38). It's checked before `tsc`, by the specifier, by the path `tsl-std` and by the file `tsc` resolved it to | `Vec`, `Slab`, typed arrays, from `@tsl/alloc` |
| TSL1020 | `@tsl.global-allocator` on anything but a top-level `const h = globalAllocator(f)`, or a `globalAllocator` call with no tag or not at the top level (3.5, D43) | Write it as 3.5 does |
| TSL1021 | A second `@tsl.global-allocator` in a program, counting every module it imports. Reported at the second, naming the first | One allocator. Without one, it's the default over the page source |
| TSL1022 | `tmk lower` of a module importing `@tsl/std`, which is TSL proper's | JS's own `Map`, `Set` and strings (D42) |
| TSL1023 | Importing `@tsl/lowered`, or a module of a lowered package, from a package whose tsl.json has no `"lowered"`; a `"lowered"` block beside another package setting, `"unsafeModules"` included (R18: so no module of a lowered package can import `@tsl/unsafe`, which is TSL5001 without the listing); and misuse of `@tsl/lowered`'s forms (D62) | Only `tmk lower` writes lowered TSL: compile the ordinary TS |
| TSL1019 | A `tsl.json` setting with a value it can't have: `"memory"` other than `strict`, `leak`, `manual` or `rc`, or `"noStd"` not a boolean. Reported at the value in `tsl.json` | Fix the setting |
| TSL3003 | A capturing closure stored or returned (3.5), and a slice given to a closure kept in a local outside it (D43) | Pass it down. Use the slice in the closure |
| TSL3009 | A local read after it was consumed by a `@tsl.moves` parameter of a handle type (`@tsl.handle`, such as `@tsl/gc`'s `Counted<T>`), on some path, before it was assigned again (3.5, D63). Reported at the read, naming the move | `share` it first if both need it |
| TSL3010 | A dispatch interface (3.4, D70) whose classes can't be told from the program: a value flowing into it from a type parameter, from another interface (even one of the same shape), or of anything but a class instance; a generic class reaching it; or nothing reaching it at all. Reported at the place the value flows in, at the generic class, or at the first use | Give it objects of plain, non-generic classes, of the class's own type where they flow in |
| TSL3008 | A raw reference from a `manual` package stored in a field or global of a `strict` or `leak` package, directly or through calls | A safe API that hands out values |
| TSL1014 | A constructor on a layout class | `make(T, …)` |
| TSL1015 | A class mixing layout-helper fields with plain fields, or a plain class used where a layout class is needed | Every byte is declared |
| TSL1024 | A tail (`units = tail(u16)`, 3.4, D69) that isn't its class's last field, a second tail, a tail of anything but a scalar (`be16` and the like included), a tail in a layout class or a generic class, and `tail()` used as a value. Reported at the field, or at the call | One tail of scalars, declared last, in a plain class |
| TSL1025 | A dispatch interface (3.4, D70) that's generic, extends another, or has a generic or optional method or one taking a function; a class reaching one whose method isn't a method of its objects, is generic, or takes or gives other TSL types than the interface's (`u32` for `usize`, fewer parameters), or a layout class reaching one; and a dispatch interface's method read as a value. Reported at the declaration, the class's method or the read | Say the interface's types exactly in each class; call the method |
| TSL1026 | A numeric literal given as the code of `trap`, of `assert` (D72), or of `@tsl/lowered`'s `trapNow` or `builtin("assert", …)` (3.10, D71), parenthesised or signed included, and in a lowered package's `assert` anything but a member of `Trap` (`cast<i32>(2)` too); the enum or constant that names it is where the number goes. Reported at the literal. A TSL error, not an audit finding: tslc sees every call, the printer's output included, at every compile | `trap(Trap.Bounds)`; a program's own code, from 1000, by its own enum or constant |
| TSL3011 | An object of a class with a tail used where TSL copies or lays out by a fixed size: moved into a `@tsl.moves` parameter not tagged `@tsl.tailed` (`Slab.add`, `Rc.make`), held in place by a field (D37), `nested`, `arrayOf`, `set`, `make`, `over`, `viewAt`, `sizeOf`, `alignOf`, an arena's `make`, `placeObject` and an inline `Ptr.write` (D69). Reported at the argument or the field | Hold it by reference. `withTail(n, new T())`, or an `Rc` store's `makeTail` |
| TSL3012 | Making an object of a class with a tail any way but `withTail(n, new T(…))` or a move into a `@tsl.tailed` parameter: a plain `new`, a static one, `withTail` given anything but a direct `new` of such a class, `withTail` in a `strict` package, which has no heap; and a constructor reading its own class's tail (D69) | `withTail` in a `leak` or `manual` package; an `Rc` store's `makeTail` anywhere. Fill the tail after it's made |
| TSL2006 | An expression whose type doesn't widen to its target | `tsc` sees `number`, so only tslc can catch it. `toX`, `wrapX`, `>>> 0`, `Math.fround` |
| TSL2007 | A condition that isn't `bool` | Truthiness of `0`, `NaN` and `0n` has no place in a typed condition. Compare explicitly |
| TSL2013 | `~` on a `u64` outside a wrap context | `BigInt.asUintN(64, ~x)` |
| TSL1016 | `assertSize` or `@tsl.size` disagreeing with the layout | Fix the layout or the size |
| TSL1017 | A `@tsl.noalloc` path reaching `arenaOver`, or a call through a function value held in memory, directly or through callees, which is what anything calling a `PageSource` does | The error names the chain. Pass the function as a parameter, which the caller's closure is checked with |
| TSL9001 | A construct TSL allows but this milestone's compiler doesn't implement yet | Temporary by design. M1 uses it for classes, closures, `isize` and the like. In an `rc` package, what the expansion can't write out yet (D74) |

An indexed read must be `a[i]!` (traps if out of bounds) or `a[i]` narrowed by `=== undefined`. V8 returns
`undefined` out of bounds where native traps
under `!`. This is an allowed divergence (3.10). Writes out of bounds trap in TSL, whereas V8 ignores them.
Same allowed-divergence rule. Down-lowering treats
unasserted writes differently (see 4.5).

An escaping allocation needs a declared memory mode (D28, D38, 3.5). In a `strict` package, which is the default, it's a compile
error that says what blocked it and suggests a `Slab` or `Vec`, or a mode.

### 3.7 Function attributes

Attributes are JSDoc tags, because decorators aren't erasable. tslc verifies them transitively.

| Tag | Meaning |
|-----|---------|
| `@tsl.noalloc` | No heap, slab, arena or frame-allocator allocation, no recursion, and no callee that does. Stack `new` and non-escaping closures are allowed. Required on trap and IRQ paths. The compiler knows no container, so what counts as allocating is `arenaOver` and a call through a function value in memory, which is what reaches a `PageSource`: `Slab.add` and `Vec.push` fail, and `Slab.remove` and `Vec.get` pass (TSL1017). |
| `@tsl.nosleep` | Doesn't block. Implied in trap context. |
| `@tsl.inline`, `@tsl.noinline` | At `-O1` and `-O2`, `@tsl.inline` is always inlined where the inliner may inline at all, up to a hard limit on size, and `@tsl.noinline` never is (D46). Neither changes what a program does, and at `-O0` neither does anything. On a function, a method or (R16) a constructor |
| `@tsl.export-c name` | Fixed AAPCS64 calling convention, exported with that symbol name, so assembly can call it |
| `@tsl.section name` | Places the function in a named section |
| `@tsl.size n` | On a plain class: tslc checks its size |
| `@tsl.moves p` | Parameter `p`'s object is copied into place, so the argument must be a direct `new` or `make`, or the caller's own moved parameter |
| `@tsl.global-allocator` | On a top-level `const h = globalAllocator(f)`: `@tsl/std`'s allocator is over `f` (3.5, D43). At most one in a program (TSL1021), in an unsafe module |
| `@tsl.sharedSlots` | On a class whose methods place objects (`placeObject`, `placeTail`) in slots another class may hold later, as `@tsl/gc`'s `Rc` does (3.5, R1b): every use of a reference to a class it places is checked, wherever the reference came from, but where every count of the class is the `rc` expansion's (D74). Placing is unsafe, so it means something only in an audited module |
| `@tsl.links l... < b...` | On a class (R29, D79): its fields `l`, `JsArray`s of `u32` held in place, hold links (2 to 2^31 - 1, naming position link - 2), each below the length of every field `b`. A claim tslc proves over every write to them, or refuses, and which changes nothing a program does: where proved, a `JsArray` read whose index it shows in bounds loses its check at -O1 and -O2 (3.5) |

### 3.8 Unsafe boundary

- Unsafe primitives (`Ptr`, `ptrAt`, `viewAt`, `staticView`, `bytesAt`, `sliceOf`, `copyBytes`, `addrOf`,
  `mmioAt`, `placeObject` and its relatives, `unsafeFree`, `setPageSource`, `sourcePages`, `pageRunFreed`, `onPageRunFreed`, `keyHash`, `keySame`, `fnAddr`, `asmFn`, `setLogSink`) exist only in `@tsl/unsafe`.
  `@tsl/alloc` is built with them and exports a safe API, and so is `@tsl/std`, with one unsafe module, the global allocator's, of 72 LOC; `JsArray`'s buffer (D66) is an unsafe module of `@tsl/jsrt` since D71, beside `JsString`'s. Its `Map` calls `keyHash`, which can depend on an address, and it's not unsafe for that: it shows nothing that depends on one, which is what 3.8's last point asks, and memory safety doesn't rest on a hash.
- Privileged intrinsics exist only in `@tsl/arch-aarch64`.
- A package with `"memory": "manual"` is unsafe code all through: every module in it must be listed under `"unsafeModules"` (TSL5006),
  and `tmk audit` counts it, wherever it is. `unsafeFree` is only for such a package (TSL5007), and takes only what its heap allocated (TSL5008).
  A package with `"memory": "leak"` needs none of this. Registering a page source is unsafe, wherever the allocation is: `setPageSource`
  takes a top-level function by name (TSL5009), and that function is trusted to return what it promises. Naming a global allocator is the same trust, so its module must be listed too (TSL5001), and its argument is a top-level function by name (TSL5009).
- `kernel-core` stays `"memory": "strict"` by policy, as do drivers (5.6, D38).
- A module may import either only if its path is listed in its package's `tsl.json` under `"unsafeModules"`,
  otherwise TSL5001. Enforce with tslc **and** with
  `no-restricted-imports` in oxlint.
- Every call to an unsafe primitive must have a preceding `// SAFETY:` comment, otherwise TSL5002. The comment may be on the
  statement holding the call or on anything around it, up to the function or class member, so one comment can give the reason for
  one function. `Ptr`'s methods count. `ref`, `inlineOf`, `elemSize` and `checkLive` don't: the first three are descriptors, and `checkLive` traps or does nothing, so none is a memory operation.
- `tmk audit` prints unsafe modules, unsafe LOC as a share of total (including `@tsl/alloc` where it's linked
  at EL1), privileged intrinsic uses by function, and assembly LOC including `asmFn` bodies. S8 is checked
  from
  this output.
- A safe API exported from an unsafe module has the same trust as the kernel. Keep these modules small.
  Asterinas's framekernel is the benchmark for this: it reports its
  TCB as 14.0% of its codebase, against 43.8% for Tock, 62.4% for Theseus and 66.1% for RedLeaf (self-reported) [P8].
- Unsafe code doesn't write an object's class id, or a field tslc found nothing writes after construction (3.4's "Class ids
  don't change"), while the object lives: those are the compiler's, and the optimiser reads one once (D73). Forging an
  object in memory no object holds, as `dispatch_forged.ts` does, isn't that.
- **Addresses are unobservable in safe code.** JS has no way to obtain one, so no safe program's results can
  depend on where anything lives. That's what leaves the compiler
  free to place things. `addrOf` takes only a layout-class object in host-visible memory, from `viewAt` or
  `staticView` (TSL5005). On the host, addresses point into simulated memory, or come
  from a registry in `fnAddr`'s case, so anything that depends on real addresses (page tables taking effect,
  `VBAR` contents) is only tested under QEMU.

### 3.9 Hardware access: MMIO, barriers, atomics, interrupts, assembly

**MMIO** uses typed register descriptors. A read of a write-only register or a write of a read-only one is a
`tsc` error (MEASURED). tslc compiles `read`/`write` to one naturally
aligned single-copy-atomic `ldr`/`str` of the declared width, never merged, split, elided or reordered
relative to other device accesses on the same thread. Registers stay explicit
calls, because a device access should look like one, and `bits` isn't available on them because it would hide
a read-modify-write. The register offsets below are from virtio 1.2
section 4.2.2 [P1].

```ts
// file: ex-mmio.ts
import { mmio, reg, type MmioRef, type Result, type u32, type u64 } from "@tsl/core";
import { mmioAt } from "@tsl/unsafe";

export const VirtioMmioRegs = mmio(0x200, {
  magic: reg.ro32(0x000),
  version: reg.ro32(0x004),
  deviceId: reg.ro32(0x008),
  vendorId: reg.ro32(0x00c),
  deviceFeatures: reg.ro32(0x010),
  deviceFeaturesSel: reg.wo32(0x014),
  driverFeatures: reg.wo32(0x020),
  driverFeaturesSel: reg.wo32(0x024),
  queueSel: reg.wo32(0x030),
  queueNumMax: reg.ro32(0x034),
  queueNum: reg.wo32(0x038),
  queueReady: reg.rw32(0x044),
  queueNotify: reg.wo32(0x050),
  interruptStatus: reg.ro32(0x060),
  interruptAck: reg.wo32(0x064),
  status: reg.rw32(0x070),
  queueDescLow: reg.wo32(0x080),
  queueDescHigh: reg.wo32(0x084),
  queueDriverLow: reg.wo32(0x090),
  queueDriverHigh: reg.wo32(0x094),
  queueDeviceLow: reg.wo32(0x0a0),
  queueDeviceHigh: reg.wo32(0x0a4),
  configGeneration: reg.ro32(0x0fc),
});
export type VirtioMmio = MmioRef<typeof VirtioMmioRegs>;

const VIRTIO_MAGIC: u32 = 0x74726976; // "virt", MEASURED on QEMU

export type ProbeError = "bad-magic" | "bad-version" | "empty-slot";

export function probeDevice(base: u64): Result<u32, ProbeError> {
  // SAFETY: base came from the Mmio capability granted to this domain, and is 0x200 bytes long.
  const regs = mmioAt(VirtioMmioRegs, base);
  if (regs.magic.read() !== VIRTIO_MAGIC) return { ok: false, error: "bad-magic" };
  if (regs.version.read() !== 2) return { ok: false, error: "bad-version" }; // QEMU needs force-legacy=false
  const id = regs.deviceId.read();
  if (id === 0) return { ok: false, error: "empty-slot" };
  return { ok: true, value: id };
}
```

**Barriers and atomics.**

- Memory is normal WB inner-shareable. `atomic.load/store/fetchAdd/cas(ref, "field", …, order)` apply to a
  scalar field of a layout class with natural alignment. Orderings: `relaxed`, `acquire`,
  `release`, `seqcst`.
- On AArch64: `ldar`/`stlr` for acquire/release, LSE instructions if present (fold from `ID_AA64ISAR0`),
  otherwise LL/SC loops.
- The QEMU `virt` DTB marks virtio-mmio nodes `dma-coherent` (MEASURED), so virtqueue memory uses normal
  cacheable mappings with `dmb ish`-class barriers. This follows the virtio specification's memory-barrier requirements [P1] and hasn't been separately verified; test it under TCG and HVF. Real hardware
  without coherent DMA needs `dcCvac`/`dcIvac` and is out of scope until M12.

**Non-atomic races give an unspecified value, never undefined behaviour.** The compiler must not assume
data-race freedom in ways that break safety. In particular, a bounds-checked index or
length is loaded **once**, never rematerialised from memory after its check. Because memory can only contain
scalars and single-word references (no fat pointers), a race can't forge a
reference or tear one.

**Interrupts and traps.** The vector table and register save/restore are assembly. Each entry calls a function
tagged `@tsl.noalloc @tsl.nosleep @tsl.export-c`, like `trapSyncLower` below. IRQs
are acknowledged and masked by the kernel, then delivered to the owning domain as a notification. Driver logic
never runs in interrupt context.

**Function addresses.** `fnAddr(f)` returns a function's address as a `u64`, for `VBAR_EL1`, thread entry
points and PSCI `CPU_ON`. It accepts only `@tsl.export-c` and `asmFn` functions
(TSL5003), because any other function uses an internal calling convention that may change. An `@tsl.export-c`
function that's reached this way must also be `@tsl.noalloc @tsl.nosleep`. On a
PC-relative build it returns the address at the current mapping, so don't store one taken before the MMU is on.

**Assembly-bodied functions.** `asmFn` declares a function whose whole body is assembly, with a typed
signature and AAPCS64 arguments. It's for code that can't be compiled safely, because it
swaps the stack and registers that the compiler is using or needs exact placement: vector tables, context
switches, register save and restore. The body must be a template literal with no holes (TSL5004).
Because the compiler never allocates registers inside one, there's no constraints or clobbers language. The
body goes through the same assembler and the same `bincheck` rules as `.s` files, so each privileged
instruction stays attributable to a named function. On the host, `asmFn` returns a stub that a test replaces
with `hostStub`, or that traps with code 12.

```ts
// file: ex-entry.ts
import { array, assertSize, u64 } from "@tsl/core";
import { asmFn, fnAddr } from "@tsl/unsafe";
import { writeVbarEl1 } from "@tsl/arch-aarch64";

export class TrapFrame {
  regs = array(u64, 31); // x0..x30
  spEl0 = u64();
  elr = u64();
  spsr = u64();
}
assertSize(TrapFrame, 272);

export const switchContext = asmFn<(from: u64, to: u64) => void>`
  stp x19, x20, [x0, #0]
  stp x21, x22, [x0, #16]
  stp x23, x24, [x0, #32]
  stp x25, x26, [x0, #48]
  stp x27, x28, [x0, #64]
  stp x29, x30, [x0, #80]
  mov x9, sp
  str x9, [x0, #96]
  ldp x19, x20, [x1, #0]
  ldp x21, x22, [x1, #16]
  ldp x23, x24, [x1, #32]
  ldp x25, x26, [x1, #48]
  ldp x27, x28, [x1, #64]
  ldp x29, x30, [x1, #80]
  ldr x9, [x1, #96]
  mov sp, x9
  ret
`;

export const vectors = asmFn<() => never>`
  .balign 2048
  // 16 slots of 128 bytes: each saves registers into a TrapFrame and calls a handler
  .space 2048
`;

export let lastSyndrome: u64 = 0n;

/** @tsl.noalloc @tsl.nosleep @tsl.export-c trap_sync_lower */
export function trapSyncLower(frame: TrapFrame): void {
  lastSyndrome = frame.spsr;
}

export function installVectors(): void {
  // SAFETY: vectors is part of this image and aligned to 2 KiB.
  writeVbarEl1(fnAddr(vectors));
}
```

**Inline assembly: none in v1 (D10).** Assembly mixed into a compiled function would need a constraints and
clobbers language in the register allocator, the C backend and `bincheck`, and the kernel's hard cases
can't use it safely anyway. `@tsl/arch-aarch64` is a **closed list** of named intrinsics, each one instruction
with fixed encoding, and these compile inline. To add one, add a named intrinsic and a backend encoding.
The list is in Appendix A. True inline assembly stays available as a future extension if a measured need
appears, such as the IPC fast path at M6, and adding it later breaks nothing.

Plain `.s` files remain only for code that runs before any compiled code exists: `boot0`, `start.s` and the seed chain.

**`.s` and `asmFn` dialect (normative):** the subset accepted by both `llvm-mc` and tslc's own assembler.
Labels, numeric local labels, `.global .section .text .data .balign .word .quad .ascii .asciz .space .ltorg`,
`ldr xN, =imm`, base A64
instructions, `//` comments, and system registers by name or `s3_0_cX_cY_Z` form. No macros, conditionals or
includes, which keeps the seed chain's `asm2` small.

### 3.10 The refinement contract and allowed divergences

Let `N(P)` be `P` compiled by tslc, `V(P)` be `P` on V8 with host `@tsl/*`, and `C(P)` be `P` compiled with
`--emit=js-checked` on V8. For all inputs, if `N(P)` doesn't trap, `N(P)` and `V(P)` have identical
observable results (return values, bytes written to simulated memory, MMIO sequence). If `N(P)` traps with
code `c`, `C(P)` traps with code `c`.

`V(P)` runs the source through `tools/ts-hook.mjs` on Node (3.1) and directly on Bun. Neither path involves
any tslc code, which is what keeps V8 and JSC independent oracles.

Allowed divergences, and only these:

1. Traps as above (`V` keeps going with an out-of-range value or `undefined`, or throws a `TypeError` on null). This includes a trap inside a `using` scope
   whose dispose traps too, such as `push` during a `withSlice` under `using`: `V` runs the dispose while unwinding and reports a `SuppressedError`, and `N` traps once with the first code and doesn't run it.
2. NaN payload bits.
3. `usize` above 2³² on wasm32.
4. Stack overflow, memory exhaustion and timing.
5. Access through a local reference after its object was removed from a slab, where the reference was known to be live when obtained
   (3.5): `V` traps with code 5, and `N` reads stale, well-typed data, or writes to whatever now occupies the slot.
6. The values of `addrOf` and `fnAddr`, which are simulated on the host.
7. Accepted by the owner on 2026-11-03, delegated to the author. The last bit of a JS `Math` function with no TIR operation (`math.*` in 4.3). `V` itself isn't one function here (MEASURED
   2026-11-03): V8 on arm64 is fdlibm compiled with fused multiplies, so it differs from V8 on x86-64, and V8 and JSC disagree on
   4 to 10% of random `sin`, `cos`, `exp`, `log` and `atan2` results, and V8's `Math.pow` is the host's libm. So agreement in the
   last bit is against V8 on the development host, for those five exactly, and for `pow` within one unit in the last place, exact
   when the result is exactly representable. Corpus programs that also run on JSC use only values on which the engines agree.
8. Use after `unsafeFree`, in a `manual` package (D38). `V` poisons the object, so any access traps with code 5, as does freeing it twice, and `N` is a
   real bug: it reads or writes whatever now occupies the block. This is why `manual` isn't safe, and why its modules are unsafe modules.
9. A `WeakRef` under `rc` (D39, D41). `N`'s `deref()` gives `undefined` once the target's count hits zero, or once the cycle collector has decided it's garbage. `V`'s can keep giving the target for as long as its collector likes, and there's no telling when it stops. So
   corpus programs compared with `V` only use a target that's still strongly held, where both must give it, and the cleared case is pinned in `corpus/lower/rc-only`, which isn't compared with `V`.

10. Where ECMAScript itself says "implementation-approximated" and V8's digits aren't reproduced (D42): `x.toString(r)` with `r` other than 10 and `|x| >= 2^53`, and `parseInt` in a radix other than 2, 4, 8, 10, 16 or 32 past 2^53. `N` traps with code 4. V8's result depends on its own rounding, and in the second case on the host's fused multiply.
11. A sort whose comparator isn't consistent (D42). JS leaves the result implementation-defined, and `N`'s merge sort and V8's TimSort can differ. With a consistent comparator both are the same stable sort.
12. A string past `2^29 - 24` units: `V` throws `RangeError`, as does `N`, where memory lasts. Before that `N` can trap 14 where `V` has more memory (item 4).
13. An Error's `stack` (D49). `N` gives the line V8's starts with, `name: message`, and no frames, which have no meaning without V8's stack. Corpus programs don't print it.
14. Recursion too deep (D49), part of item 4. In a module where something can catch, a function in a cycle of calls tests the stack on entry, and below the limit its caller set throws `RangeError("Maximum call stack size exceeded")`, as `V` does past its own. The depth where each gives up differs, and so a program can see the error in one and a result in the other. A cycle through closure values has no test, and runs into the guard page as before.
15. Down-lowered `throw`, where nothing can catch (D49): a module with no `try`, no `using` and only `throw new <Error>(message)` the trap path can say keeps the trap path, as before this work. Where something can catch, a runtime failure `V` throws as an exception is one in `N` too (4.5's table). Where nothing can, a bad array length traps where `V` would throw an uncaught `RangeError`: item 1.

**Optimiser levels (D44, D46).** None of these depend on the level. `N(P)` at `-O1` and `-O2` gives the results and trap codes `N(P)` gives at `-O0`, and only time, memory and stack use may differ, as item 4 already allows. Two things follow that the optimiser has to do on purpose. A load can fault, which is how an unchecked null dereference traps 6, so a load that ran at `-O0` still runs, even where inlining or folding left its value unused (4.3). And an explicit null check is left to the load after it (D75's R7) only where that load's fault through null is the check's own trap: natively, by the image's table of such loads, which the runtime reads, inside a driver's case and outside one alike; never on Wasm, where a load near 0 reads memory. And a trap reports its code and, where anything reports one, its trap site's location, which inlining copies unchanged: a trap inside an inlined function is reported as it was at `-O0`.

`@tsl/std` adds no divergence. It's the same source on every engine, so `V(P)` and `N(P)` differ only where these already let them: memory (4, as the host's default source has no limit, and a stride in a `Slab` is simulated, 6), a stale local (5), and a trap inside `using` (1). Its `Map` and `Set` are JS's (D47), held to JS's own by `tools/std-map-oracle.ts`, and `ExactMap` isn't, by design: it traps 2 on a missing key and 13 on a change during `forEach`, on every engine alike, so that's no divergence either.

Any other difference is a compiler bug or a spec bug, and blocks the milestone.

**Trap codes (normative).** On the host, `trap(code)` throws `TslTrap`, a class exported by `@tsl/core` with a
numeric `code` property. Every code is named (D71): `@tsl/core`'s `Trap` names the table's, `Trap.Overflow` (1), `Bounds`
(2), `DivZero` (3), `Conversion` (4), `Stale` (5), `Null` (6), `Assert` (7), `ShiftCount` (8), `Misaligned` (9), `Panic`
(10), `NoAddress` (11), `NoStub` (12), `Loan` (13), `OutOfMemory` (14), `Hole` (15), `RcCheck` (16), `BadCast` (17) and
`Dispatch` (18), and a program names its own, from 1000, with its own enum or constant. A numeric literal given as `trap`'s or
lowered `trapNow`'s code is TSL1026, at the literal; printed TSL says `trapNow("narrow", Trap.BadCast)`. A member is a
constant, so `trap(Trap.Bounds)` is `trap(2)`'s tree, TIR and trap site exactly. `Trap` is a constant object and a type of the
same name, which tslc reads as a numeric enum, rather than a TS `enum`: Node's type stripping, which loads `@tsl/core`
without the hook where the Wasm glue and checked JS import it, rejects `enum`. In Wasm glue, the same class is thrown. Natively, EL0 means domain death with the
code reported, and EL1 core means
`TMK:PANIC`. In the bare-metal test runtime (4.5), a trap inside a call the driver made reports `TMK:C <case> T <code>` and
unwinds to the driver. A load or store near address 0 is code 6 there: an unchecked null dereference faults, it never reads 0.

| Code | Meaning | Code | Meaning |
|------|---------|------|---------|
| 1 | Integer overflow | 7 | Failed `assert` with no code (reserved) |
| 2 | Index out of bounds | 8 | Negative bigint shift count |
| 3 | Division by zero, or MIN / −1 | 9 | Misaligned layout overlay |
| 4 | Checked conversion out of range, or unknown `enumOf` value | 10 | `panic` |
| 5 | Stale reference, including one about to reach a closure from a `@tsl/std` collection (`checkLive`), or a bad `Slab.remove` | 11, 12 | Host only: `addrOf` with no simulated memory; `asmFn` with no stub |
| 6 | `!` on null | 13 | `Vec` changed during a `withSlice` loan, or a `@tsl/std` collection during its `forEach` or `sortInPlace` |
| 14 | Down-lowered code: arena, memory or shadow stack exhausted. `leak` and `manual`: the page source has run out, or none is registered (divergence 4). `@tsl/std`: the global allocator's source has run out, on the host and natively alike, where it's one source and the same arithmetic. `rc`: the same, and only after everything pending has been freed and, with the collector, it has run to completion | 15 | Down-lowered code: a write that would leave a hole in a scalar `Array`, or at a negative or fractional index |
| 16 | Test builds of `rc` only: an access through, or a count on, a reference to a dead object, or to one the cycle collector has decided on. A release build can't report it | 17 | Down-lowered code: an `unknown` used as a class or primitive it isn't, after a type predicate or an `as` cast that lied (D49, 4.5). The checker's own narrowing can't reach it |
| 18 | A dispatch interface's object whose class id is none of the classes that reach it (3.4, D70): only memory reused or written through `manual` or `@tsl/unsafe` can give one. Native only: on the host the call is JS's own | 19 to 999 | Reserved (down-lowering's `rc` probe uses 999 in test builds; it's never printed) |
| | | ≥ 1000 | Program-defined, via `trap(code)` and `assert(cond, code)`. In down-lowered code, codes from 100000 are `throw` sites, whose message is in the trap table (4.5) |

---

## 4. The compiler

### 4.1 Pipeline

```text
ordinary TS
        |
 down-lowering (TS checker: types, numbers, escape, layouts, can-throw)
        |
 TSL text, in a "lowered" package (tmk lower --emit tsl, D62)
        |
TSL source                                 TSL source only
        |                                        |
 tslc-host (TS checker, then TSL's)      tslc (own parser + checker)      <- M8
        |                                        |
 subset check and elaboration                    |
        +------------------+---------------------+
                           v
                  TIR (typed SSA, canonical text, SHA-256 = tirhash)
                           |
          verify -> opt (-O0 | -O1 | -O2, D44, D46, D73): inline, SROA, const-fold,
                 copy propagation, DCE, branch folding [built: phase A];
                 value numbering, LICM, unswitching, peeling, check
                 elimination [built: phase B]; specialisation constants [unbuilt]
                 -> verify
                           |
             +-------------+--------------+
             v             v              v
           wasm            c           aarch64 --> image --> bincheck
           M1              M3              M5
```

`tslc-host` and `tslc` must produce the same `tirhash` for all pure-TSL corpus files (checked from M8).

Ordinary TS reaches TIR through TSL (D62): down-lowering prints its lowered tree as a TSL package, and tslc compiles that
like any other. The direct route, lowered tree straight to TIR, is kept as the reference until every feature has moved, and
`tmk milestone pipe-a` compiles every program the TSL route takes both ways and runs both. In phase 1 the TSL route takes
every program with no closure values in `strict`, `leak` and `manual`, strings, `Map`, `Set`, exceptions and inheritance
included, and is the default for those it printed exactly, which give the same TIR; the rest, and `rc`, still take the
direct route (4.5).

### 4.2 Stage plan and implementation language

- **M1 to M7:** `tslc-host`, all backends and TIR tools are strict ordinary TS on Node, in a "TSL-ready"
  style from `compiler/tir` onwards: no capturing closures on hot paths, monomorphic data, integer-indexed
  tables. Not enforced by the checker, just reviewed, so the M8 port is mostly mechanical.
- **M8:** `tslc` is written in TSL. Because TSL runs on V8, the first self-compile needs nothing new.
- Keep `tslc-host` afterwards. It remains the only path for down-lowering full TS, because that depends on
  the TS checker.

**TS version: pin `typescript@5.9.3`** (verified installed in Moire, verified API behaviour for this design).
TypeScript 7 (Go) shipped in 2026 with no stable programmatic API until 7.1, and tooling relying on the API
stays on the 6.0 API [P14]. Revisit when 7.1's API exists. The dependency is confined to `compiler/host` and
the `tools/ts-hook.mjs` test hook.

### 4.3 TIR

TIR is a typed SSA control-flow graph with block parameters. It has no aggregates: SROA runs during
lowering, so value records become multiple SSA values and memory aggregates become byte offsets.

**Types:** `i8 i16 i32 i64 f32 f64 ptr ix`. Signedness is in the operation. `ix` is the target's pointer-width integer
and carries `usize` and `isize`, so TIR stays target-independent and `tirhash` is the same for all backends. Checked
`ix` arithmetic traps at 2³² on wasm32 and at ±(2⁵³−1) on 64-bit targets.

**Module:** `types`, `globals` (name, size, align, section, optional bytes), `funcs`, `traps` (id, kind,
source location, and for a lowered `throw` its message), `externs` (name and signature of a function outside the module;
only a JS host's fallback shims have any, 4.5).

**Function:** `func @name(params) -> (rets) attrs { blocks }`. Attributes: `export` (visible to the embedder),
`noalloc`, `nosleep`, `inline`,
`noinline`, `export_c`, `section`. Multiple returns are allowed.

**Operations (complete for v1):**

| Group | Operations |
|-------|-----------|
| Constants | `iconst.T`, `fconst.T`, `globaladdr`, `funcaddr` |
| Int wrap | `add sub mul and or xor shl lshr ashr neg not`, `.T` |
| Int shift, JS | `shl.js32 lshr.js32 ashr.js32` (count mod 32); `shl.big lshr.big ashr.big` (count ≥ width defined) |
| Int checked | `add.chk.{s,u}.T trapid`, `sub.chk…`, `mul.chk…`; `range.chk.{s,u}.T lo hi trapid`, where `hi` may be `ixmax`, the target's largest `ix`  |
| Division | `sdiv udiv srem urem`, `.T`, with `trapid` on zero, and for `sdiv` on MIN/−1. `srem` MIN/−1 is 0, as in JS |
| Float | `fadd fsub fmul fdiv frem fneg fabs fsqrt ffloor fceil ftrunc fnearest fmin.js fmax.js fcopysign`, `.T`. `frem` is JS `%`: exact, with the dividend's sign. A target with no instruction uses `tir/helpers.ts` |
| Compare | `icmp.{eq,ne,slt,sle,sgt,sge,ult,ule,ugt,uge}.T`, `fcmp.{eq,ne,lt,le,gt,ge}.T` |
| Convert | `zext sext trunc`, `fpromote fdemote`, `sitofp uitofp`, `fptosi.sat fptoui.sat`, `js.toint32`, `bitcast` |
| Select | `select.T` |
| Memory | `load.T.{na,rlx,acq,sc}`, `load.T.inv` (a class id: plain, and nothing writes it while its object lives; only the optimiser makes it, D73), `store.T.{na,rlx,rel,sc}`, `load.dev.T`, `store.dev.T`, `alloca size align trapid` (traps if the stack is exhausted) |
| Atomic RMW | `rmw.{add,sub,and,or,xor,xchg}.T.ord`, `cas.T.ord`, `fence.ord` |
| Safety | `bounds.chk idx len trapid -> idx'` (speculation-hardened if enabled, see 7.3); `gen.chk slotgen handlegen trapid` |
| Address | `gep base index scale offset` |
| Call | `call @f args -> rets`, `call.indirect sig tableIndex args -> rets`, `intrinsic name args -> rets`. Intrinsics grow by name: `mem.base`, `mem.ensure`, `mem.fill`, `mem.copy` back the arena, `math.sin` and the like are JS `Math` functions with no operation here, and `native.*` belong to the bare-metal runtime (`native.putc`, `native.counter`, `native.frequency`, `native.off`, `native.try`, `native.unwind`, `native.fma`) and exist on no JS host |
| Terminators | `br bb(args)`, `brif cond bbT(args) bbF(args)`, `switch val [k: bb(args)…] default bb(args)`, `ret vals`, `trap id`, `unreachable` |

A non-escaping closure lowers to a code pointer plus an environment pointer, passed as a hidden first
argument. A stored reference is an `i64`, and `gen.chk` guards each dereference of one. As built: `gen.chk ref trapid -> ptr` reads the word
before the object itself and gives the pointer, and `ref.addr ref -> ptr` gives the pointer with no check, which every other member access uses. A
value of function type is two leaves in native TSL, and a top-level function used as a value gets a thunk that takes and ignores the environment. A
closure's environment holds a pointer for a variable that changes and the value for one that doesn't. Each `alloca` is in the entry block, so a stack
`new` in a loop has one slot. What a static object can't have in its initial bytes, addresses and its generation prefix, goes in by a generated `__statics`
function, which the image calls first: it's the equivalent of a loader's relocations, with no user code in it, so TSL1010 still holds. Classes, closures and pointers
compile to the native backend only so far, with no Wasm and no `--emit=js-checked`; a program using none of them gets the TIR it always did.

**Rules:**

- Every value has exactly one definition, which dominates its uses. Every block ends in one terminator.
- `load.dev`/`store.dev` and all atomic operations are never removed, duplicated or reordered past each other.
- A check (`*.chk`) may be removed **only** if a proof dominates it, from `tir/range.ts`. A check may never be
  moved ahead of a side effect or out of a loop unless the moved version dominates all original uses and
  its trap would still occur on the same path. Lucet's loop-invariant-code-motion bug was exactly this
  class, and it could bypass safety checks [P11].
- The verifier (`tir/verify.ts`) runs after each pass in a test build (`TMK_OPT_VERIFY=1`, which `tmk` sets for `test`,
  `milestone`, `corpus` and `ci`), naming the pass that broke the TIR, and always at the start and end of the pipeline.

**The optimiser, as built (phases A and B, D44, D46, D73).** `compiler/tir/passes/`, run by `optimizeModule` in `manager.ts` on each
module `tslc` lowers, between lowering's verifier and canonical text, so `tirhash` is the optimised module's. `-O0` returns
the module untouched, the same object, so no `-O0` output can move. The passes:

- `simplify`: constant folding, identities (`x + 0`, `x * 1`, a conversion undone, a gep at nothing, a reference made from
  a frame slot's address read back as that address, a second `ref.addr` of one reference in a block (D64)), and copy propagation, which replaces a block parameter given one
  value on every edge by that value. A fold computes what the backend computes: none folds a float to NaN or a subnormal,
  and none folds an `ix` operation whose answer could differ between wasm32 and a 64-bit target. A check folds only where
  its constant operands prove it can't fire, and a checked `x + 0` or `x * 1` can't. *Strength reduction* (R1f, found with
  `tmk profile`): an `i32` or `i64` `urem` or `udiv` by a power of two from 2 is an `and` or an `lshr` (the divisor isn't zero, so
  neither could trap); a 64-bit shift whose count is a constant below 64 needs no guard for a count of 64 or more (`lshr.big` to
  `lshr.i64`); and `lshr (shl x, c), c` is `x` where x has at most 64 − c bits (32 − c for `i32`), counted from its definition (a
  constant, an `and`, a zero extension or truncation, an `i32` or `i64` right shift; not an `ix` shift, which wasm32 takes modulo
  32), which is how a checked `<<`'s test for bits lost folds. `TMK_TSL_OPT_OFF=pow2,bigshift` turns them off, for measuring. The
  injected bugs `fold-pow2-mask` (an `and` with 2^k) and `fold-shift-back` (the width ignored) are caught by corpus/pos/pow2_divrem.ts
  and corpus/trap/shift_const.ts (opt-a box 12).
- `cfg`: a branch or `switch` on a constant becomes a jump, unreachable blocks go, a block with one predecessor that jumps
  to it joins it, and an empty block that only jumps on is jumped past. Each keeps the graph reducible, for Wasm.
- `dce`: a pure operation or block parameter nothing needs goes. Loads, checks and effects never do.
- `inline`, `partial` and `devirtualize`: the inliner, by D46's cost model, bottom-up over the call graph. R20: `partial` takes a
  callee whose entry gives a frame slot that nothing it copies uses, and leaves the slot out of the copy (D46). R26: a call
  in a loop's block, inlined, splits the block; the callee's copy and the rest of the block are in the loop as the block
  was, so a call after it in the block is still weighed as a call in a loop (-O1's small leaf, -O2's loop factor), where it
  had been weighed as one outside (reshape_order.ts's `note`, after an inlined array read, at -O1: M5's R26 record).
- `sroa`: a frame slot used only by loads and stores at constant offsets, zeroed at entry, becomes SSA values.
- `keep`: a load that ran at `-O0` runs at every level. The backend has always dropped a plain load nothing uses, and
  natively a load through null is how trap 6 happens (3.10), so where inlining or folding leaves a load's value unused that
  `-O0` used, its value is stored to `__opt_keep`, a word nothing reads. A load `-O0` itself dropped stays dropped, so no
  level runs a load `-O0` didn't. Which loads `-O0` dropped is the backend's own rule, tested equal to it.
- `gvn` (phase B, D73, `-O1` and `-O2`): value numbering over the dominator tree. A pure operation, or a check, with the
  same operation, operands and immediates as one that dominates it is that one: a check that passed with the same operands
  can't fire, whatever its trap. A plain load is a dominating load of the same type at the same address, or the value a
  dominating store of that type put there, where nothing between them may have written those bytes; between a block and
  its dominator is every block on a path from one to the other, so a load after an if/else still sees one from before it
  unless an arm wrote there. What writes is `memory.ts`'s: a plain store writes its bytes (an address is a base and a
  constant offset, two accesses at one base alias only where their bytes overlap, and a global and a frame slot are objects
  of their own); an atomic, a device access, a fence, an intrinsic with effects, an indirect call, and a call to anything
  that may write write everything, a function writing nothing only where it and all it calls store to nothing but their own
  frame slots. `rc`'s counts are calls or plain loads and stores of the count word, under the same rules. A load whose
  value stands for a later one must have run at `-O0` (`keep`): one `-O0` dropped didn't run, and running it now could
  fault earlier. A class id's load (`load.T.inv`: at `-O1` and `-O2` the optimiser's first step, `invariant`, makes it of
  each load lowering noted, outside the canonical text, so `-O0`'s TIR is as it was) is changed only by a plain store at
  its own base over its bytes, so it stands for a later one across calls, intrinsics and stores elsewhere (3.4's "Class ids
  don't change"); LICM and peeling treat it the same way.
- R27, fresh-allocation separation (D77, `-O1` and `-O2`, for `gvn`, `licm` and `peel`): lowering notes, outside the
  canonical text, a separated field's read (tslc's rule, 3.5) and every object field's read and write. An address worked out
  from a separated field's read (an offset from it, a cast, an add of it and something that isn't one, a block parameter every
  edge gives one) is in a block no object is in, so an access there and an object's field's, a global's or a frame slot's
  don't alias; and a call writes only such blocks where the callee and all it calls store nowhere but their own frame slots
  and such blocks (memory.ts's `writeSummaries`, settled over the call graph from each function's own writes), as a fill or
  copy into one does. A length read before such a store or call is the length after it, so a check the loop's test made goes
  by the rules below. `TMK_R27_OFF=sep` turns it off (the pins tool); its injected bugs are a summary missing a write
  (`r27-summary-miss`) and an alias it misses (`r27-alias-any`), in `OPT_FAULTS`.
- R28 (`-O1` and `-O2`): `simplify` takes `ref.addr (or x, y)` as `ref.addr x` where `y` has no bit below 48 (a constant
  tag, as a static's 0xffff, or a value shifted left by 48 to 63, as a slot's generation is put on its address): a reference's
  pointer is its low 48 bits, so the tag can't change it, and the tag's own work is left for DCE (`r28-tag-keep-wrong`, an
  injected bug, keeps the tag and drops the address). `conds` takes two integer constants of one type and value as one
  operand, so a test of `1 < len` answers `get`'s own `1 >= len` where each made its own constant (relative_import's second
  check; `r28-consts-any` takes any two constants as one). The inliner lets a callee no bigger than its call in past the
  caller's growth limit, as it can't grow the caller (forced copies can take a caller past its soft limit, after which a
  three-instruction method was left a call; `r28-shrink-store` copies such a callee without its first store). And `-O2`
  runs `version` a second time after the copying rounds, over every loop the first pass didn't version (an unswitched copy
  or peeled loop, whose lengths value numbering and LICM have since moved out, as a view's buffer length in a scan), with the
  same guards and limits; a loop the first pass versioned, either copy, isn't looked at again (`r28-version-again` lets the
  second pass's fast copy run one turn too many). `TMK_R28_OFF` with `tag`, `consts`, `grow` or `version` turns each off.
- R29 (`-O1` and `-O2`, D79): a call tslc's table-links proof marked in bounds (`Instr.inb`, compiler/host/links.ts) is
  inlined with the callee's leading bounds check's compare (noted `chk` where lowering made it, the test of that parameter
  against `this.len`) as false, and the length load it compared with left unkept (keep.ts): the receiver is one of a live
  object's arrays held in place, so the load can't fault, and with the check gone nothing needs it. Both notes are outside the
  canonical text, so -O0 is untouched; a call not inlined keeps its check. `TMK_R29_OFF=links` turns the proof off; its injected
  bug is `r29-inb-any` (every call's copy loses the check), in `OPT_FAULTS`.
- R30 (`sroa`; `-O2`, and its first part at `-O1`): a copy out of a frame slot (`mem.copy` from it, of a constant length
  within it, to anywhere else), which is how `make` places a new object in its counted slot, is written as a store of each
  field's value at that point at its offset from the copy's destination, and a store of zero over each run of bytes no field
  covers, which only the fill wrote; a copy that would split a field keeps the slot. The fill may be the first accesses of a
  block that dominates every access, stores of zero that cover the slot exactly a word at a time, as a new object's fields
  are cleared after its constructor's tests (the entry block's `mem.fill` or one store, before). At `-O1`, only a slot copied
  out is replaced, nothing else of `-O2`'s; -O0 is untouched. `TMK_R30_OFF=sroa` puts it back; its injected bug is
  `r30-copy-stale` (each field stored as the fill left it), in `OPT_FAULTS`.
- `licm` (D73, `-O1` and `-O2`): loop-invariant code motion into the loop's preheader, made where there isn't one. A
  load with an invariant address that nothing in the loop may write moves from anywhere if it's from a global or a frame
  slot, which can't fault; any other only from the path every first turn takes from the header, with only pure operations
  and loads before it there (a fault is a fault at either load), and never one `-O0` dropped. A check moves on the same
  path with only pure operations before it, so its trap is the first thing that could happen, as at `-O0`; passing once
  with the same operands, it passes every turn. Pure arithmetic dearer than one instruction moves from anywhere; a cheap
  pure operation (a constant, a rename, a constant offset, a compare, arithmetic with a constant) only where something that
  moves needs it, as out of the loop it holds a register across all of it (the JPEG decoder's scan spilled 43 values with
  everything moved, 29 this way, 25 with none: M5's phase B record). At `-O2` the path goes past the loop's test where
  `range.ts` proves which way the first turn goes from what holds on every edge into the loop, so `i * n` leaves
  `for (k = 0; k < n; k++)` inside `for (j = 0; j < n; j++)`, `i < n` having made `n` at least 1.
- `unswitch` and `peel` (D73, `-O2`): a loop branching on a value it computes from nothing that changes in it (a class
  test) becomes a copy for each way, chosen before it; a loop whose every turn loads something it doesn't write, which
  can't move because the loop may run no turn, has its first turn copied in front of it, and value numbering gives the
  later turns the first turn's load (a chain walk's lengths read once a lookup). Nothing runs that didn't, nor in another
  order. A loop is copied only up to a cost of 160 (unswitching) or 64 (peeling), and copies add at most 640 to a function.
  R26: in up to three rounds, with value numbering, LICM and check elimination between, the 640 and the loops peeled shared
  by all of them. A peeled first turn's loads are the later turns' only once value numbering has run, so a test on one (a
  string's buffer's null test, a view against a flat string) is an invariant branch only in the next round, which unswitches
  it; each way's loop may then be peeled once more, where its own loads (a view's start, its buffer's length and units)
  dominate its latches, and value numbering gives the rest of its turns the copy's loads. A round after the first copies
  only loops a round peeled and the copies unswitching them makes: every other loop was there to copy in the first round,
  and copying it again once value numbering changed it grew code no peeled turn made worth it (`JsMap`'s `advance`, 0.4%
  more instructions on number-keyed maps, M5's R26 record). Each round only copies as before.
- `checks` (D73, `-O2`): check elimination by `range.ts`'s proofs: each integer value's interval, read unsigned and
  signed, from constants, operations, checks passed and the branches above a block, loops gone round to a fixpoint
  (widened, then narrowed); and facts `a <= b + c` from compares, bounds checks, masks (`x & m <= m`), a length less one
  and renames. A checked add, subtract or multiply that can't leave its type becomes the operation without its check; a
  range check whose operand is in range, and a bounds check whose index is below its length, go; a compare whose answer is
  proved becomes it, and branch folding takes the branch and its trap away (an array's `get`, a string's index); and
  `js.toint32` of an `i32` converted to a float is that `i32`. Nothing is moved. An `ix` interval holds on wasm32 and a
  64-bit target alike, so a checked `ix` result is proved only below 2^32, or where it's at most an `ix` value read
  unsigned, a usize, which is never above 2^53 − 1 (D23). Divisions keep their checks. R26: a signed test gives its fact,
  read unsigned, where its smaller side isn't negative (`k < m` with `k >= 0` puts `m` above `k`, so not negative either,
  and two values that aren't negative compare alike signed and unsigned), where both sides had to be: a loop's `i < n` with
  `n` a load. A fact reaches a target through the target's own definition, `zext n` or `range.chk n`, the same number read
  unsigned (the target is asked about where it's used, so its definition has run). And a float compare of two `i32`s
  converted exactly (`sitofp`, rounded or not) is decided from the integers as they're known in the compare's block, a
  branch above may have said one isn't negative, not as they were where they were converted: `charCodeAt`'s test of its
  index against the length in a loop over the string. With `spec-hardening` (7.3, not
  built yet) a proved bounds check is to keep its hardening.
- R32 (`-O2`, `checks`): a float compare's edge gives facts too (`range.ts`'s `floatRange`). A block reached by one edge
  alone, from a two-way branch whose ways differ, knows which way its test went, as for an integer test, and so does every
  block it dominates; a test of `c == 0` or `c != 0` reads as `c`'s, the other way or the same. A compare of a float `x` with a
  float constant, or with an `i32` `n` converted (`sitofp`, which is exact), bounds `x`; `Math.trunc(x) === x` (an `ftrunc` of
  `x` compared with `x`) says `x` is an integer. NaN answers every ordered compare (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `==`) false and `!=`
  true, so a compare that held, or a `!=` that failed, says `x` isn't NaN; an ordered compare that failed says its opposite
  (`!(x >= n)` is `x < n`) only once some compare in force says `x` isn't NaN, and otherwise nothing. Where `x` isn't NaN and
  its bounds put it at least 0 and at most a constant or `n`, `js.toint32 x` is `Math.trunc(x)` (it can't wrap: `x` is below
  2^31), which for `x` at least 0 is its floor: from `x >= c` at least `ceil(c)` for an integer `x` and `floor(c)` for any
  float, from `x > c` `floor(c) + 1` and `floor(c)`; from `x < c` at most `ceil(c) - 1`, from `x <= c` `floor(c)`. So -0
  (at least 0, ToInt32 0), a fraction (truncated toward 0, inside the bounds), ±Infinity (outside one of them) and a float at
  2^31 or more (outside the upper one, where ToInt32 would wrap) are all answered as JS answers them. Below `n` it's the fact
  `toint32(x) <= n - 1` (at most `n`: `toint32(x) <= n`), true wherever the result is, as it's defined only where the compares
  are in force; and there `n` is at least the lower bound plus one (or the lower bound), so a signed test of the two reads as
  the unsigned one. The range `[0, n)` needs no integer `x`; an integer is what makes a strict or fractional lower bound
  tighter (`x > 0` puts an integer's ToInt32 at 1 or more, a fraction's at 0). Check elimination then takes a test the fact
  proves (the unit read's own test of its index against the length, under class printing's nested `s[x]`, 4.5), and makes a
  `js.toint32` whose float is so bounded `fptosi.sat.i32`, the saturating conversion, which gives the truncation exactly there
  as it never saturates, so ToInt32's slow way for a float out of range goes. Nothing moves, no check goes unproved, and
  `-O0` and `-O1` are untouched. Injected bugs: `r32-float-le` (`x <= n` taken as `x < n`), `r32-float-int` (every float an
  integer), `r32-float-nan` (a failed compare's opposite taken where `x` may be NaN) and `r32-sat-any` (every ToInt32 made the
  saturating conversion), each caught by a wrong answer (pipe-d box 84, and opt-a box 12, whose first step is R32's program).
  `TMK_R32_OFF=range` turns it off.
- `conds` (R15, D73, `-O1` and `-O2`): a test a test above it answered goes, by one walk down the dominator tree, with
  no intervals and no fixpoint. A block reached by one edge only, from a `brif c` whose two ways go to different blocks,
  isn't the entry block, and knows which way `c` went; so does every block it dominates, as every path to them took that
  edge and an SSA value never changes (nor do the operands of the compare that made `c`, whose definitions dominate it).
  Past a `bounds.chk i, n`, in its block and those it dominates, `i < n` unsigned holds, or it trapped. Where those facts
  are in force, a `brif` on a known value becomes a jump; an integer `icmp` of the same type and operands (either way
  round) whose relation a known one implies, or whose opposite it implies, becomes its constant; and a `bounds.chk i, n`
