  with `i < n` known becomes `i`. That's the lowering's check of a read dominating `get`'s own, either way round (R13's
  double check), and a null test made twice in one turn, which the JPEG decoder's class printing did in `toRgba`'s pixel
  loop (M5's R15 record). Nothing moves, and a test that stays is where it was. Floats aren't touched (NaN answers every
  ordered compare false). The injected bug `conds-not-dominating` takes a fact from an edge whose block is also reached
  from elsewhere.
- `version` (R15, D73, `-O2`): loop versioning. A loop with checks that can't be proved where they are, but can be from
  values from outside it, becomes two: a fast copy without those checks, and the loop as it was, the fallback; a test in
  the preheader, the guard, chooses. Sound by construction: the original loop is untouched, so wherever the guard fails
  the program runs exactly as before; the guard reads only values from outside the loop, which never change, so what it
  proves before the first turn holds on every turn; and it computes only plain arithmetic and compares, with a division's
  divisor made at least 1, so it can't trap or write. For a check (a `bounds.chk`, or a compare and branch to a block
  that only traps, `JsArray.get`'s form) on index `i` against a length `n` from outside the loop: where `i` is from
  outside too, the guard is `i < n`; where `i` is the loop's counter `k` widened (`zext`, or `sext` of one never
  negative), the loop being `loopbounds`'s shape (its header ends in `k < m`, `m` from outside the loop, `k` starting at
  a constant at least 0 and stepping up) and the check past the header, so that `0 <= k < m` on every turn that reaches
  it, then for `i = k + B` the guard is `B <= n && m <= n − B`, and for `i = k × S + B` it's
  `B < n && (m = 0 || m − 1 <= (n − 1 − B) / max(S, 1))`, with `B` and `S` from outside the loop. The checked `add`
  and `mul` that make `i` lose their checks in the fast copy too: each result is at most `i`, below `n`, an `ix` value,
  so below the type's limit (as `checks`' rule). A length the loop can change (a load in it after a store that may write
  there, or a push) isn't from outside the loop, so a loop over a resized array, or one whose bound it raises, isn't
  versioned for that check; two references to one array change nothing, as each check is against its own SSA length.
  At most 8 guards a loop, a loop of cost 160 at most, and copies add at most 640 to a function; a loop is versioned
  once. matmul's inner loop (corpus/pos/matmul_f64.ts) is the shape: `a[i·n + k]` and `b[k·n + j]` lose their two
  bounds checks and four overflow checks in the fast copy. Injected bugs, each caught by corpus/trap/loop_versions.ts
  (pipe-d box 50, opt-a box 12): `version-off-by-one` (the guard allows one turn more), `version-bound-in-loop` (a bound
  or length the loop changes read once before it, for the guard), `version-wrong-length` (every guard against the first
  check's length).

No pass removes a store, a call, an atomic or device access, or a check that isn't proved; only `gvn`, `licm` and `peel`
move or share a plain load, and `licm` a check, under the rules above; and none removes a function: an export keeps its body and symbol, and the image linker drops what nothing reaches. Any pass
can be switched off by name for bisecting (`--no-pass`, `TMK_OPT_DISABLE`). `tmk lower --report` prints the remarks:
what was inlined where, partly or whole, what was made a direct call, and why each other call wasn't, with its cost and
threshold. The same module, level and switches give the same bytes, on Node and Bun.

**Canonical text** is the stable interchange format. `tirhash` = SHA-256 of canonical text. All values, including
parameters and block parameters, are numbered `%0, %1, …`: parameters first, then in order of definition, walking
blocks in reverse postorder. Source names live in a separate debug table, outside the hash. Blocks are
numbered the same way. Function order is sorted by name. Output has no timestamps,
paths or hash-map order. Source locations live only in the separate `traps` section, and paths in it are
repo-relative.

```text
func @sum(%0: ptr, %1: i32) -> (i32) {
bb0:
  %2 = iconst.i32 0
  br bb1(%2, %2)
bb1(%3: i32, %4: i32):
  %5 = icmp.ult.i32 %3, %1
  brif %5, bb2, bb3
bb2:
  %6 = bounds.chk %3, %1, t1
  %7 = gep %0, %6, 1, 0
  %8 = load.i8.na %7
  %9 = zext.i32 %8
  %10 = add.chk.u.i32 %4, %9, t2
  %11 = iconst.i32 1
  %12 = add.chk.u.i32 %3, %11, t3
  br bb1(%12, %10)
bb3:
  ret %4
}
```

### 4.4 Backends

**Order: Wasm, then C, then AArch64.** Machine code is the goal, and the first two exist to get there safely.
The C backend is an addition to the owner's original order (D6).

| Backend | Purpose | Key decisions |
|---------|---------|--------------|
| `wasm` (M1) | Scaffolding: fast feedback and V8/JSC differential, before native exists. Also Moire-usable output | Hand-written binary encoder, no wabt (not installed) and no Binaryen dependency. `wasm-opt` optional for benches. CFG to structured control per Ramsey's "Beyond Relooper" (cited from memory); TSL's control flow is always reducible. Memory: one linear memory, bump arena per export call. Multi-value returns. |
| `c` (M3) | Scaffolding: lets kernel work start before the native backend exists; a second opinion for differential tests | Emits one freestanding C file, and `asmFn` bodies as a companion `.s` file. Compile with `clang --target=aarch64-none-elf -ffreestanding -fwrapv -fno-strict-aliasing -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks -mgeneral-regs-only` (kernel) plus `ld.lld`. **Never part of the boot chain.** |
| `aarch64` (M5) | **The product** | No external tools. Own instruction encoder, own `.s` assembler for the restricted dialect, own linker for one image. Linear-scan register allocation over SSA. No instruction scheduling in v1. AAPCS64 at `export_c` boundaries; an internal convention may otherwise pass more in registers. |

**Determinism is a hard requirement of all backends.** Same input bytes and flags produce the same output
bytes, regardless of host engine, thread count or path.

**The AArch64 backend as built (`compiler/backend-aarch64`, phase A).** It reads TIR, including TIR parsed back from canonical text.
Selection first decides what needs no register: constants and symbol addresses are rebuilt at each use, a zero-extension or a
`bounds.chk` result is its operand under another name, a `gep` used only as an address in its block folds into the access, and a
compare used only by a branch or `select` in its block folds into it. Allocation is then linear scan over one interval per value,
with no holes or splitting, so a value has one register or one 8-byte slot for life. x8, x16, x17, d29, d30 and d31 are scratch, and
x18 is left alone. A value crossing a call must be callee-saved or spilled. The internal convention is AAPCS64's registers, with
x29 also allocatable and no frame chain, and any argument or result past the registers in the caller's outgoing area. Every integer
register holds its value zero-extended to 64 bits, which is what makes widening a rename. `alloca` is a static frame slot, and one in
a loop or a frame over 1 MiB is a compile error, because the stack guard is 2 MiB. `js.toint32` is a truncation in 64 bits, with
a slow path from the bits when that saturated, and no use of `FJCVTZS`. Traps branch to per-function stubs. Checked `ix` arithmetic traps at 2⁵³.
There is no `.s` assembler or `tmk repro` yet (M5). `tools/encoder-check.ts` compares `decode.ts` with `llvm-objdump`, and reassembles with `llvm-mc`.

**The backend's code shape at -O1 and -O2 (D75, B3).** At -O0 the backend is the one above, byte for byte. At -O1 and -O2 it
reshapes the program's functions (never the runtime's or the driver's) on a copy, so the TIR and its tirhash are the optimiser's,
and only the machine code differs; the level comes with the module (`Module.opt`, never printed). Five parts, each switched off by
name with the optimiser's passes (`TMK_OPT_DISABLE`), each with an injected bug a test catches (`OPT_FAULTS`, `b3-`):
- *`globals`:* a load or store of a global, or of a constant offset into one whose alignment allows it, is `adrp` and the access
  with the rest of the address in its own offset (a `lo12` fixup), two instructions where it was three, and still PC-relative, so
  an image has no data relocation (D52 to D57).
- *`thread`:* a block that only tests one of its parameters, directly or by comparing it for equality with a constant, is
  skipped by each predecessor whose own branch or constant argument already decides the test, and a predecessor that jumps to it
  unconditionally takes the test itself. That's what `&&`, `||` and an inlined boolean result leave. Nothing is copied or
  computed anew, so a definition still reaches every use; a loop header is left alone, so a loop keeps one entry.
- *`fuse`:* a compare only ever branched on, in other blocks or more than once, is computed again at each branch rather than
  kept as a value, where at most one operand needs a register; and a test of equality with zero is `cbz` or `cbnz`.
- *`remat`:* a constant offset from a register used only as an address, in any block, folds into each access; and after the
  scan, a spilled value that's a constant offset from a register, a compare only branched on, or a class id's load (`.inv`)
  whose uses are all in its block with no store or call between, is computed again at each use from operands that got
  registers, and the scan runs again, up to three times. A value passed on an edge, to a call or returned isn't, as parallel
  moves could overwrite an operand first.
- *`layout`:* blocks that only trap go last, and a branch to one goes straight to its trap stub; a loop whose header ends in
  a test with one way out, whose other blocks are together with the latch last, has its header placed after the latch, so an
  iteration takes one branch, the test's, back to the body.

*R30, values split around cold calls* (`coldsplit`, at -O1 and -O2): a call is cold where its block isn't on every turn of its
innermost loop (it doesn't dominate each source of the loop's back edges), or, outside every loop, isn't on every way out of the
function (it doesn't dominate each block that returns, but a quick way out, a block that only returns reached by a conditional
branch); `native.try` is never cold, and nothing is kept across `trap.code`, which never comes back. A value live across cold
calls only may take a register a call clobbers: it's stored to a slot of its own just before each such call (before its
arguments are moved) and loaded back just after (after its results are moved), so the way through that calls nothing needs no
callee-saved register for it, and the prologue saves fewer. A value live across any other call still takes a callee-saved
register. Which calls are cold decides only what's saved where, never what's computed. And a frame with no outgoing arguments
on the stack has its saved registers at the bottom and its slots above them, so the first pair's store makes the whole frame
and the last pair's load takes it away, where a frame with slots was a `sub` and an `add` of SP more (bare metal only; hosted
keeps its frame record on top). Machine code only: TIR and tirhashes are untouched. @tsl/gc's `freeAlloc` saved 9 to 11
registers and now saves only the link register. Its injected bugs, in `OPT_FAULTS` (`r30-split-`): a split value never loaded
back, one stored after the call's arguments are moved, and a callee-saved register taken for a split value but not saved.

*R31, quick ways out that return a constant* (part of `coldsplit`): a block that makes only the constants it returns
(`if (count === 0) return 0;`) is a quick way out, as an empty one is, so a call past such a test is on every way through that
does the function's work and isn't cold. Still only what's saved where. Found by instruction counts of the JPEG decoder at -O1:
`readBits` and `receiveExtend` stored and loaded a value around the call after their `count === 0` test on every call, and the
decoder was 0.4% slower than with no split at all. MEASURED (HVF, tower-portrait, nine interleaved runs each): -O1 7.050 →
6.989 ms (7.022 with no split at all), -O2 6.995 → 6.995 ms (7.179 with no split). `TMK_R31_OFF=split` puts R30's rule back. *Tried and taken out:* a cost check, keeping a value made
outside a loop in a callee-saved register across a cold call inside it (decodeScan stored and loaded five such values around a
reader call on most turns, 750,000 instructions a decode): JPEG -O2 0.3% faster still, -O1 the same, but twenty-one runtime
functions of a lowered `rc` program (@tsl/gc's freeFlat, freeSteps and freeRest, JsMap's lookups, JsArray's tryReserve) saved
more registers again, and adv_forof_mutation at -O2 went from 0.992 to 1.006 of the direct route; with the check only two loops
deeper, nothing measured moved.

*R23, range checks' bounds a value can't pass* (always at -O1 and -O2, not a part of its own): a 32-bit `range.chk` leaves out
the compare for a bound the operand can't pass whichever way it's read: a signed check's upper bound at 2^31 - 1 or lower at
-2^31 (`toUsize` of an i32 checks `0 ≤ x ≤ 2^31 - 1`), and, for a value whose own type is 8 or 16 bits, which a register holds
zero-extended (`select`), any bound at or beyond 0 and 2^8 - 1 or 2^16 - 1 (`toI32` of a `u16` unit). The trap is the same
wherever the value is out of range, which these never are; TIR and tirhashes are untouched. Its injected bug (`r23-range-lo`,
in `OPT_FAULTS`) leaves the lower bound out too, and corpus/trap's `i32ToUsize(-1)` then doesn't trap.

*R25, an add that can't carry* (always at -O1 and -O2, not a part of its own): a checked unsigned `add` of `ix` or `i64` whose
operands are each a constant or a value whose own type is 32 bits or fewer, held zero-extended (`select`), is a plain `add`:
its sum is below 2^33, so it can't carry, and below 2^53, `ix`'s limit (SPEC 4.3, D23). That's a view's unit index in `rc`
class printing, its u32 start plus an index from an i32, three instructions a read. Machine code only: on wasm32, whose `ix`
is 32 bits, the add can still overflow, so the TIR keeps its check, and TIR and tirhashes are untouched. Its injected bug
(`r25-add-narrow`, in `OPT_FAULTS`, so opt-a box 12 runs it) takes a 64-bit operand for a 32-bit one, and
corpus/trap/wide_add.ts's u64 at its limit plus a u32 then doesn't trap. That corpus runs on wasm32 too, where `ix` is 32 bits
and such sums of `ix` trap, so it pins the u64 form; the `ix` form is every view read of corpus/lower/r25, natively.

### 4.5 Down-lowering

This is how most code reaches machine code: everything outside the kernel and drivers is ordinary TypeScript,
and only those two are
written in TSL directly.

Input: strict TS, `tsc`-clean. Uses the TS checker for resolved types. Output: TSL, in a package whose tsl.json says
`"lowered"`, which tslc compiles to TIR (D62); `tmk lower --emit tsl` prints it. Per-function outcome: `lowered` or
`fallback`.

**The route (D62, design/pipeline.md).** The rules below are the lowering's analysis and desugaring, and they build the
typed tree tslc's elaborator builds from TSL. Their result is then printed as TSL (`compiler/host/emit-tsl.ts`), each
construct as the TSL that tslc elaborates back to the same node, so TS → TSL → tslc gives the TIR the tree gives directly, and
for every program the TSL route takes in the corpora it does, byte for byte at -O2 (pipe-a). A number's representation is its
declared type, a range the lowering proved is `wrap<T>(a + b)`, a proved conversion `cast<T>(x)`, and a statement-expression
a comma expression or statements before its statement. What TSL proper has no words for comes from `@tsl/lowered`, which
only a lowered package can import (TSL1023): in phase 1 that includes the memory layer, objects and vectors as loads and
stores at the lowering's offsets, which is the part phase 2 replaces with TSL's own classes, in TSL's own layout, with no
lowered layout and no lowered class (D62's rulings; design/pipeline.md, section 3, lists every extension and why desugaring
wasn't enough). A memory mode is a desugaring onto TSL (D63): the lowering prints plain TSL in the package's mode, and in
`rc` the counts are `@tsl/gc` calls tslc adds (D74), not a pass of the lowering's. Lowered `rc` builds take that route
when it's forced (R2: class printing of the tree before down-rc.ts counts it, in a lowered `rc` package tslc expands), and
`auto` takes it too since R4 met the speed rule (`AUTO_RC`, M5's R4 record), where the program prints exactly, and keeps the
rest on the direct route and D39's counted heap. Objects as TSL's own classes are built, and `auto`'s choice in `leak` and `manual` (D64; `--route tsl` with
`TMK_EMIT_CLASSES=1` forces them): tslc then runs its escape analysis on the lowered package, in its `lowered.memory` mode, so a `new`
is placed as TSL places any. A lowered program's arrays print as `@tsl/jsrt`'s `JsArray` (D66; `@tsl/std`'s before D71), in `auto` too since they met the
speed rule (`TMK_EMIT_VECS=0` turns that off). `tmk lower` takes the TSL route by default where the
printer printed the program exactly, with no loop or branch reshaped and no operand moved to fit a statement-expression in,
which gives the direct route's TIR byte for byte, and since R14 where phase 1's printing reshaped it only by the kinds `auto`
trusts (a statement-expression's statements before an operand, after a sequence's first part, in a conditional's arm or on
a logical operator's right side, each in JS's order: D62), which gives that TIR too, checked on every such program; a
program it had to reshape otherwise, a closure value and `rc` take the direct route by default; `--route direct|tsl|auto` or `TMK_ROUTE` picks one, and `auto` falls back to the direct route rather than
fail. The direct route stays the reference until every
feature has moved, and `tmk milestone pipe-a` runs both on every program the TSL route takes.

**Maps as TSL (D72).** With classes forced, a lowered program's `Map` and `Set` print as `@tsl/jsrt`'s `JsMap` and `JsSet`, compiler/rt/map.ts in TSL, and map.ts isn't printed: `new JsMap(u64, f64, true, false)` (the key's and value's descriptors, whether it keeps values, and whether an outgrown array goes back), `m.get(jsNumKey(k))`, `m.set`, `m.has`, `m.delete`, `m.clear()`, `m.cursor()`, `m.advance(c)`, `jsKeyNum(m.keyAt(c))` and `m.valAt(c)`. A number key is its bits, -0 as +0 and every NaN one NaN. A map whose key or value is a string, a boolean or nullable, or that's iterated through an iterator value, prints as before. Not `auto`'s choice yet (`AUTO_MAPS`).

**Printed TSL runs on V8 (D71).** The refinement rule (2.2) holds for a lowered package: `@tsl/lowered`'s words run on V8
and JSC as a host simulation, and the dual-route differential has a standing third route, which runs each printed program
unchanged (Node with `tools/ts-hook.mjs`, and Bun) through `tools/printed-exec.ts`, its arguments placed as a native caller
places them (D36), and requires the result, the arguments after and the trap code native gives, and where native traps, the
source's on V8 or one of 3.10's allowed divergences, named: traps (1), memory (4) and recursion too deep (14). Run on JSC too,
it must give V8's results. The simulation: lowered memory is a block per allocation holding each stored value at its offset
(a type argument is erased on the host, so it can't be bytes), what was never stored reads as zero; a typed array is a real
one, its address its own block; one made from a pointer and a length is a view TSL proper indexes; `rt` is the call arena's
two no-ops and the vectors of `down-rt.ts`; `intrinsic` and `builtin` are JS's `Math` and the bit operations TIR has;
`text`, `charTable` and `hashKey` lay out D42's static data; `throwJs` throws what the native trap path reports; a conversion
between integer types prints its target as a second argument (`cast<usize>(i, "usize")`), which tslc ignores, so a negative
`i32` as a `usize` is past every length on the host as natively; and past 128 MiB of simulated bytes or 4 million stored
values the host runs out, trapping 14, under a process's 3 GiB watchdog. **Switching over takes this too:** a feature takes
the TSL route by default only where its printed programs run on V8 and agree there, beside the speed rule (D44, D62).

Each of these rules converts something TSL rejects into something TIR can express. As TSL gains a construct
directly, such as plain classes and
non-escaping closures in version 2, the rule here stays only for the wider forms the checker can still prove.

| Input | Lowering |
|-------|---------|
| Generic function/type | Monomorphise per concrete instantiation; cap at 128 (fallback past that) |
| Object shape with fixed fields, no dynamic keys | Struct in the arena, or value record if it's immutable and non-escaping |
| Class without inheritance, reflection or `this` escape | As in 3.4: struct + functions, with field types inferred where they're plain `number` |
| Class with `extends`, `super()`, `super.m()`, overriding, `abstract`, `protected`, getters, `instanceof`, static members, `extends Error` | In `leak`, `manual` and `rc` (D50): a flow class's struct holds every class that reaches it, base fields first and a field a subclass adds under its own key, with a class id in the first word where anything needs one; a call is direct where the receiver's classes reach one implementation, and a switch on the class id with a direct call in each arm where they reach several; `instanceof` is a range of preorder ids; fields start in JS's order, the derived ones after `super()` returns. **fallback** in `strict` (`inheritance`), and for a generic class in a hierarchy, `extends` of an expression, mixins, prototype changes, a static method using `this`, a write to an inherited static through a subclass, and a derived field a base constructor reads before it's set whose type can't hold `undefined` (`field-before-init`). A write there is fine, as JS has it: the write happens, and the subclass's initialiser then overwrites it, so only a read, or `+=` and `++`, which read, falls back |
| Discriminated or literal union | Tagged value; literal-only unions become small integers |
| `T \| null`, `T \| undefined` on heap objects | Null pointer; on scalars a tag or sentinel, e.g. `u8 \| undefined` as `i32` with −1 |
| Known closure (single target, or local const called directly) | Inline or lambda-lift |
| Closure selected among known targets | `switch` on a tag. In `leak`, `manual` and `rc`, a function variable that isn't a `const` bound to a known target is a closure value |
| Closure stored or returned, in `leak`, `manual` and `rc` | Environment struct + `call.indirect`: see the closures rule below. In `rc` the environment is counted, and has a descriptor for its own captures |
| Non-escaping allocation | Stack |
| Allocation escaping only within an export call | Call-scoped bump arena, reset on return (results are copied out). Not in `rc`, where it's counted: see below |
| Allocation escaping further (stored in a global, returned, or kept by anything long-lived) | **fallback** in `strict`; the mode's allocator in `leak`, `manual` and `rc` (`--memory`, D38, D39) |
| `number` used only with integer ops, `.length`, integer literals and index positions | `i32` where its range is proved to fit, and `f64` where it isn't, so a result past i32 is what V8 gives, never a trap |
| `number` with fractional sources (`/`, float literal, `Math.*`) | `f64`. Integer-only again after `Math.floor/ceil/round`, `\| 0`, `>>> 0` |
| `Math.floor(a / b)` with int operands | Float division then floor, unless proved non-negative i32, then integer division |
| Parameter with literal-union type (`scale: 1 \| 8`) | Specialise per constant if call sites are known, then const-fold |
| Typed array | (ptr, len) pair. `.subarray` is pointer arithmetic with JS clamping. Stores do JS conversion (`Uint8Array` mod 256, `Float32Array` round) |
| Typed array read of `a[i]!` | Bounds check + trap. V8 yields `undefined` out of bounds; this is an allowed divergence and is reported |
| Typed array read of `a[i]` | `T \| undefined` as above. JS semantics preserved |
| Typed array write `a[i] = v` | **Silent no-op out of bounds**, as in JS. Note this differs from TSL proper, which traps |
| `Array<T>` of known element type | Arena-backed vector with nullable slots for holes |
| `.map .filter .reduce .find .forEach`, `Array.from({length}, fn)`, `for…of` over arrays | Loop with the closure inlined |
| `.shift()`, `.splice(...)`, `a.length = n`, `[a.n, b.n] = [b.n, a.n]` | Loops over the slots, in every mode. `shift` moves every element, so it's linear: V8's isn't, for a queue. `length` growing leaves holes, which only reference slots can hold, so on scalars it's trap 15. A destructuring assignment is of an array literal, as a statement |
| `new WeakRef(x)`, `.deref()` | `rc` only, with a cell the target shares (3.5). Otherwise **fallback** `weakref` |
| Destructure, spread of a known shape | Field-wise copy |
| `Math.max(...arr.map(f))` with known array | Loop |
| `String.fromCharCode(...bytes) === "lit"` | Byte comparison with static bytes; other string uses **fallback** |
| `throw` in a module where nothing can catch | `trap id`; the export glue rethrows `new Error(msg)` from the trap table, including template parts captured as scalars. Natively, it is the trap path, and the message goes to serial (see the native ABI below). In a memory mode this is only for `throw new <Error>(message)` in a module with no `try` and no `using`: everything else is the next row |
| `throw` of any value, `try`, `catch` with and without a binding, `finally`, `using` | In `leak`, `manual` and `rc` (D49): the thrown value is an `unknown` in two words of module state, a call to a function that can throw is followed by a test of the first, and a `try` is labels, a completion code and jumps, made before `rc` and TIR see the tree. `Error`, its six standard subclasses and `SuppressedError` are classes in `compiler/rt/exc.ts`. `using` disposes in reverse order on every way out, with `SuppressedError` when the body and a disposal both throw. **fallback** in `strict` (`try-catch`) |
| `unknown`, as a catch binding, an Error's `cause` or a parameter | In a memory mode (D49): one pointer, null for `undefined`, a class instance as itself, and a primitive in a box. Narrowed by `typeof`, `instanceof` and `=== null` or `undefined` to a class or a primitive, with the class id checked (trap 17). `e as C`, as in `(e as Error).message`, is the same checked narrowing, and a lie traps 17 where V8 would read on (3.10 item 1); `as string`, `as number` and `as boolean` unbox the same way. `String(e)`, `Number(e)` by JS's ToNumber (a class with its own `valueOf` or `toString` that can be in it stays a fallback), `typeof e` as a value, and passing it on lower; anything else is `any-type` |
| A runtime failure V8 throws: a string too long, a bad `repeat` count, `toFixed` and `toString` arguments, a bad code point, a bad array length, recursion too deep | In a module where something can catch, V8's `RangeError` with V8's message (3.10 item 14 for the depth). Elsewhere, and for TSL's own checks (`!` on null, an index with `!`, overflow in a conversion, a hole), the trap it always was: 3.10 item 1 |
| `any`, `eval`, `Proxy`, reflection, prototype mutation, computed keys, `async`, generators, `RegExp`, `Date`, `FinalizationRegistry`, `WeakMap`, `WeakSet`, `Symbol`, `JSON`, `Intl`, `localeCompare`, `normalize` | **fallback**, in every memory mode, with its root cause. A `for...of` over a user iterator, whose `return()` an exception would have to call, is one of these: only arrays, `Map` and `Set` iterate, and theirs have nothing to close |
| Run-time strings: `string`, concatenation, templates, `length`, indexing, `charCodeAt`, `codePointAt`, `at`, `charAt`, `slice`, `substring`, `indexOf`, `lastIndexOf`, `includes`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `split` on a string, `trim` and its kin, `repeat`, `padStart`, `padEnd`, `replace` and `replaceAll` of a string, `toUpperCase`, `toLowerCase`, `String.fromCharCode`, `fromCodePoint`, `for...of` by code point, `===` and ordering by code unit, `parseInt`, `parseFloat`, `Number()`, `String()`, `toString`, `toFixed` | **fallback** in `strict` (`string-use`). In `leak`, `manual` and `rc`, code in `compiler/rt`, lowered into the module that reaches it (3.5, D42). `toPrecision`, `toExponential`, and `replace` with a callback are `string-use` |
| `Object.is(a, b)` | Lowered for numbers, booleans and bigints, and strings in a memory mode: `===`, with NaN itself and -0 not +0, and just `===` where both are known to be integers. **fallback** on anything else (`reflection`, `TSLD0202`) |
| `new Map()`, `new Set()` with no type arguments | TS's first overload is `Map<any, any>`, whatever it's assigned to, so the destination decides: the declared type of a field, variable, parameter, return or assignment target (`getContextualType`), the `Map` member of a union. With no destination it stays `any`: **fallback** (`any-type`, `TSLD0201`) in a memory mode, and `map-set` in `strict`, as any `Map` is |
| `Map`, `Set`, `for...of`, `keys`, `values`, `entries`, `forEach`, `new Map(iterable)`, spread, `Array.from`, explicit `.next()` | **fallback** in `strict` (`map-set`). In `leak`, `manual` and `rc`, the class in `compiler/rt/map.ts`, per key and value type (3.5, D42), growing incrementally (D47). A `Map` whose value can be `null` is `nullish-both`: `get` would need three states. There's no `ExactMap` in ordinary TS: it isn't on V8, and a program wanting a trap on a missing key writes the test, or a class over `Map` of its own, which lowers like any (D47) |
| `.sort`, `.reverse`, `.join`, `.concat`, `.at`, `.toString` on an array, a tuple of mixed types | In `leak`, `manual` and `rc`: `compiler/rt/array.ts`, a stable merge sort, and a tuple like `[string, number]` is a struct with fields `0` and `1`, where a tuple of one kind stays a vector. Otherwise **fallback** |

**How the rules are applied (M2).** `tmk lower` takes any strict TS file, whether or not a `tsl.json` is above it. The pass
walks each reachable function using the checker's types, and repeats until what it knows stops changing:

- *Numbers.* JS has one number type, and `f64` is exactly it, so `f64` is always correct and an integer representation is
  an optimisation that has to be earned. Every location of `number` (variable, parameter, return, field, element)
  collects facts from what flows into it: a range, whether anything fractional reached it, and whether it can hold −0. It
  gets `i32` if its range fits, `u32` if that fits and `i32` doesn't (only `>>>` and `Uint32Array` produce one), and
  otherwise `f64`. Mixed `i32` and `u32` is `f64`, and so is any `+ - *` with a `u32` operand, because the exact value may
  be outside both. An integer `+ - *` or negation whose operands' ranges don't prove the result fits i32 is done in `f64`, which is JS's number
  exactly, so nothing traps where V8 gives a result: before the Maps phase it was a checked i32 that trapped with code 1, a
  bug (M5). A loop's condition bounds a counter it compares, for `for` and `while`: in the body a read of `i` in `i < e` is
  within `e`'s range, widened by each plain write to `i` there in walk order, unless an inner loop writes it, a destructuring
  does, or a closure sees it. So a counter bounded by a length stays an `i32`, and one bounded by an exported parameter,
  which is an `f64`, is an `f64`, as is a sum or product that can pass i32.
- *Exports.* A parameter from JS can be any number, so an exported function's `number` parameters are `f64`, and
  anything that must be an integer inside converts with `| 0` or by being an index. An exported integer-looking parameter
  is not narrowed on a guess.
- *−0.* An integer register can't hold −0, and only a float consumer can see the difference. So `*`, unary `-`, `%` and
  `Math.ceil/round/trunc` note when they may produce −0, and if such a value reaches a float consumer (including a return
  to JS), its source stays `f64`.
- *`Math.floor` and kin* yield an integer by a checked conversion, which traps with code 4 if the value doesn't fit `i32`. Where
  the result flows only into `f64` locations, it stays `f64` and never traps.
- *Bit operations* keep only the low 32 bits of an exact value. Inside one, `+ - *` wrap if the exact value is proved below
  2⁵³, and otherwise compute in `f64` and take `js.toint32`, which is what JS does.
- *Objects.* Values of one TS type share a layout, and an assignment between types unifies them, so a struct holds the
  union of its fields. Discriminated unions are one such struct, with the tag as a field. Typed arrays and vectors get one
  class per flow, not per type, so `number[]` of integers and of fractions can differ. A `const` bound to an object
  literal and used only through `.field` has no memory at all.
- *Allocation.* An object or fixed-size typed array that is never returned or stored, and isn't allocated in a loop, uses
  `alloca` (a shadow stack on Wasm, between statics and the arena). Anything else is in the call arena.
- *Closures.* A closure's body is walked in place at each call, in its defining scope, so captures just resolve and a
  mutated capture needs no box. A variable selecting among targets is a tag, and a call is a `switch` over inlined bodies.
  A callback argument inlines its callee. A recursive local function is lambda-lifted if its captures are never assigned.
  In `strict` no environment struct exists: a closure stored in a field or returned is a **fallback**, and so is one kept past
  the scope of a binding it captures.
- *Closures in `leak`, `manual` and `rc`.* What's known still inlines. A closure used as a value gets an environment struct, `[code pointer][captures]`, made
  where it's used, and its value is a pointer to that. A call loads the code pointer and does `call.indirect` with the environment as a hidden first argument. Every
  closure that can reach one place shares a calling convention, because function types unify like objects do: one representation per parameter and for the
  result. A captured binding nothing assigns is copied into the environment. One that's assigned after it's made lives in a heap cell the closures share,
  so mutation is seen on both sides. A `for` loop's `let` gets a fresh cell per iteration, copied before the incrementor, as JS's per-iteration bindings do, and
  a `let` only its own incrementor changes needs no cell, since nothing changes an iteration's binding during its body. A function that would be inlined into itself takes its
  callback as a value. An environment follows the placement rules of any object below. Comparing two function values is a **fallback**,
  since one function can have several environments. So are generic and overloaded function values, a method used as a value, and locals
  captured before they're declared.
- *Memory modes (`--memory`, D38).* The order stays: stack, then call arena, then, for what truly escapes, the mode's allocator instead of a fallback. What truly
  escapes is what can outlive the export call: anything reachable from module state, a result, whatever is stored in memory a caller gave, and everything those can reach,
  to a fixed point over the same flow classes as the rest of this list. It's a whole class, so an object escapes if any of its class does.
  `leak` allocates these from a bump allocator over the page source (3.5), never frees, and has no prefix, as lowered code has no `Slab`. `manual` allocates from the heap. Nothing else is linked:
  no collector and no std. A mode is native only, as there's no page source or glue on the other side of Wasm. `--no-fallback` then means what it says for much more.
  A plain array growing in `leak` leaks its old buffer. In `manual` it frees it, because that's provable: a vector's buffer is only ever reached through its header, every access
  loads the pointer afresh, and no temporary holds it across a call that can grow it. A vector a caller placed could have its buffer known to that caller, so it leaks those, as it
  does a run of whole pages. Ordinary TS has no `unsafeFree`, so that's the only freeing lowered `manual` does.
- *`rc` (3.5, D39).* What isn't on the stack is counted, including what `leak` would put in the call arena. **That part of D38's order doesn't survive here, measured:** the call arena has no way to give back one iteration's allocation, so a loop in a single export call that allocates and drops runs it out. `localsInALoop` in `corpus/lower/memory/churn.ts` traps 14 at 96 MiB in `leak` and `manual`, with nothing escaping. Keeping it would need a proof that an allocation runs a bounded number of times per export call, across the whole call graph, and the saving would only be on what doesn't loop. The arena stays for a caller to place arguments that aren't counted.
  Counts are added in `compiler/host/down-rc.ts`, once, to the finished tree, after everything is known about which classes are counted, so the other modes don't change by a byte. Stage A says of each expression whether its value is owned or borrowed, and adds increments and temporaries. Stage B gives each counted local a scope, the smallest list of statements holding every use of it, and releases it after its last use there and on every jump out. A local's count moves rather than being copied where a statement is its last use, as does a block's result, so `new P()` and `return x` count nothing extra.
  A plain array in `rc` frees its old buffer as it grows, for the reason `manual` can, and its header and buffer are one count. Arguments a caller placed count as its own: see the ABI below.
  The cycle collector (3.5, D41) is added in the same pass. `--cycles`, or `"cycles"` in `tsl.json`, sets it, and it's on by default. Which types can be in a cycle is settled before any site is written, over the type graph and every environment an allocation in the tree makes. With no such type, or with it off, nothing here or in the runtime differs by a byte, which a tirhash pin says. Otherwise a site for such a type has the barrier after an increment, and after a decrement that leaves a count, a test of whether the object's a candidate yet, and a count-preserving move of an element has the barrier too.
- *Literal unions.* A parameter of up to 4 integer literals gets a copy per value. A call with a value known only at run time
  switches among the copies.
- *`Array<T>`.* Reference slots use 0 for a hole. A scalar slot has no spare value, so a write that would leave a scalar
  hole traps with code 15, and `new Array(n)` of scalars with no whole `.fill` is a fallback.
- *Module state.* Top-level `const` numbers fold, and `const` typed arrays of constants are static bytes. Other initialisers
  and top-level statements run once in `__init`, whose allocations are never reclaimed. At run time, a reference stored
  in a module binding, or an allocation reachable from one, is `escape-global`. If a function stays JS, module state it
  touches stays JS too (`shared-state`), and so do the functions that read it. If an initialiser stays JS, so do its readers (`global-init`).
- *Strings, `Map` and `Set` (D42).* `compiler/rt` is ordinary TS, part of the program only in a memory mode, and nothing in it is lowered unless something reaches it. A `declare function` in `compiler/rt/intrinsics.ts` is what TS has no words for: a string's memory, a vector with no bounds check, what a type parameter is in this instantiation, a double's bits. Each is lowered in place by shape. So a module's first non-literal string starts its walk again with `strRt` on, every string in it is then a pointer, and one with none is byte for byte what it was. A prelude method is an instance like any other: its counts, its elision, its barrier and its descriptors are the compiler's, which is why there's no count in `compiler/rt`. Why it isn't over `@tsl/alloc`: a `Vec` holds no counted reference and takes a heap, its stored references have generation checks, and the collector doesn't know it. To be traced, freed in bounded steps and borrowed from as `rc` requires, a map has to be made of what `rc` knows, and that's lowered vectors. A class in the mode's allocator costs no more runtime than the classes a program already has.
- *Limits.* `T | null | undefined` together is a fallback (`nullish-both`). So `a?.next`, where `next` is `T | null`, is one too. Lengths stay below 2³¹, as `__alloc` refuses
  more.
- *Casts and widened shapes.* A struct can't say a field is absent. So `x as T` on an object type is a fallback
  (`unsound-cast`, TSLD0226) unless `x`'s type is assignable to `T`, and an object literal that reaches JS without a non-optional field
  that a wider shape unified into its type is a fallback (`shape-widened`, TSLD0227), unless its type is a discriminated union, whose
  tag says which fields are there. Before this, the first read 0 where V8 read `undefined`, and the second showed an extra field of 0.

**Export glue (Wasm for JS hosts).** Generated per export. Scalars pass directly. Typed arrays are copied into linear
memory on entry. A returned object shape is a pointer to its struct in the call arena: the glue reads the fields, copies
any typed arrays out, and builds the JS object. `null` is pointer 0. A trap becomes a thrown `Error` with the message
from the trap table.

**Native ABI (accepted by the owner on 2026-11-03, delegated to the author, D36).** There's no JS glue, so no copy-out. An export's TIR signature is
what's called, with AAPCS64's registers: typed arrays as (pointer, length), objects as pointers, and null as 0. A program says where
its memory comes from (D28), so the caller supplies an arena: `__arena_use(start, limit)` sets the module's arena, and a module's
`__init` runs in the first one, with its data kept for the module's life. An allocation past `limit` is trap 14. Returned objects and
buffers live in the arena until the caller calls `__arena_reset`, which rewinds to where `__arena_use` or `__init` left it. Nothing
resets by itself, as the JS glue does on each call. The arena is module state, not a hidden parameter: every internal function would
otherwise pay a register for it, and a call never changes arena. A caller reads a returned object at offsets from the layout
`DownMeta` records. The bare-metal runtime is the arena provider in this phase, with everything from the 8 MiB stack's top to the end of
RAM, and the native libm covers only `sin`, `cos` (|x| below about 2¹⁹·π/2, past which they panic with code 10 rather than guess),
`exp`, `log`, `atan2` and `pow`, see 3.10 item 7. The decoder uses none of them.

**The ABI with a memory mode (D36, D38).** The arena stays, and so does `__arena_use`. It holds what's bounded by the export call. A caller also registers a page source
with `__page_source_use(code)`, a function taking a page count in `x0` and returning a zeroed run or null. D36's promise about results changes: in `leak` and `manual`, a result is in long-lived memory, never in the arena,
because a result is what the caller keeps, and a result the arena could rewind would be a stale reference, which `leak` says can't happen. So `__arena_reset` reclaims only the module's internal bounded allocations,
and a result survives it, and nothing frees it in `leak`. The other direction has a rule too: `DownMeta` marks a class or typed array `long` if the module can keep it, and a caller places such an argument
with the mode's allocator (`__leak_alloc` or `__heap_alloc`, and `__vec_new_leak` or `__vec_new_heap`), not `__alloc`, and places the rest wherever it likes. A returned closure is a pointer to its environment, with the ABI of the closures rule above.
Class instances cross as pointers in a mode, where `strict` keeps them out (`export-signature`) for JS glue's sake. A native caller sees no more than a struct, at `DownMeta`'s offsets.

**The layout, listed, through both routes (D36, R5, R6).** What a native caller reads and writes is `DownMeta.heap`'s list, whichever route built the module: for each class that crosses an export, its size and each field's offset and description, and for an array D36's header (the buffer's address at p, the length at p + 8, the capacity at p + 16) and its element's slot. Since R6 the rule is TSL's own (3.4, D62's ruling: "lowered objects take TSL's own layout rules, with no lowered layout"), in the direct route and phase 1's printing as in class printing: the lowering's field order, a hierarchy's class id first, each field at its natural alignment; a number 4 or 8 bytes by its representation, a `bool` 1, a literal union or a strict closure's tag 4, a typed array 16 as its pointer and length, a reference 8; an optional scalar a `bool` flag and then its value at the value's own alignment (an `f64` at 8 past its flag, an `i32` at 4, a `bool` at 1), so the two fields TSL would print for it (D62's ruling) are where it is; and the size its fields' end rounded up to the largest alignment, not to 8 and with no minimum, though every object is allocated at least 8 bytes, by the module and by a caller (`allocBytes`), as TSL's own `new` asks. An array element's slot is its value's size, a `bool`'s 1. Before R6 a `bool` was 4 bytes, an optional scalar's flag a word of its own, and every size a multiple of 8, at least 8; nothing had shipped, and `tools/r6-pins.ts` lists every pinned build the change moved, each with what in it the two rules lay out differently. The TSL route prints each class that crosses with its fields in D36's order, which TSL then lays out exactly where D36 lists them, with nothing added (R5's padding fields, `pad$17: u8` after a `bool` at 16, are gone), tagged `@tsl.size` and exported. Before anything is built, tslc checks that each such class is plain (no prefix, its references plain addresses, D64) and that its size and every field's offset are D36's, and refuses the printing otherwise, so the direct route builds the program instead (`checkBoundary`): a layout that moved is never one a caller sees. An array that crosses is `@tsl/jsrt`'s `JsArray`, whose first three words are D36's header; a caller places one with the module's own export, `__vec_place_<id>(length)` (the heap entry's `place`), which gives one of that many holes, in place of `__vec_new*`, and writes its elements at the address at p as before. `DownMeta.tslClasses` names each class and field as the printed TSL has them, which only a host caller of the printed TSL needs (D71's third route makes and reads the classes by it). Since R7 an optional number or boolean field crosses as its two printed fields (the flag at D36's offset, the value where D36 lists it, both checked), a typed-array field as its runtime class held in place (pointer at the field's offset, length 8 past it), and a `Map` or `Set` as `JsMap` or `JsSet`: a caller builds one with the surface exports D36 already names (`make` and `put`, printed from compiler/rt/map.ts onto JsMap's `new` and `set`), and reads one through `size`, `has`, `iter`, `step`, `key` and `val` the same way, or from memory by JsMap's layout as tslc laid it out (`DownMeta.tslMaps`: the offsets of its tables, each a `JsArray` held in place whose first two words are D36's header, and of the move it may be in, and of the JsMap a JsSet holds in place), which the test driver does. Not built through the TSL route, which leaves such a program on the direct route: a closure, a union, a tuple, and a program of several modules; and in `rc`, a string, a `Map` or a `Set` crossing (strings aren't printed in `rc` yet, nor are a map's counts at the boundary). `rc`'s counted objects and arrays cross since R8 (the ABI in `rc`, below). `auto` doesn't take it yet (`AUTO_BOUNDARY`, M5's R5, R6 and R7 records).

**The per-call region (R6, D62's third ruling, 3.5).** In a lowered `leak` or `manual` package, tslc places each heap `new` its escape analysis proves no export call outlives in a region each export gives back when it returns, as the direct route's call arena holds what the lowering bounds by the export call; the printed TSL says nothing of it (no annotation beside `new`) and runs on V8 and JSC unchanged. The analysis is tslc's own, on the package's typed tree, a class (an instantiation) at a time (compiler/host/region.ts): a class is *long* if one of its objects can be reached after an export call returns, which is only from module state, from what an export gives back or is given (whatever is stored into what a caller passed in, it keeps), from a field or a type argument of a long class (a generic library class keeps values of its type arguments in its own memory), or from anything tslc can't follow (a reference given to the runtime, an intrinsic, a builtin or a conversion, but for a generic class's method keeping its own type argument, and asking where an object is). A `new` escape analysis put on the heap of a class that isn't long goes in the region, and so does one it put on the stack of a class that keeps memory beside its objects where they are (one of whose methods asks `inCallRegion(this)`: `JsArray`, whose buffers then come from the region too, as the direct route's call-bounded vectors keep theirs in the arena); an object with a tail stays in the heap until R9, and since R9 goes in the region at its real size like any other (a flat string doesn't, as `tailAddr` of it is a reference given to a builtin). **R9:** a view of an object's storage (a layout class's `array(…)` field read, or a tail, as a typed array made in a function prints) holds that object's memory with no reference to it, so region.ts follows views too, through locals, parameters and results, a conditional, `subarray` and `fill`, to a fixed point over the package: a view only indexed, written, measured, copied from or given to `set`, or whose pointer @tsl/lowered's `part` takes to read or write an element at, keeps nothing; one an export gives back, or given anywhere else (its pointer kept as an integer in a field or module state, a function value's call), makes its class long. Finer than a class it can't see: one object of a class kept in module state makes every object of the class long, and a class an export takes or gives is long where it never crosses. The region is the call arena the module already has (`__alloc`, over what `__arena_use` gave it), zeroed as it's taken; an export whose call can reach a `new` placed there marks the arena's top on entry and puts it back at every return (lower.ts), so what an export call made there is given back as it returns, whoever calls it, and a caller that never rewinds the arena (`__arena_reset`) no longer needs to. A call that makes more bounded objects than the arena holds runs out with code 14, as the direct route's does. Not retired, then, as the ruling allowed if it measured no slower: without it, what a churning call makes goes in the mode's heap, which `leak` never gives back, and the TSL route ran out of memory where the direct route doesn't (M5's R5 record); the region is that ruling's "smallest TSL-level form", placed by tslc and measured in M5's R6 record.

**Arrays in `strict` (R13, D36, D66, pile item 7).** A lowered `strict` package has no heap, and its call arena is the caller's: an export doesn't give it back, and what it holds lives until the caller resets it (`__arena_reset`), as the direct route's results do (D36). Class printing there prints arrays as `@tsl/jsrt`'s `JsArenaArray` (3.5's `// file: ex-jsrt-arena.ts`), whose buffers come only from that arena; typed arrays made in functions as R9's layout classes and tails; an array of typed arrays as an array of R7's holders (`Uint16ArrayField`), one made for each typed array stored (`<holder>_of`, `<holder>_get`, a hole a typed array of no storage, as the lowering reads one); closure values as environment classes; and exports taking or giving objects in D36's listed layout (R5). tslc places them (region.ts, with `giveBack` false): what escape analysis puts on the heap goes in the arena, and since nothing in the arena outlives the caller's reset but what module state reaches, a class is long only where module state reaches it, never because an export gives it back or is given it. Module state can hold what's in the arena where it's made by the module's `__init` before it commits the arena (`__arena_commit`, below which no reset goes), so tslc refuses a package (TSL3001) where, after `__init`, module state is set to something it didn't already hold, a field of an object it reaches is, a typed array's pointer is kept in one, or a library method that can grow (reaches `callRegionBytes`) or keep a reference is called on one: `stateHazard`, followed through locals, parameters, results and fields to a fixed point. A typed array's pointer kept in a holder is followed through the holder's class rather than given up on as an integer, and its length (the second leaf) and an element copy or fill at its pointer (`mem.copy`, `mem.fill`) keep nothing. The lowering itself keeps a program that allocates where module state reaches on the direct route (`escape-global`), so tslc's check is the second line, tested on hand-written lowered packages (tools/r13-tests.ts's `KEPT_CASES`). A reference that crosses an export is the Wasm backend's i64 there, its address the low 32 bits, which the Wasm glue converts (`DownMeta.refI64`), and the native callers type each call by the module's own signature. `auto` takes arrays in `strict` where the printing is exact and the speed rule is met (`AUTO_STRICT_ARRAYS`, M5's R13 record); closures and the boundary in `strict` as in every mode.

**The ABI in `rc` (D36, D39).** A result crosses with one count, and that count is the caller's. An object, an array or a closure is released with `__rc_release(p)`, and a typed array with `__rc_release_arr(p)`, where `p` is its pointer. Until then it stays valid whatever the caller does, including `__arena_reset` and further calls. Arguments are borrowed: the caller keeps its own count across the call, and what the module keeps, it counts for itself, so the caller can release an argument straight after the call whether the module kept it or not. A caller places a class `DownMeta` marks `long` with `__rc_new(size, rcDesc)` and `__vec_new_rc(len, slot, rcDesc)`, taking `rcDesc` from `DownMeta`, or `__rc_new(size, 0)` for a typed array. These start at count one, which is the caller's. A pointer it stores into one of them holds a count too, so it does `__rc_retain` (or `__rc_retain_arr`) for each. `__rc_collect` runs everything pending, cycles included, for a caller who wants that now: it's a pause, by choice. An `rcDesc` is opaque to a caller, and in a module with the collector it holds a bit besides the descriptor's index. A caller's counts are like any other, so a count a caller holds keeps what it reaches from being collected, and nothing else about this ABI changes with the collector. A non-`long` class is the same as in any other mode: no counts, placed where it likes. A trap leaves counts as they were, and what the frames it unwound were holding stays held, which is a leak in a test driver and doesn't matter to a domain that dies.

**The ABI in `rc` through the TSL route (R8, D36, D39).** The ownership is the same: a result's count is the caller's, arguments are borrowed, a caller holds a count for each reference it stores into an object it placed, and gives back each count it holds. What differs is whose functions it calls, as the TSL route has no `__rc_new` or `__rc_release` of the direct route's counted heap: `@tsl/gc`'s heap is the package's, and the package prints what a caller counts with, in plain TSL tslc's `rc` expansion counts (D74), each named in `DownMeta.heap`'s entry for the class or array (`place`, `retain`, `release`). `__rc_place_<id>()` is `return new C();`: a new object, zeroed, at one count, the caller's (a result is owned), which the caller fills in at D36's offsets as it fills in `__rc_new`'s; an array is placed by its `__vec_place_<id>(length)` (R5), the same way. `__rc_retain_<id>(p)` is `return p;`: the expansion shares a borrowed parameter it returns, so the caller holds one more count, and ignores the result, the same object. `__rc_release_<id>(p)` is an empty function whose parameter is tagged `@tsl.moves p`: the expansion takes such a parameter over as an owned local (a function that takes one over can't be called inside the package, where nothing would give it a count to take), so it drops the caller's count at its scope's end. `__rc_collect()`, `__rc_live()` and `__rc_steps()` are `@tsl/gc`'s `rcCollect`, `rcLive` and `rcSteps`, the direct route's `__rc_collect` and its live-object and freeing-step figures. A counted object crosses at its address (3.5's "A counted reference is an address"). Every object and array that crosses is counted through the TSL route, as `rc` has no arena there for what the direct route proved call-bounded, so `DownMeta` marks each `long`, and a caller follows the `long` rules for all of them; a typed array crosses only borrowed, as a lowered `rc` package keeps none and makes none, so it isn't `long` and the caller places it in the call arena. A release takes a reference that isn't null, and a caller doesn't release what it was still filling in when a trap stopped it (a half-built object can hold null where its class says none), which is a trap's leak like any other. A program the direct route builds with call-bounded objects in the arena can run out of memory through the TSL route where the direct route doesn't, after a trap left what its frames held: `corpus/lower/pipe/region.ts`, named in tools/r8-tests.ts's `RC_TSL_ROUTE_OOM` with why. `auto` doesn't take it (`AUTO_BOUNDARY`, M5's R8 record). **Strings (R10):** a string crosses as the program's own `JsStr`, counted the same way, by a pair of the package's own, `__rc_retain_str(p)` (`return p;`) and `__rc_release_str(p)` (an empty function, `@tsl.moves p`), named in `DownMeta.rcStr`: a string the caller places with `__str_place(n)` is one count, its own, a string result is one count of the caller's, an argument is borrowed, and the caller retains a string it stores into an object it placed; each it holds it gives back with `__rc_release_str`. A build whose strings cross publishes `rcTsl` too, for `__rc_collect`, `__rc_live` and `__rc_steps`. corpus/lower/strmap/rc_churn.ts ran out of memory through the TSL route alone once strings printed in `rc`, in its sets of numbers, not its strings, and was named in `RC_TSL_ROUTE_OOM` (M5's R10 record) until R11 made a map's tables at the counted heap's pace (3.5's "Maps' tables at the counted heap's pace"): it agrees through both routes now, and `RC_TSL_ROUTE_OOM` names region.ts alone. **Exceptions (R11):** a module that can throw through the TSL route in `rc` prints `__exc_release`, which a caller gives a taken exception back with (4.5's "The ABI with exceptions").

**The ABI for strings, `Map` and `Set` (D36, D42).** A string crosses as one pointer, null for `null` or `undefined`, with `DownMeta`'s `{ "k": "string" }`. To read one: `len` is the `u32` at `p`, `off` the `i64` at `p + 8`, and the UTF-16 units are at `p + off`, in the module's memory, including non-ASCII and lone surrogates, or from `__str_length(p)` and `__str_units(p)`. **Where strings are `@tsl/jsrt`'s `JsString` (D67, D70; `DownMeta.strLayout`, pipe-split),** the build publishes their layout instead, as the two classes are laid out: the `u32` class id at `p` says which; a `JsFlat`'s length is the `u32` at `p + flat.len` and its units start at `p + flat.units`; a `JsView`'s length is the `i32` at `p + view.len` and its units at the address in the word at `p + view.addr`. As built, `{ flat: { id: 1, len: 8, units: 12 }, view: { id: 2, len: 8, addr: 16 } }`: what moved from D36's is the length (from `p` to `p + 8`, where the class id now is) and the units (inline at a fixed 12 for a flat string, and an address, not an offset, for a view). A string still crosses as a TSL reference, and `__str_place`, `__str_units` and `__str_length` are the same calls. **In `rc` through the TSL route (R10),** a string is the program's own `JsStr` (3.5), and the build publishes its layout as `DownMeta.rcStr.layout`, as tslc laid the two classes out: the length is the `i32` at `p + len`; if the word at `p + buf` is null the units are the string's own, from `p + units`, and otherwise they're its buffer's, from that buffer's address `+ bufUnits + 2 × start`, `start` the `i32` at `p + start`. As built, `{ len: 16, start: 4, buf: 8, units: 24, bufUnits: 12 }`. It's a layout of its own because `JsString`'s can't be kept there: a class id and a view's unit address are what a dispatch interface and an unsafe module give, and an `rc` package has neither. `__str_place`, `__str_units` and `__str_length` are the same calls, and what counts a string is 4.5's ABI in `rc`, below. To pass one: `__str_place(len)` gives a flat string of that length, with a count of one in `rc`, and the caller writes units at `__str_units(p)` before the module sees it. In `rc` a result is released with `__rc_release(p)`, and arguments are borrowed, as with any object. A `Map` or `Set` crosses as a pointer, and is opaque (D47, D54): its layout is the runtime's own, and changes as the runtime does, as it did when its growth became incremental, so `DownMeta` lists no fields for it, and a caller uses the exports its `heap` entry's `map` field names, with `key` and `val` giving the descriptions of what it holds. `make()` and `put(m, k, v)` (`put(m, k)` for a `Set`) build one, and exist only if an export takes that type as an argument. Where one can cross either way: `size(m)`; `has(m, k)`; `iter(m)`, a cursor; `step(m, c)`, which moves it to the next entry and says whether there was one; and `key(m, c)` and `val(m, c)` (no `val` for a `Set`), what it stopped at. These are `compiler/rt/map.ts`'s `mapLen`, `mapHas`, `mapIter`, `mapStep`, `mapKey` and `mapVal`, made for that key and value type. A cursor follows JS's rules under change, as `for...of` does. In `rc` the cursor and a counted key or value from `key` and `val` are the caller's, released with `__rc_release`. The test harness reads a dump of one by a description only it uses (`internal`), which isn't the ABI. A tuple of mixed types is a struct whose `heap` entry has `tuple` set. A thrown message with a string part prints printable ASCII as itself, and anything else as `{uXXXX}`. `__hash_key_use(a, b)` sets the hash key, and must come before any table exists.

**The ABI with exceptions (D36, D49).** In a module where something can throw an exception, an export that can let one out is a wrapper around the function itself (`name$x`), and what a native caller gets depends on what it asked for. By default nothing changes for a caller that knows nothing of exceptions: an exception that reaches it is the trap path, as `throw` always was, with one site (`meta.exc.uncaught`) whose message is the thrown value described as JSON (its constructor, `name`, `message`, `cause`, and a SuppressedError's parts, or the primitive), and the module is left with nothing in flight. A caller that calls `__exc_catch_use(1)` once gets zeros back instead, with the exception in flight: `__exc_pending()` says so, `__exc_take()` gives the thrown value, an `unknown`, and clears it, and in `rc` its count is the caller's, to give back with `__rc_release` (through the TSL route, R11: with the module's own `__exc_release(p)`, an empty function whose parameter is tagged `@tsl.moves p`, R8's pattern, named in `DownMeta.exc.release`, and the description, a string, with `__rc_release_str`). `meta.exc.describe` names the function that turns one into that JSON, as a run-time string. The frames the exception left released what they held on the way out, so nothing leaks, which the trap path can't say. `__exc_stack_use(limit)` sets the address below which a recursive function throws `RangeError` rather than run off the stack (3.10 item 14); with none set it never does. A class instance in a hierarchy doesn't cross the boundary as a value in this phase.

Natively, a lowered `throw` is the trap path. Its code from 100000 finds its site in the trap table, the template parts captured in
`__trap_args` are formatted in the guest, and the report is one serial line: `TMK:C <case> T <code> <Ctor>: <message>` in a test image,
or `TMK:PANIC trap <code> <Ctor>: <message>` outside any `native.try`. `i32`, `u32`, `bool` and literal-union parts print as JS prints
them, as does a float with an integer value below 2⁵³. Any other float prints as `{<16 hex digits>}`, since there's no shortest-digits
printer in the guest, and the harness turns that back into JS's text before it compares.

**Fallback behaviour by target:**

- **Wasm for JS hosts:** the function stays JS and is linked through a marshalling shim. Calls across the
  boundary copy typed arrays and pass scalars. A hot lowered function calling a fallback produces warning
  TSLD0100, since it's probably a performance problem.
- **Native, kernel and any `--no-fallback` build:** fallback is a hard error, reported with the diagnostics
  below. There's no runtime for it to fall back to (D28), so in `strict`
  a program with an allocation that truly escapes doesn't compile natively until it's changed to use a `Slab`
  or `Vec`, or declares a memory mode (D38). M5 measures how often real code hits this.

**Diagnostics** are written as JSON lines and as readable text. Every fallback names a root cause and the
span that blocked it, and if a caller fell back only because of a callee it says so:

```json
{"code":"TSLD0203","fn":"decodeJpeg","file":"jpeg.ts","line":595,"col":13,
 "blocker":"string-from-spread","detail":"String.fromCharCode(...x) compared with a non-literal",
 "suggest":"compare bytes with lit(\"JFIF\")","outcome":"fallback","blocked_callers":[]}
```

`tmk lower --report` prints a table: function, outcome, root blocker, and whether it's on a hot path if a
profile is given. Language phase A changed what these mean in a memory mode: `try-catch` and `throw-non-error` are now `strict`'s only, `inheritance` is `strict`'s and the forms the class row lists, and `field-before-init` (TSLD0230) is new. `tmk coverage` (9.3) counts them over the corpora and real projects.

### 4.6 What the Moire JPEG decoder demands

Target: `~/projects/moire/packages/file-formats/src/image/jpeg.ts`, 729 lines,
SHA-256 `215182f153d002e73d414f6a2d5dfc9fa27fc6d6ccd5e4731b4191515cc2ac44`, commit `d126a70`.

Vendor a copy into `bench/jpeg/vendor/jpeg.ts` with its hash recorded, and replace its one type import
(`./raster`, `ImageData`) with a local type. Don't edit anything else, since S3 requires "no source edits".

It's real full TS, not TSL: Node's strip mode rejects it because of parameter properties (MEASURED).
For the V8 baseline, use `ts.transpileModule` first.

| Lines | Construct | Rule needed |
|-------|-----------|------------|
| 89-98 | `class BitReader` with parameter properties, `private`, getter | Class to struct |
| 100-121 | `this.acc`, `(x << 8 \| b) >>> 0` | Int inference, wrap forms |

| 265, 364, 426, 499, 572 | Small local closures (`refine`, `q`, `put`, `clamp`, `u16`) | Inline |
| 321, 495, 501 | `Math.floor(x / y)` on ints | Division rule |

Corrupt-input behaviour: for `a[i]!` reads out of bounds the lowered code traps, whereas V8 continues with
`undefined` → `NaN` → 0 or the like. Valid fixtures must match exactly. Corrupt inputs must not crash the
host and must either trap or match. Report the count.

### 4.7 Self-hosting and bootstrap chain

**Stage sizes are EST** except where sourced.

| Stage | Written in | Output, or role | Size EST |
|-------|-----------|----------------|----------|
| `seed0` | Raw AArch64, hex-commented | Converts hex text to bytes. Reads input via the seed ABI. | ≤ 512 B. stage0-posix's seed is 256 B (SOURCE [P5], its page doesn't give an AArch64-specific size) |
| `asm1` | `seed0` hex | Hex with labels and relative offsets | 1 to 2 KiB |
| `asm2` | `asm1` | A64 assembler for the restricted `.s` dialect, with macros | 8 to 16 KiB binary, 2 to 4 KLOC |
| `tslc0` | `asm2` assembly | Compiles **TSL0**: `u8 u32 u64`, plain classes with fields only, top-level functions, `if`, `while`, static arrays. No generics, no checking beyond types. | 60 to 100 KiB binary, 8 to 12 KLOC |
| `tslc1` | TSL0 | All of TSL, non-optimising | 15 to 25 KLOC |
| `tslc` | TSL | All of TSL, optimising | 40 to 70 KLOC |

**Why this and not hex0 to M2-Planet to Mes to TinyCC:** stage0-posix and live-bootstrap solve a harder
problem (reach GCC and a whole Linux userland from bytes), with an interpreted Scheme stage in the middle,
and it takes hours [P5][P6]. We control the source language of the top compiler, so we can write it in a
subset that a small native compiler handles directly. No interpreter, no C, no GCC.

**TSL0 is a frozen language.** `tslc1` must stay in it. Changing this is costly, so `tslc1` grows only with
new TSL features, and `tslc` may use all of TSL. Every TSL0 file is also valid TSL, so tsc, V8, `tslc-host`
and `tslc` can all process it. That's what makes `tslc0` testable before it exists on bare metal, and the
reason this chain can be deferred until the end (M10).

**Seed ABI.** Each chain program runs at EL0 under `boot0`, with three `svc #0` calls. `x8=0`: read up to
`x1` bytes of the input blob into `x0`, returns count in `x0`. `x8=1`: append `x1` bytes from `x0` to the
output blob. `x8=2`: exit with status `x0`. The output blob's SHA-256 is compared to the expected value in
the manifest, and it then becomes the next stage. This ABI is implemented in `boot0` in under 200 lines
of assembly (EST).

### 4.8 Feasibility: "a KB-scale seed compiles a TS compiler at boot"

**Verdict: feasible for the TSL compiler, not for full TypeScript, and not useful on every boot.**

1. **Full TypeScript in the chain is not feasible.** `typescript.js` 5.9.3 is 200,276 lines and 9.1 MB
   (MEASURED). It's a dynamic, GC-dependent program. TS 7 is a Go program. Neither can be built by a small
   static compiler, so down-lowering stays on the host. Kernel, drivers and compiler must be pure TSL.
   A full-TS userspace component can enter the system only as checked-in TIR, which is **not** bootstrapped
   from seed, and the manifest marks it as such.
2. **A TSL-only chain looks feasible and fast because it's native all the way.** Estimates for M1 Max under
   HVF, single core, ±3× confidence. These are not measurements; every stage is unbuilt:

   | Step | EST |
   |------|-----|
   | `seed0` to `asm2` | < 10 ms |
   | `asm2` assembles `tslc0` | < 100 ms |
   | `tslc0` compiles `tslc1` (25 KLOC naive) | 0.1 to 1 s |
   | `tslc1` compiles `tslc` (70 KLOC, slow compiler code) | 1 to 5 s |
   | `tslc`(slow) compiles `tslc` (optimising a large program with slow code) | 5 to 20 s |
   | `tslc`(fast) compiles `tslc`, fixed-point check | 1 to 3 s |
   | `tslc` compiles kernel and drivers (40 KLOC) | 0.5 to 2 s |
   | **Total from seed** | **≈ 8 to 30 s** (TCG or slow boards: 1 to 5 min) |
   | **Specialise on cache miss** (`tslc` binary from store, kernel + bincheck + write) | **≈ 1 to 3 s** |
   | **Cached boot** (no compile) | **≈ 100 to 250 ms** (probe alone: 72 to 80 ms) |

   Reference points: TCC reported about 859,000 lines/s on a 2.4 GHz Pentium 4 for a single-pass C compiler
   (self-reported, old) [P9]. Midori's AOT took 1.5 years of work to get from about 40× to 3× to 5× the C#
   compiler's time, largely because of generics [P3]. Zig's bootstrap from a 637 KB compressed Wasm seed takes
   about 10 minutes, and compiler memory is the main bottleneck [P10]. Live-bootstrap takes "many hours", with
   the first GCC at about 30 minutes on x86 per an informal IRC report [P6].

3. **It's not useful on every boot.** Doing it at each boot costs tens of seconds to prove something that
   doesn't change, so it's a mode (`tmk.boot=from-seed`) for install, audit and CI. Normal boots use the cache.

4. **What the seed actually buys, honestly:** no pre-built binary needs to be trusted for the compiler. The
   auditable part becomes `seed0` + `asm1` + `asm2` + `tslc0` (hand-reviewable, EST about 15 KLOC with assembly)
   plus the whole source above it (about 130 KLOC with kernel, EST), which someone must still read. It doesn't
   shrink the trusted base; it removes *binary blobs* from it. Also still trusted: QEMU or firmware, `boot0`, and
   the CPU.

5. **The real cost is human, not CPU.** `tslc0` is about 10 KLOC of assembly, and the chain is frozen against
   language change. This is why M10 comes last and is optional (see 12.2).
